aage.ety: From Old Norse Áki. Cognate with Swedish Åke.

aaliyah.ety: Popularized by American singer Aaliyah Haughton (1979–2001). Transliteration of Arabic عَالِيَة.

aarón.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Aaron See English Aaron for more.

aashild.ety: Variant of Åshild, retaining the traditional spelling ⟨aa⟩ for ⟨å⟩.
aashild.m: god; one of the Æsir + battle

abbigail.ety: A rare nonstandard spelling of Abigail.

abbigale.ety: A rare non-standard spelling of Abigail.

abbygail.ety: A rare nonstandard spelling of Abigail.

abdoulaye.ety: A French spelling of a name ultimately derived from Arabic عَبْدُ اللّٰهِ, i.e. Native spellings include Wolof Abdulaay and Pulaar Abdullaye etc.

abe.ety: A shortening from Abraham. In the slang sense for money, refers to the picture of Abraham Lincoln on the currency.

abilio.ety: Perhaps from Latin abilius (“not vindictive”). Possibly related to Abelardo.

abrahan.ety: From American Spanish Abrahán. Doublet of Abraham and Avraham and Ibrahim and Abramo.

abram.ety: From Latin Abram, from Koine Greek Ἀβράμ, from Hebrew אַבְרָם (ʾaḇrām), from אָב (áb, “father”) + רָם (rám, “high, exalted”). Doublet of Abramo and Avram.

abrielle.ety: Modern coinage possibly shortened from Gabrielle. Compare Brielle, Aubrielle.

abubakar.ety: Borrowed from Arabic أَبُو بَكْر. This surname is predominantly found in Nigeria.
abubakar.m: father of a young camel; father of a person named Bakr

achille.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Achilles Latin Achilles.

achilles.ety: Borrowed from Latin Achillēs, from Ancient Greek Ἀχιλλεύς.

adalyn.ety: Rare non-standard variant of Adeline with -lyn. Can also be construed as Ada + -lyn.

adalynn.ety: Rare non-standard variant of Adeline with -lynn. Can also be construed as Ada + -lynn.

adan.ety: Borrowed from Spanish Adán, ultimately from Biblical Hebrew אָדָם (ʾāḏām, “earth, man, soil, light brown”).

adao.ety: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese Adan, from Latin Ādām, Ādāmus, from Ancient Greek Ἀδάμ, Ἄδαμος, from Biblical Hebrew אָדָם (adam, “earth, man, soil, light brown”), from אדמה (adamah, “red earth, ground”).

addison.ety: A patronymic surname from a medieval diminutive form of Adam + -son.

adel.ety: Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *aþalaz. The female name is a rare variant of Adele.

adelaide.ety: Borrowed from French Adélaïde, from Old High German Adalheid (from adal (“noble”) + heit (“nature, character”)), modern German Adelheid; doublet of Alice.

adelar.ety: Old High German, from adal (“noble”) + aro (“eagle”).

adelina.ety: From Adelina. Latinate form of French Adèle, short form of Germanic compound names beginning with Proto-Germanic *aþalaz (“noble”).

adeline.ety: From Old French Adeline, a diminutive form of Adela and Adele brought to England by the Normans.

adem.ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish آدم Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish آدم (adem).

adilynn.ety: A rare non-standard variant of Adeline with -lynn.

adnan.ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish عدنان (Adnan), from Arabic عَدْنَان (“settler”).

adolf.ety: From Old High German adal (“noble”) + wulf (“wolf”). Doublet of Ethelwolf from Old English Æþelwulf.

adolphus.ety: From Latin Adolphus. Doublet of Adolph.

adonai.m: sir, my lord (used when addressing a man)

adria.ety: From Latin Adria, Hadria. Compare Adriatic.

adrian.ety: From Latin Hadrianus (“from the Roman harbor Hadria”) a place name ultimately from Etruscan 𐌇𐌀𐌕𐌓𐌉𐌀. Doublet of Hadrian.

adrienne.ety: From the French Adrienne, the feminine form of Adrien (equivalent to English Adrian).

adélaïde.ety: From Old French, from Old High German Adalheid (modern German Adelheid), from adal (“noble”) + heit (“nature, character”), from Proto-Germanic *aþalaz (“noble”) + *haiduz (“character”).

afonso.ety: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese Afonso Compare Spanish Alfonso.

agapito.ety: From Latin Agapētus, from Ancient Greek Ᾰ̓γᾰπητός, from ᾰ̓γᾰπητός (“beloved”), from ᾰ̓γᾰπᾰ́ω (“to love”) + -τός (“masculine suffix”).

agatha.ety: Borrowed from English Agatha, from Ancient Greek Ἀγαθή, from ἀγαθός (“good”).

agathe.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἀγαθή, from ἀγαθός (“good”).

agnaldo.ety: From the Germanic name Aginal, from agin ("sword") + wald ("rule").

agnar.ety: Old Norse Agnarr, from age (“awe”) or egg (“sharp point”) + herr (“army”) or geirr (“spear”).

agne.ety: Old Norse Agni, short form of compound names beginning with Agn-, from age (“awe”) or egg (“point of a weapon”). Cognate to German Egon.

agnes.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἁγνή, coming from Ancient Greek ἁγνός (“pure, chaste”), Ancient Greek ἁγνεία (“purity, chastity”). Doublet of Inez.

ahad.ety: From the older Ahadi, with word-final vowel deletion.

ahmet.ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish احمد (ahmed), from Arabic أَحْمَد.

aicha.ety: Borrowed from Arabic عَائِشَة Borrowed from Arabic عَائِشَة.

aida.ety: Borrowed from Italian Aida, made famous by Giuseppe Verdi's opera Aida, which premiered in 1871.

aidan.ety: Name of an Irish saint, Anglicized from Irish Aodhán and Scottish Gaelic Aodhan, diminutives of Aodh (literally "fire", the name of a Celtic sun god).

aila.ety: From Sami; an Inari Sami variant of Aili. Possibly related to Laila.

ailish.ety: Phonetic rendering of Irish Ailís (“Alice”) or Eilís (“Elizabeth”).

aimar.ety: From Vulgar Latin Aymarus, Aimarus, from a Germanic proper name Eimar.

aimee.ety: Borrowed from French Aimée (“beloved”). A variation of the English Amy.

aine.ety: A derivative of Old Irish án (“bright, brilliant; splendid, noble”).

ainhoa.ety: Borrowed from Basque Ainhoa. Shortened from Virgen de Ainhoa (“Virgin of Ainhoa”), a Roman Catholic epithet of the Virgin Mary, from the place name Ainhoa.

ainsley.ety: Habitational surname for someone from Annesley, Nottinghamshire or Ansley, Warwickshire, both from Old English anne (“alone, solitary”) or ānsetl (“hermitage”) + lēah (“woodland, clearing”).

aira.ety: From airene (“ryegrass”), from Airisa as a rendering of the English Iris, or a phonetic coinage.

aissata.ety: A French spelling of a name ultimately derived from Arabic عَائِشَة (“Aisha”). Native spellings include Pulaar Aysata.

aissatou.ety: A French spelling of a West African name ultimately derived from Arabic عَائِشَة (“Aisha”).

akiva.ety: From Hebrew עֲקִיבָא (akíva), from Aramaic עֲקִיבָא (ʿăqīḇā).

akram.ety: Borrowed from Arabic أَكْرَم Borrowed from Arabic أَكْرَم.

alaia.ety: Borrowed in the 21st century from Basque Alaia, from alai (“joyful”). For earlier use among English-speakers, compare Hebrew עֲלִיָּה ('alīyá, “ascent”), Arabic عَالِيَة (“high, exalted”).

alaina.ety: A variant of Alana coined in the 20th century from Alain, the French equivalent of Alan.

alan.ety: From Old Breton Alan, name of early Breton saints, of disputed origin and meaning; brought to England by Normans. It may have been the name of a Celtic deity, the brother of Bran, Welsh Alawn, Alun.

alana.ety: Alana (“awakening”); the modern usage is reinforced by English Alana.

alanah.ety: Rare spelling variant of Alana, the feminine form of Alan.

alanis.ety: A feminine form of Alan best known for the Canadian singer Alanis Morissette whose father was named Alan.

alanna.ety: A feminine form of Alan; variant spelling of Alana. Compare also Alannah.

alannah.ety: Modern variant of Alana, the feminine form of Alan. Also associated with the affectionate Anglo-Irish term of address alanna (“child”).

alastair.ety: From Scottish Gaelic Alasdair (“Alexander”). Doublet of Alexander.

alban.ety: From Latin Albānus (“resident of Alba”) (a mountain region and an ancient city of Latium).

alberta.ety: From Albert + -a. The province was named after Princess Louise Caroline Alberta.

albertina.ety: A feminine diminutive form of Albert. Latinate variant of Albertine.

albertine.ety: Borrowed from French Albertine. Variant of Albertina.

albin.ety: Early saints' name, from the Roman cognomen Albīnus, derivative of Latin albus (“white”). In the case of individuals from Germanic nations, partly also from Germanic (cf.

albina.ety: From Latin Albina (name of a third-century martyr), feminine form of the Roman cognomen Albīnus, derivative of Latin albus (“white”).

alden.ety: From Old English Ealdwine, from eald (“old”) + wine (“friend”); equivalent to Alwin. In some cases a variant of Haldane.

alderico.ety: From a Germanic given name which contains Proto-Germanic *aldaz (“old”) + Proto-Germanic *rīks (“king”). See English old, Old English eald and English rich.

aleah.ety: Probably a fanciful spelling of Alia, Arabic عَالِيَة.

aleks.ety: Short form of Aleksander and Alexius. Cognate with English Alex.

aleksandar.ety: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic Алеѯандръ, from Ancient Greek Ᾰ̓λέξᾰνδρος. Older variant without "fleeting a": Александр.

aleksander.ety: A Norwegian spelling of Alexander, from Latin Alexander, from Ancient Greek Ἀλέξανδρος (Aléxandros), traditionally analysed as ἀλέξω (aléxō, “to ward off, defend”) and ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man”), genitive ἀνδρός (andrós).

aleksandrs.ety: From Russian Алекса́ндр. Cognate to English Alexander.

alesha.ety: One of the modern variations of Alicia.

aleshia.ety: One of the modern variations of Alicia, meaning "of noble kind".

aletha.ety: Derived from Ancient Greek ἀλήθεια, meaning "truth", "speaker of truth, one who speaks truth".

alex.ety: Short form of Alexander, from Ancient Greek Ἀλέξανδρος 'he who wards off men', i.e. protector, possibly of Hittite origin.

alexa.ety: From Alex + -a. A feminine form of Alex.

alexandre.ety: Borrowed from French Alexandre and Portuguese Alexandre.

alexandria.ety: Inherited from Middle English Alexandria From Middle English Alexandria, from Old English Alexandria, from Latin Alexandrīa, from Ancient Greek Ἀλεξάνδρεια, from Ἀλέξανδρος (“Alexander”) + -εια (“-ia: forming place names”).

alexandrina.ety: Latin Alexandrīna, feminine of Alexandrīnus. Alexandra + -ina.

alexandros.ety: Transliteration of Greek Αλέξανδρος, a male given name used in (modern) Greece. Cognate with English Alexander.

alexandru.ety: From Spanish Alejandro from Latin Alexander, from Ancient Greek Ἀλέξανδρος. Compare Xandru.

alexis.ety: From French Alexis, from Latin Alexis, ultimately from Ancient Greek Ἄλεξις (“helper, defender”).

alexzander.ety: Modern non-standard spelling variant of Alexander.

alf.ety: From Old Norse Alfr, alfr (“elf”), with an identical meaning in modern Danish. Also a medieval contraction of Adolf, and later used as a pet form of Alfred.

alfhild.ety: From Old Norse Álfhildr, from álfr (“elf”) + hildr (“battle, strife”). The spelling Alfhild was revived through Jacob Aall’s 1838 Norwegian translation of Snorri Sturluson’s kings' sagas.

alfons.ety: Of Germanic origin. Cognate to German Alfons and English Alfonso.

alfreda.ety: Originally a variant of Elfreda, used as a feminine form of Alfred since the 19th century.

alia.ety: Borrowed from Arabic عَالِيَة. The feminine form of Ali.

alin.ety: Probably the masculine of the name Alina, or perhaps derived from the verb alina.

alina.ety: Borrowed from Italian Alina, or a Latinate form of French Aline, ultimately from diminutives of the same Germanic name Adela, Adele.

alisha.ety: A modern spelling variant of Alicia.

alison.ety: From Middle English Alisoun, from Old French Alison, itself from Alis + -on, with Alis ultimately being from Old High German Adalheid or Adalhaid (“of noble kind”).

alissa.ety: Variant of Alyssa, from Alicia or from alyssum.

alistair.ety: From Scottish Gaelic Alasdair, from Norman Alexandre or Latin Alexander, from Ancient Greek Ἀλέξανδρος, from ἀλέξω (“to defend”) + ἀνδρ-, the stem of ἀνήρ (“man”).

alister.ety: From Old Irish Alaxander, from Latin Alexander, from Ancient Greek Ἀλέξανδρος, from ἀλέξω (“to defend”) + ἀνήρ (“man”).

alivia.ety: From 20th-century fiction, possibly influenced by Olivia.

allison.ety: From a Middle English diminutive form of Alan, Alexander or Alice + -son.

almeda.ety: From Spanish Almeda, from Arabic الْمَائِدَة.

almir.ety: From Arabic أَمِير Compare Slovene Almir, Serbo-Croatian Almir, Albanian Almir.

almira.ety: Coined name, possibly inspired by Elmira, of a queen of Castile in C. Handel's opera Almira (1705) to an Italian libretto.

alojzy.ety: Borrowed from Old High German alwisi Compare German Alois.

alon.ety: Four main origins: Borrowed from Macedonian Alen; Borrowed from English Alan.

alora.ety: From Botswana, it means "my dream" in the Bantu languages.

aloysius.ety: Latinization of Occitan Aloys, an Occitan form of Louis. Doublet of Louis.

alphonse.ety: From French Alphonse, from Spanish Alfonso, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *Aþalafunsaz, from *aþalaz + *funsaz. Doublet of Alfonso.

alphonso.ety: Anglicized form of Italian or Spanish Alfonso.

althea.ety: From Althaia or of Greek mythology, from Ancient Greek Ἀλθαία.

alton.ety: From Old English ǣwell (“river source”) + tūn (“settlement, town”).

alv.ety: From Old Norse Alfr, from Proto-Germanic *Albiz, and alfr (“elf, supernatural being”). Also a short form of compound names with the element, such as Toralv.

alvar.ety: Old Norse Alfarr, from alfr (“elf”) + herr (“army”). Revived in the 19th century, partly because it was mistaken for a translation of German Ernst from Swedish allvar (“seriousness”).

alvaro.ety: Inherited from Late Latin Alvarus, from Spanish-Visigothic. The Germanic proper name consists of two parts.

alvhild.ety: Old Norse Alfhildr, from alfr (“elf”) and hildr (“battle”).

alvin.ety: From Old English Ælfwine, made up of ælf (“elf”) + wine (“friend”).

alwin.ety: From Old English Æþelwine, from æþel (“noble”) + wine (“friend”); partly merged with Ælfwine (“Alvin”), literally “elf friend”.

alycia.ety: A rare spelling variant of Alicia.

alyssa.ety: A 20th-century invention. Possible origins: From alyssum + -a.

alzira.ety: Latinized form of Alzire, the name of the titular character of Voltaire's 1736 play Alzire.

amadeo.ety: From Amadeo. From Latin Amadeus, from Latin amo (“love”) + deus (“god”).

amadeu.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Amadeus Latin Amadeus.

amadeus.ety: From Latin Amadeus, from Latin amo (“love”) + deus (“god”).

amadou.ety: A French spelling of a name ultimately derived from Arabic أَحْمَدُ, i.e. Native spellings include Wolof and Pulaar Aamadu etc.

amand.ety: Borrowed from Latin Amandus, name of early Christian saints, from amandus (“lovable”).

amanda.ety: From Latin Amanda, feminine form of the saint's name, from amandus, future passive participle of amāre (“to love”): thus meaning "who/which is to be loved".

amandine.ety: From Amanda + -ine, reinforced by the common noun amandine.

amari.ety: The surname is of multiple origins, including: A variant of Amaro, from Italian Amaro. A variant of Amar, from Arabic عَمَّار.

amaro.ety: From the name of a local saint, San Amaro, not officially recognised by the Catholic church.

amaya.ety: Heroine of a Spanish historical novel Amaya o los vascos del siglo VIII (1877) by F. Navarro Villoslada, explained as Basque amai (“the end”).

amber.ety: From amber, from Middle English ambre, from Old French ambre, from Latin ambar, from Arabic عَنْبَر (“ambergris”).

ambrose.ety: From Latin saints' name Ambrosius, from Ancient Greek ἀμβρόσιος (“immortal, divine”). Compare Athanasius.

ambrosio.ety: Borrowed from Spanish Ambrosio, from Latin Ambrosius, from Ancient Greek ἀμβρόσιος (“immortal, divine”).

amelie.ety: Derived from Proto-Germanic compound names beginning with the element *amal (“vigor”).

america.ety: New Latin America, feminine Latinized form of the Italian first name of Amerigo Vespucci (1454–1512).

amie.ety: Perhaps a variant spelling of the female given name Amy.

amiel.ety: Borrowed from French Amiel, itself from Occitan.

amine.ety: Borrowed from Arabic أَمِين Borrowed from Arabic أَمِين.

amirah.ety: Borrowed from Arabic أَمِيرَة (“princess”), feminine of أَمِير (“prince”).

amiya.ety: Variant of Amiyah, from Hebrew אמאיה (āmíjah), literally “My mother is Jah”.

ammon.ety: From Latin Ammōn, from Ancient Greek Ἄμμων, itself from Egyptian jmn (jmn).

amund.ety: From Old Norse Ǫgmundr and from Ámundi "great" + " protection". Cognate with Faroese Øgmundur, Icelandic Ögmundur, and Swedish Amund.

amy.ety: Anglicized form of Old French Amee (modern French Aimée), which was both a nickname and a form of the Latin name Amata (“beloved”).

anabella.ety: Rare spelling variant of Annabella, the Latinate form of Annabel.

anais.ety: From Ancient Greek Ἀναῗτις, from Old Persian 𐎠𐎴𐏃𐎡𐎫.

anakin.ety: Coined by George Lucas as early as 1974 in early drafts of Star Wars, which included a character named Annikin Starkiller.

anastasija.ety: From Ancient Greek Ἀναστασία. Cognate with English Anastasia.

anastasio.ety: Inherited from Latin Anastasius, from Ancient Greek Ἀναστάσιος.

anastazja.ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Ἀναστασία.

anatol.ety: Borrowed from Latin Anatolius, from Ancient Greek ἀνατολή (“sunrise”).

anatole.ety: From French Anatole, from Ancient Greek ἀνατολή (“sunrise”). Cognate with Latin Anatolius.

anatoli.ety: From Ancient Greek ἀνατολή (“sunrise”). Cognate with English Anatole and Latin Anatolius.

anaís.ety: From Ancient Greek Ἀναῗτις, from Old Persian 𐎠𐎴𐏃𐎡𐎫.

anaïs.ety: From Ancient Greek Ἀναῗτις, from Old Persian 𐎠𐎴𐏃𐎡𐎫.

anderson.ety: From enm:Ander (“Andrew”) + -son, after Saint Andrew, patron saint of Scotland. In the United States, sometimes an anglicization of Danish and Norwegian Andersen or Swedish Andersson.

andoni.ety: Coined by Sabino Arana, based on Latin Antonius.

andra.ety: A modern feminine form of Andres (“Andrew”).

andre.ety: Borrowed from French André (“male given name”), from Latin Andreas (“male given name”), from Ancient Greek Ἀνδρέας (Andréas, “male given name”), derived from ἀνδρεῖος (andreîos, “manly, brave”), from ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man”). in Norway.

andreina.ety: Feminine (diminutive) form of Andrea (“Andrew”), comparable to the English female name Andrea.

andres.ety: Patronymic surname, borrowed from Spanish Andrés.

andressa.ety: From Spanish Andreza, variant of Andreia.

andria.ety: Borrowed from the Ancient Greek Ανδρεία.

andrina.ety: A rare feminine form of Andrew.

andriy.ety: From Ukrainian Андрі́й (“Andrew”). Doublet of Andrew.

andré.ety: Borrowed from French André (“male given name”), from Latin Andreas (“male given name”), from Ancient Greek Ἀνδρέας (Andréas, “male given name”), derived from ἀνδρεῖος (andreîos, “manly, brave”), from ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man”). in Norway.

ane.ety: Variant of Anne, itself a variant of Anna..

anes.ety: One variant name of the daughter of Gruffudd ap Cynan.

angeles.ety: From ángeles (“angels”), shortened from María (de los) Ángeles, a Roman Catholic epithet of the Virgin Mary as the Queen of Angels.

angeline.ety: Borrowed from French Angeline, from female>.

angelino.ety: From Angelo, from diminutive suffix> From Angelo (“a male given name”) + -ino.

anh.ety: As for the country name, contracted from Chinese 英國 (Anh quốc, “United Kingdom”), from Chinese 英 (Anh) (as in Mandarin 英吉利 (Yīngjílì, Anh Cát Lợi, “England”) or 英格蘭 (Yīnggélán, Anh Cách Lan, “England”)) + 國 (quốc, “country”).

anibal.ety: Borrowed from Latin Hannibal, Annibal, from Punic 𐤇𐤍𐤁𐤏𐤋.

aniceto.ety: From Latin Anicetus, from Ancient Greek ἀνίκητος (“invincible”).

anina.ety: Of unknown origin. Store norske leksikon describes Anina as possibly derived from one of the female given names Anna, Anne or Ane.

anine.ety: Of unknown origin. According to Store norske leksikon, Anine may be derived from one of the female given names Anna, Anne or Ane.

anita.ety: From Spanish Anita, diminutive of Ana (“Ann”).

aniya.ety: Said by some references to be Hebrew.

ann.ety: From Late Latin Anna chiefly in reference to St Anne the apocryphal mother of Mary mother of Jesus but appearing in the Vulgate in reference to Anna the Prophetess, from Koine Greek Ἄννα (“Anna”) in the New Testament.

annabel.ety: Originally a mishearing or misreading of Latin amabilis (“lovable”) (= Amabel, Mabel), used since the 12th century and by folk etymology interpreted as Anna + belle, "beautiful Anna".

annabelle.ety: A variant of Annabel, by folk etymology, "beautiful Anna".

annalena.ety: From Anna. From Latin Anna, which see.

anne.ety: From French Anne (“Ann”), from Late Latin Anna chiefly in reference to St Anne the apocryphal mother of Mary mother of Jesus but appearing in the Vulgate in reference to Anna the Prophetess.

annette.ety: From French Annette, diminutive of Anne, from Ἄννα, the Ancient Greek New Testament form of the Hebrew female name חַנָּה (ḥannâ, “grace, gracious”) with the French suffix 'ette meaning cute, adorable or little.

anni.ety: Borrowed from English Annie (“female given name”), adapted in spelling. English Annie is a pet form of Ann and Anne.

annick.ety: From Breton Annig and Annaig, from Anna + -ig.

annie.ety: Borrowed from English Annie (“female given name”), an English pet form of Ann and Anne.

annina.ety: Borrowed from Italian Annina, made known in Germany by 19th and 20th century opera characters.

anniston.ety: The city in Alabama, originally Woodstock, was renamed by town officials in 1873 (after realizing there was another village named Woodstock in central Alabama) in honor of Annie Eliza Scott Tyler (1838–1914).

anny.ety: Borrowed from English Anny (“female given name”), a dated spelling variant of Annie, originally a pet form of Ann and Anne.

anouk.ety: From French Anouk, popularised by actress Anouk Aimée, who adopted the name after her role in the film La Maison sous la mer (1947).

ansgar.ety: From Old High German ans (“god”) + Old High German gēr (“spear”). Cognate with Ásgeir, Asger, Norwegian Nynorsk Åsgeir, and English Oscar.

ansley.ety: From Old English ānsetl (“hermitage”) + lēah (“woodland clearing, glade”).

anson.ety: From Ann + -son (the former word is a diminutive).

antero.ety: Vernacular form of Andreas (from Ancient Greek). Cognate with English Andrew.

anthony.ety: From Latin Antōnius, name of a Roman gens (with excrescent -h- suggested by an unetymological association with Ancient Greek ἄνθος (“flower”)).

antoine.ety: From French Antoine. Doublet of Anthony.

antoinette.ety: From French Antoinette, feminine diminutive of Antoine, equivalent to Anthony.

anton.ety: Borrowed from German Anton and from other northern European languages. Doublet of Anthony.

antoni.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Antōnius Latin Antōnius.

antonin.ety: Borrowed from Latin Antōnīnus, in many cases via Czech Antonín.

antonina.ety: Borrowed from Latin Antōnīna, feminine form of Antōnīnus, derivative of Antōnius. Name of obscure early martyrs venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church.

antonino.ety: Inherited from Latin Antonīnus Inherited from Latin Antonīnus. Cognate with Sicilian (A)ntuninu.

antony.ety: From Latin Antōnius, name of a Roman gens, of uncertain etymology, but not Greek or Hebrew; most likely of Etruscan origin, possibly derived from Ani, the Etruscan god of the sky. Doublet of Antoine.

antwan.ety: Anglicization of French Antoine. Compare Antoine, Antwon.

anuar.ety: Ultimately derived from Arabic أنور. Doublet of Enver.

aníbal.ety: Borrowed from Latin Hannibal, Annibal, from Punic 𐤇𐤍𐤁𐤏𐤋.

aparecida.ety: From Nossa Senhora da Conceição Aparecida (Our Lady of the Revealed/Appeared Conception), the original name for Our Lady of Aparecida, a clay statue of the Virgin Mary that, according to tradition.

apollo.ety: From Latin Apollō, from Ancient Greek Ἀπόλλων.

april.ety: From Middle English apprile, Aprill, re-Latinised from Middle English aueril, from Old French avrill, from Latin Aprīlis (“of the month of the goddess Venus”), perhaps based on Etruscan 𐌀𐌐𐌓𐌖, from Ancient Greek Ἀφροδίτη (“Venus”).
april.m: of the month of the goddess Venus

aquiles.ety: From Spanish Aquiles, from Latin Achilles, from Ancient Greek Ἀχιλλεύς.

arabella.ety: Used in Scotland since the sixteenth century; possibly from Latin orabilis (“yielding to prayer”) or a variant of Annabel.

araci.ety: Coined by Q455703, as the name of a character in Ubirajara. Navarro derives it from Old Tupi eíra + sy, making it a doublet of Iraci.

aranzazu.ety: Borrowed from Basque Arantzazu, literally “hawthorn place”. The given name is a shortening of María de Aranzazu, to whom the sanctuary is dedicated.

aras.ety: From Turkish Aras, from Persian ارس (aras), ultimately from Proto-Iranian *Raxsā- (“swift-flowing”). Compare Sanskrit रङ्घते (“to hasten, run”).

arch.m: pure, holy, genuine, precious + strong, bold

archibald.ety: From Anglo-Norman Arcebald, Arcenbald or Ercenbald, from Old French Archaunbault, from Proto-West Germanic *Erknabalþ, from *erkn (“pure, holy, genuine, precious”) + *balþ (“strong, bold”).
archibald.m: pure, holy, genuine, precious + strong, bold

archie.m: pure, holy, genuine, precious + strong, bold

arden.ety: Derived from the Brythonic ardu (“Arden”) ardu meaning "high".

are.ety: From Old Norse Ari, from ari (“eagle”).

ari.ety: Of the first sense, derives directly from Hebrew: אֲרִי (arí, “lion”); compare Yiddish: לייב (leyb, “Leib”), English: Leo, Leon, French: Léo, Léon, Czech: Lev, Polish: Lew, Russian: Лев, and Ukrainian: Лев.

aria.ety: As a 21st century English name from TV and fantasy fiction, explained as "a musical aria". Similar sounding names exist in many languages, e.g.
aria.m: God has promised. Also, lion of God

ariah.ety: From Hebrew אַרְיֵה (“God has promised. Also, lion of God”).
ariah.m: God has promised. Also, lion of God

ariana.ety: Modern simplification of Arianna, Ariane and Arianne, all forms of the Greek name Ariadne ("most holy"; Cretan Greek αρι (ari) "most" and αδνος (adnos) "holy").

ariane.ety: From French Ariane, from Ancient Greek Ἀριάδνη.

ariele.ety: From Biblical Biblical Hebrew אֲרִיאֵל (ari'él), literally “lion of God”, a compound of אֲרִי (arí, “lion”) and אֵל (él, “God”).

arif.ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish عارف (arif), from Arabic عَارِف (“knowing”), active participle of عَرَفَ (“to know”).

arik.ety: Transcription of a modern Hebrew diminutive of the Hebrew equivalent of Ariel.

arild.ety: A Norwegian 15th century variant of Harald. Also a Danish variant of the German Arnold.

arina.ety: From Russian Арина, a variant of Ири́на (“Irene”).

arizona.ety: From O'odham alĭ ṣonak, from Basque haritz ona.

arkaitz.ety: From Harkaitz, in turn, derived haitz (rock).

arlene.ety: A nineteenth-century coinage probably based on similar-sounding names such as Charlene and Arlette.

arlette.ety: From a derivative (possibly a diminutive) of Old French Herleva, a Germanic compound name beginning with *harjaz (“army”). The mother of William the Conqueror was called both Herleva and Arlette.

armand.ety: Cognate to English Herman and German Hermann, possibly also to German Hartmann.

armel.ety: Name of a Breton saint, from Late Latin Armagilus, of Celtic origin; compare Welsh Arthfael.

arnav.ety: From Sanskrit अर्णव (“ocean, sea”). Doublet of Arnab.

arne.ety: For the given name, a short form of Old Norse compound names beginning with arn- (“eagle”).

arnfinn.ety: From Old Norse Arnfinnr, from ǫrn (“eagle”) + finnr (“Sami”). Cognate with Arnfinnur.

arnhild.ety: From Old Norse Arnhildr, from ǫrn (“eagle”) + hildr (“battle”).

arnold.ety: From a French version of a Germanic name, from Proto-West Germanic *Arnuwald, from Proto-Germanic *arô (“eagle”) + *waldą (“power”).

arnstein.ety: From Old Norse Arnsteinn, from ǫrn (“eagle”) + steinn (“stone”).

arnt.ety: Low German variant of Arnold, borrowed into Norwegian in the 15th century.

arnulf.ety: From Old High German *Arnwolf, from Proto-Germanic *Arôwulfaz, equivalent to Old High German arn (“eagle”) + wulf (“wolf”).

arnulfo.ety: From German Arnulf derived from Germanic elements German arn (“eagle”) and German ulf (“wolf”).

arran.ety: From Scottish Gaelic Arainn, but the name is ultimately probably of non-Indo-European (substrate) or Pictish origin, along with other uncertain names in Scotland such as Skye, Lewis, and Islay.

arsenio.ety: From Ancient Greek Ἀρσένιος, from ἄρσην (“masculine, virile”).

artemis.ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Ᾰ̓́ρτεμις Further etymology is uncertain.

arthur.ety: From the name of the legendary king, from Middle English Arthure, from Medieval Latin Arthurus, probably from Middle Welsh arth (“bear”).

arve.ety: From Arved (pronounced Arve) reanalysed as weak masculine; from Old Norse Arviðr. Also from Old Norse *Arfi, from arfi (“heir”).

arvid.ety: From Old Norse Arnviðr, arn / ǫrn (“eagle”) + viðr (“tree, wood”).

ascension.ety: From ascensión (“Ascension (of Jesus to heaven)”), shortened from María (de la) Ascensión, a Roman Catholic epithet of the Virgin Mary; also referring to birth on Ascension Day.

asgeir.ety: From Old Norse Ásgeirr with a shortened due to the following consonant cluster.

ashby.ety: From Old English æsċ (“ashtree”) + Old Norse býr (“farm, town”).

ashley.ety: From Old English *Æsċlēah, composed of æsċ (“ash tree”) + lēah (“wood, clearing”). Equivalent to Ash + -ley.

ashling.ety: From Aisling, to match English spelling.

ashlyn.ety: An anglicized form of Irish Aisling (“dream, vision”) with -lyn.

ashton.ety: From Old English æsc (“ash (tree species)”) + tūn (“enclosure, settlement”).

asif.ety: From Hebrew אסף (asef, “to gather”); or Persian, Urdu آصف (āsaf, “name of Solomon's vizier”).

aslak.ety: From Old Norse Áslákr, from áss (“god”) + leikr (“play, sport”). Cognate with Old English Ōslāc.

asle.ety: From Old Norse Atli with a change of tl to sl, cf. netle > nesle. Also a short form of names beginning with Asl- (e.g.

asmund.ety: Ås + -mund; from Old Norse Ásmundr, from áss + -mundr. Cognate with Ásmundur.

asta.ety: Old Norse Ásta, a medieval diminutive of Ástríðr (hence Astrid).

asuncion.ety: From asunción (“assumption (of Mary to heaven)”), shortened from María (de la) Asunción, a Roman Catholic epithet of the Virgin Mary.

athan.ety: [//www.alt-usage-english.org/sdc2005/questions61_90.html Perhaps] from Nathan, via rebracketing of "my Nathan" as "mine Athan"; compare Ned, derived from Ed via rebracketing in the opposite direction.

athanasios.ety: From Greek Αθανάσιος and Ancient Greek Ἀθανάσιος, from α- (“a-, un-, non-”) + θάνατος (“dying”) + -ιος (“-y: forming adjectives”). Doublet of Athanasius and Afanasy.
athanasios.m: a-, un-, non- + dying + -y: forming adjectives

athena.ety: From Middle English Athena, from Latin Athēna, from Ancient Greek Ἀθηνᾶ. Doublet of Athina.

athina.ety: From Greek Αθηνά, from Ancient Greek Ἀθηνᾶ. Doublet of Athena.

atle.ety: From Old Norse Atli, from late Proto-Germanic *Attilô, diminutive of *attô (“father”). Cognate with Atli.

aubin.ety: From the Latin given name Albinus. Cognates include Albino, Albin.

aubrey.ety: Inherited from Middle English Aubrey From Middle English Aubrey, Aubry, from Norman Auberi, Alberi, from Latin Alberīcus, Latinized form of Old High German Alberich, from Proto-Germanic *Albirīks, from *albiz (“elf.

aubrie.ety: Modern altered spelling of Aubrey as a feminine name.

aubriella.ety: Modern coinage, probably a Blend of Aubrey + Gabriella.

aubrielle.ety: Modern coinage, probably a Blend of Aubrey + Gabrielle.

aud.ety: From Old Norse Auðr, from auðr (“riches”). Cognate with German Oda and Ute, and with English Eda.

aude.ety: From the short form of compound names beginning with Frankish *ald- (“old”) or *aþal- (“noble”); cognate to Italian Alda.

audun.ety: From Old Norse Auðunn, from older *Auðvinr, from Proto-Germanic *Audawiniz. Cognate with Faroese Eyðun, Icelandic Auðun, Swedish Öden and Edwin.

august.ety: From Middle English August Early Middle English August(us), re-Latinized from Old English Agustus, from Late Latin Agustus, from Latin augustus (“month of August”).

augusta.ety: From Latin Augusta From Latin Augusta, feminine of Augustus. The places are mostly named for British royalty.

augusto.ety: Inherited from Latin Augustus Inherited from Latin Augustus.

aura.ety: The name of the deity is from Ancient Greek Αὔρα, from αὔρα (“breeze”).

aurea.ety: From the feminine form of the Latin adjective aureus (“golden”).

aurélia.ety: Borrowed from Latin Aurelia. A Latinate variant of Aurélie.

aurélien.ety: Borrowed from Latin Aurelianus, derivative of the Roman gens name Aurelius, from aureus (“golden”). Doublet of Orléans.

austin.ety: From Middle English Austin, from Anglo-Norman Aostin, Austin, similar to Old French Aostin, Austin, a popular variant of Old French Agustin, from Latin Augustīnus, from Augustus, literally “majestic”.

avalyn.ety: From Ava + Lyn, or a variant of Aveline.

avalynn.ety: From Ava + -lynn, or a variant of Aveline.

avery.ety: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman Averay From Anglo-Norman Averay, Auveray, Alverey, from Latin Alveredus, Aluredus, from Old English Ælfræd, from ælf (“elf”) and ræd (“counsel”). Doublet of Alfred.

aviana.ety: From the female given name Ava and the feminine Latinate suffix -ian(n)a, or possibly from a feminine elaboration of the adjective avian (“of birds”) through the suffix -a.

avianna.ety: From the female given name Ava and the feminine Latinate suffix -ian(n)a, or possibly from a feminine elaboration of the adjective avian (“of birds”) through the suffix -a.

avigail.ety: Borrowed from Hebrew אֲבִיגַיִל (avigáyil, “Avigail”), literally “my Father's joy” or “fountain of joy”.

avraham.ety: From transliterations of modern pronunciations of Hebrew אַבְרָהָם (Avrahám). Doublet of Abramo and Abraham and Ibrahim and Abrahan.

avril.m: of the month of the goddess Venus

axel.ety: From Danish Aksel, first used for the bishop and statesman Absalon Hvide (1128–1201), from biblical Absalom.

axton.ety: From Axton, Kent, Old English Acca (a personal name) + Old English stan (“stone”).

ayan.ety: Meaning Eon in Arabic. May be related to the greek word Aeon.

aydin.ety: From Turkish Aydın, from Ottoman Turkish آیدین (Aydın) named for Aydin Mehmet Bey, from آیدین (aydın, “light; clarity; shining; bright; enlightened, educated, intelligent”).

azalia.ety: From azalia, an archaic form of azalea.
azalia.m: A plant of the obsolete genus Azalea.

aïcha.ety: Borrowed from Arabic عَائِشَة Borrowed from Arabic عَائِشَة.

badr.ety: Borrowed from Arabic بَدْر Borrowed from Arabic بَدْر.

balder.ety: From Old Norse Baldr, from the adjective baldr, ballr (“brave”).

baltazar.ety: From Akkadian 𒁹𒀭𒂗𒈗𒋀 (“Bēl-šarra-uṣur”), literally “May Bel protect the king”. Cognate with English Balthazar.

balthazar.ety: From, from Latin Baltassar, from Ancient Greek Βαλτάσαρ, from Hebrew בֵּלְשַׁאצַּר (bēlšaṣṣar), attested in the Tanakh and the Old Testament (Daniel 5:1), from Akkadian 𒁹𒀭𒂗𒈗𒋀 (Bēl-šarra-uṣṣur), literally “May Bel protect the king”.

bambi.ety: Borrowed from Italian Bambi, from bambina (“young girl”).

baptiste.ety: From Jean-Baptiste (“Saint John the Baptist”), from baptiste (“baptist”). From the epithet of John the Baptist (Jean-Baptiste).

barbara.ety: From Latin Barbara, the name of Saint Barbara, feminine form of barbarus, from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (“strange, foreign”). Doublet of Varvara.

barbro.ety: From Latin Barbara, reshaped in Scandinavian. The Latin name is from Ancient Greek Βαρβάρα, the feminine form of βάρβαρος (“foreign, non-Greek”).

barnaby.ety: English surname of Aramaic origin, from בַּר נְבִיָּא (bar nəḇiyyā), literally “prophet’s son”.

barney.ety: From either the Old English personal name Bera (genitive singular Beran) or from Old English beren (“growing with barley”) + īeġ (“island”).

baron.m: The male ruler of a barony.

barron.ety: As a Scottish surname, from Scots baron, sometimes found as McBarron; see Baron. As an Irish and Manx surname, from Ó Bearáin, literally “descendant of Bearán”, a personal name from bior (“spear”).

barry.ety: Anglicized form of Irish Bairre, short form of Fionnbharr, from fionn (“white”) + barr (“head”).

bart.m: son of Talmai; son of Ptolemy

bartolome.m: son of Talmai; son of Ptolemy

bartolomeu.m: son of Talmai; son of Ptolemy

barton.ety: From Old English bere (“barley”) + Old English tūn (“enclosure”).

bartłomiej.m: son of Talmai; son of Ptolemy

basil.ety: Name of several early saints, particularly in the Orthodox Church, from Latin Basilius, from Ancient Greek Βασίλειος. Doublet of Vasilios and Vasily.

basile.ety: Latin Basilius, from Ancient Greek Βασίλειος.

basilio.ety: From Spanish Basilio, from Latin Basilius, from Ancient Greek Βασίλειος.

baxter.ety: From Middle English bakster, bakestre, from Old English bæcestre (“baker”), equivalent to bake + -ster.

baylee.ety: Variant of Bailey, possibly influenced by Lee.

bazyli.ety: Latin Basiliī, from Ancient Greek Βασίλειος.

bear.ety: As an English surname, related to bear As a German surname, spelling variant of Baer and Bahr.

beat.ety: From Latin Beatus, a masculine form of Beata.

beatrix.ety: From viātrīx (“female wayfarer, traveller”), altered under influence from beātus, beāta (“happy, fortunate”).

beau.ety: Shortened from surname type given names such as Beauregard or Beaumont, or from the French word beau.

beckham.ety: From Old English personal name Becca + hām (“homestead”).

becki.ety: A fanciful respelling of Becky, diminutive of Rebecca.

beckie.ety: Variant of Becky, diminutive of Rebecca.

belchior.ety: Alteration of Melchior, from Latin Melchior, from Hebrew מלכיאור.

belinda.ety: From Belle + -inda, base from various Romance sources such as French belle, Italian bella (“beautiful”), suffix Latinate form of German linde (“soft”) (English linden, lithe).

bella.ety: From Italian: a diminutive of Isabella and Arabella, by folk etymology interpreted as bella (“beautiful”).

bellamy.ety: Of Norman origin, from Old French bel (“fair”) + ami (“friend”). Could also be a locational surname from the Norman town of Bêlleme (Belesme).

belle.ety: From French belle (“beauty, beautiful”), from Latin bella.

benedicta.ety: From Latin Benedicta, feminine of Benedictus.

benedikt.ety: Borrowed from Late Latin Benedictus, from Latin benedictus (“blessed”), perfect passive participle of benedīcō (“to speak well of, bless, praise”), from bene (“well”) + dīcō (“to speak”).

benedykt.ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin benedictus.

bengt.ety: Cognate with Swedish Bengt. Recorded in Norway since the 14th century.

beniamin.m: son of the right/south or son of days

benjamim.m: son of the right/south or son of days

benjamín.m: son of the right/south or son of days

benji.m: son of the right/south or son of days

bennet.ety: See French Benoît, Norman Beneît. Doublet of Benoit and Benito.

bennie.m: son of the right/south or son of days

benno.m: son of the right/south or son of days

benoit.ety: From Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin Benedictus, from benedictus (“blessed; well spoken of”), from Latin benedicō.

benoît.ety: From Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin Benedictus, from benedictus (“blessed; well spoken of”), from Latin benedicō.

bent.ety: Medieval contraction of Late Latin Benedictus. Cognate with Swedish Bengt.

bente.ety: Contraction of Benedikte. The feminine equivalent of Bent.

bentlee.m: A motor car manufactured by this company.

bento.ety: From Old Galician-Portuguese Bẽeito, from Late Latin Benedictus, from benedictus (“blessed”), from Latin benedicō. Doublet of Benedito and bendito.

benton.ety: From either Old English bēan (“bean”) or *beonet (“bentgrass”) + tūn (“enclosure; settlement, town”).

berengere.ety: From the name of medieval queens, called Berengaria in English. Feminine form of Bérenger, from Proto-Germanic *beraną (“carry”) and *gaizaz (“spear”).

berenice.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Βερενῑ́κη (“bringer of victory”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Macedonian (compare the native word Φερενῑ́κη), from φέρω (“to bear, to carry, to bring”) + νῑ́κη (“victory”).

bergljot.ety: Berg + ljot; from Old Norse Bergljót and Bergljótr, from an element meaning (compare bjǫrg and bjarga) + ljót and ljótr (“light, shining”).

berkeley.ety: From Old English beorc (“birch”) + leah (“meadow, leigh”). Equivalent to birch + -ley (“lea”).

bernadette.ety: From French Bernadette, made famous by St. Bernadette of Lourdes.

bernard.ety: Inherited from Old High German Bernhart, from Old High German bero (“bear”, cf. Bär), + Old High German hart (“hard, strong”, cf. hart).

bernardete.ety: From French Bernadette with influence from Bernardo//Bernarda.

bernhard.ety: From Old High German Bernhart, from Old High German bero (“bear”, cf. Bär), + Old High German hart (“hard, strong”, cf. hart).

bernie.ety: From Bernard + -ie. From Bernadette + -ie or Bernice + -ie.

bernt.ety: Borrowed in the Middle Ages from a Low German variant of Bernhard, equivalent to modern German Bernd.

berry.ety: Variant of Bury and (in dialects with Mary-marry-merry merger) Barry. The given name is also a pet form of names beginning with Ber-.

bert.ety: Shortened version of Bertrand, Albert, Bertram, Robert, Herbert, Gilbert or any name containing the Germanic element bert/berht/beraht/brecht "bright".

bertha.ety: Definitely from Old English Berþa as a result of metathesis of h, from earlier Old English Berhte (“bright one”), influence of Latin Bercta.

bertil.ety: Medieval equivalent of modern German Berthold, from Germanic berht "bright" + wald "rule".

beryl.ety: From beryl or an anglicization of Yiddish בערל, literally “little bear”.

bess.ety: Variant of Beth, a Short form of Elizabeth.

bethan.ety: Shortened form of Bethany, from Ancient Greek Βηθανία, from Aramaic בית עניא (beth anya, “house of wretchedness”).

bethany.ety: From Ancient Greek Βηθανία, from Aramaic בית עניא (beth anya, “house of wretchedness”). This etymology is highly disputed; see Bethany.

betsy.ety: From the Short form of Elizabeth + -sy.

beulah.ety: A biblical name applied to the land of Israel in Isaiah 62:4, from Biblical Hebrew בְּעוּלָה (bəʿûlâ, “married (woman)”), taken up as a given name by Puritans and used figuratively for the New Earth.

beverley.ety: From Old English befer (“beaver”) + lēah (“clearing”). Equivalent to Beaver + -ley (“lea”).

bexley.ety: From Old English byxe (“box tree”) + leah (“wood”), equivalent to box + -ley (“lea”).

beyonce.ety: The recent use of this name is due to the American singer Beyoncé Knowles (born 1981), after her mother's maiden name, which was different from her own parents' surname, Beyincé, due to a clerical error on her birth certificate.

beñat.ety: Originally a diminutive of Bernart, with expressive palatalization.

bianka.ety: Borrowed from German Bianka Borrowed from German Bianka.

bill.ety: Hypocorism of William. It is unclear how the initial W became a B; this could have been part of the medieval trend of swapping letters, similar to Dick for Rick.

birdie.ety: From birdie (“little bird”). Also used as a diminutive of Bertha.

birgit.ety: Short form of Birgitte and Birgitta.

birgitta.ety: From Old Irish Brigit. Borrowed from Swedish Birgitta.

birgitte.ety: Borrowed from Danish Birgitte and Norwegian Birgitte.

birk.ety: From the Anglo-Norman surname, from Old English burh, burg (“fortification, city”).

bjarne.ety: From Old Norse Bjarni, short form of names starting with Bjarn-, from bjǫrn (“bear”).

bjarte.ety: Old Norse Bjartr, short form of names containing the element bjartr (“bright”). Comparable to English Bert.

bjørg.ety: From Old Norse Bjǫrg, from bjǫrg (“salvation”). Also a short form of compound names with the element.

bjørn.ety: From Old Norse Bjǫrn, from Old Norse bjǫrn (“bear”), whence also bjørn. Also a medieval short form of compound names containing the element.

bjørnar.ety: From Old Norse Bjarnar, influenced by the word bjørn (“bear”). Cognate with Danish Bjørner.

blaise.ety: Borrowed from Old French Blaise in the Middle Ages and revived partly due to the modern French equivalent, from Latin Blasius. Doublet of Blasius.

blake.ety: A surname derived from either Old English blæc (“black”) or from Old English blāc (“pale, fair, shining, white”), or as an anglicisation of Irish Ó Bláthmaic.

blanche.ety: From Old French blanc (“white”). The surname originated as a nickname, or as a matronymic.

blandine.ety: From Blandina, a second century martyr of Lyons, derived from Latin blandus "pleasing".

blue.ety: From the German surname, Americanized from Blau or its French cognate bleu.

blythe.ety: English surname, from Old English blīþe (“merry”). Many senses are derived from placenames, such as the River Blythe, all from the Old English adjective.

bo.ety: From Old Norse Búi (“dweller, long-time resident”), originally a medieval byname.

bob.ety: Probably from a medieval hypocorism of Rob.

bode.ety: As a Dutch and German surname, from bode (“messenger”). As a German and Danish surname, from the name Bodo, derived from Old Saxon bodo (“messenger”), related to above.

bodie.ety: As a Scottish surname, variant of Body, Boddy, Boddie. As a French surname, variant of Bodi, see Beaudin.

bodil.ety: Borrowed from Danish Bodil, ultimately from Old Norse Bóthildr, a female given name formed from bót (“remedy, help, improvement”) and hildr (“battle, fight”).

bogumił.ety: Inherited from Old Polish Bogumił, from Bóg.

bonifacio.ety: Inherited from Late Latin Bonifātius From Late Latin Bonifātius, literally “the one with a good fate”. The city was named Named after Boniface II of Tuscany.
bonifacio.m: the one with a good fate

bonifacy.ety: Late Latin Bonifātius, from Latin bonus + fātum.

bonnie.ety: Originally an American nickname from Scottish bonnie (“fine, beautiful”).

borys.ety: From Ukrainian Бори́с. Compare Belarusian Барыс, Russian Бори́с.

boston.ety: The US city is named after the English town (from which several prominent colonists had come).

bowen.ety: From Welsh ab Owain (“son of Owen”).

boyd.ety: From Scottish Gaelic, either buidhe (“blond, yellow, fair”), or a habitational surname from the Isle of Bute in Scotland.

braden.ety: Anglicised from an Irish surname Ó Bradáin (“descendant of Bradán”), from a personal name meaning "salmon," from bradán (“salmon”).

bradford.ety: Various place names in England, from Old English brād (“broad”) + ford (“ford”).

bradley.ety: Ultimately from Old English brād (“broad”) + lēah (“woodland”). Equivalent to broad + -ley.

brady.ety: From Old English brād (“broad”) + ēage (“eye”) and brād (“broad”) + ēġ (“island”); or from Irish Ó Brádaigh.

braelyn.ety: 20th-century coinage with -lyn, compare Braylen, Braylon. Variant: Braelynn.

braelynn.ety: 20th-century coinage with -lynn, compare Braylen, Braylon. Variant: Braelyn.

brage.ety: From Old Norse Bragi, from bragr (“first, foremost”) or bragr (“poetry”).

branca.ety: From a nickname related to branca (“paw, claw, hand”).

brandon.ety: From Middle English Brandon, Brampdon, Bramdun, Bremedon, Bromdun, from, from brōm (“broom shrub”) + dūn (“hill, dune”). Doublet of Branton.

brandt.ety: Contraction of given names containing the Germanic element *Brand-, -brand (“fire/ sword”) such as modern German Hildebrandt.

brantley.ety: Anglicized from Alemannic German Brändle, Brändli, "firebrand.".

braxton.ety: Perhaps a habitational surname from the village of Branxton, in Northumberland.

braylee.ety: Modern coinage, compare Brylee, Kaylee, Jaylee.

brenda.ety: Possibly from Old Norse brandr (“sword”); by folk etymology seen as a feminine form of Brendan.

brendan.ety: Anglicized form of the name of Irish saints, Irish Bréanainn (via Latin Brendanus), from Old Irish Brénainn, from Old Welsh 5=prince, king, ultimately from Proto-Celtic 5=(someone) preeminent, outstanding.

brendon.ety: Transliteration of Brandon. From Middle English Brandon, Brampdon, Bramdun, Bremedon, Bromdun, from, from brōm (“broom shrub”) + dūn (“hill, dune”).

brenna.ety: An American coinage used since the 1970s, possibly based on the male given name Brennan or Brendan.

brennan.ety: From Irish Ó Braonáin (“descendant of Braonán”), a diminutive of braon (“moisture, drop”). Alternatively, from Irish Ó Branáin (“descendant of Branán”), a diminutive of bran (“raven”).

brent.ety: English surname from placenames in Devon and Somerset, from Old English brant (“steep”), referring to hills. Compare Brents.

brentley.ety: Possibly an invented name. Compare Brent, Brantley.

brett.ety: Related to Breton, Brittany, and more distantly Briton.

brian.ety: Borrowed from Irish Brian. Doublet of Brendan.

brianne.ety: A feminine form of Brian, taken to regular use in the 1970s.

briar.ety: As a surname Middle English brere (“briar”).

bridget.ety: English form of the Irish saints' name Brighid, Brigid. Doublet of Bride.

brit.ety: First use appears c. 1901, either a shortening of Britisher or Briton, or a.

britt.ety: From Britta. From Old Irish Brigit.

brittany.ety: Inherited from Middle English Bretany, Brytany, itself borrowed from Medieval Latin Britannia, applied to Brittany from at least the 6th century, and reinforced by Middle French Bretagne.

brixton.ety: Thought to originate from Brixistane, meaning "the stone of Brixi (a Saxon lord)".
brixton.m: the stone of Brixi (a Saxon lord)

brodie.ety: Scottish habitational surname of uncertain meaning. Probably of Pictish or Gaelic origin.

brogan.ety: Anglicized form of Irish Ó Brógáin (“descendants of Brógán”), probably from a diminutive of bróg (“shoe”).

bronisław.ety: Of Slavic origin, from Proto-Slavic *borniti (“to protect”) + *slava (“fame, glory”).

bronson.ety: From Middle English Brun (“a man named Brown's”) + son.

bronte.ety: Used by Patrick Brontë (1777–1861) as a rendering of Brunty, Prunty, an Anglicization of the Irish Ó Proinntigh (“descendant of a person named Proinnteach (“Generous”)”).
bronte.m: descendant of a person named Proinnteach (“Generous

brook.ety: As an English surname, from the noun brook. As a north German surname, from Low German Brook (“swamp, marsh”), related to the above.

brooke.ety: A topographic surname for someone who lived near a brook.

brooklyn.ety: From Dutch Breukelen, from broek (“wetland, marsh”).

bror.ety: From bror (“brother”), a suitable name for a younger son.

bruce.ety: From a Norman place name, Brix, of disputed meaning.

bryn.ety: From Welsh bryn (“hill, mound”), or Cumbric *brınn (“hill”) in the Greater Manchester place-name.

brynhild.ety: From Old Norse Brynhildr, from Proto-Germanic *Brunjōhildiz, from *brunjǭ (“breastplate”) + *hildiz (“battle, fight”).

bryony.ety: From the bryony plant in the 19th century.

buck.ety: For both the English surname and given name, originally a nickname for someone who resembled a buck. Also as an English topographic surname, from Middle English buk (modern beech).

buffy.ety: A pet form of Elizabeth (cf. Bethy), based on a child's unsuccessful attempts to pronounce the name.

burton.ety: Usually from Old English burhtun (fortified farmstead, farmstead near or belonging to a stronghold or manor), from burh + tun.

byron.ety: A habitational surname from Old English byrum (“at the byre or cattleshed”).

bérénice.ety: Through Latin Berenicē, borrowed from Ancient Greek Βερενίκη. Doublet of Véronique.

børge.ety: Variant of Birger. Cognate with Swedish Börje.

błażej.ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin Blasius.

cade.ety: As an English surname, from an old personal name Cada, from a Germanic root meaning "lump, swelling" and perhaps related to the next sense.

caden.ety: Invented by American parents in the 1990s to rhyme with the equally fashionable Aidan, Braden, Hayden and Jayden.

cadence.m: The act or state of declining or sinking.

caetano.ety: Latin Caiētānus (“inhabitant of Gaeta”), re-Latinized from Italian Gaetano, name of a saint. Compare Sicilian Caitanu.

caio.ety: From Latin Caius, variant of Gaius.

caitriona.ety: From French Catherine, from Medieval Latin Catharīna, from Latin Ecaterīna, from Ancient Greek Αἰκατερίνη, *Ἑκατερίνη.

caius.ety: The spelling with C is a holdover from an era when the letter C represented the phonetic value. Compare ecō and vircō.

calebe.ety: Borrowed from Hebrew כלב (kéleb, “dog”) (possibly referring to dogs’ unconditional devotion to their masters).

calista.ety: From Latin Callistus, from Ancient Greek Κάλλιστος (“most beautiful”), from καλός (“beautiful”). Compare Callisto.

calixte.ety: From Latin Callistus. Historically most prevalent in Martinique.

calixto.ety: From Old Spanish Calixto, via Latin Callixtus, ultimately from Ancient Greek Κάλλιστος (“most beautiful”), from καλός (“beautiful”). Compare Calisto.

callahan.ety: From Irish Ó Ceallacháin, from Ceallachán, diminutive of the given name Ceallach. Doublet of Kelly and Kellogg.

callan.ety: Borrowed from Irish Ó Cathaláin (“descendant of Cathalán”).

callista.ety: Borrowed from Italian Callista, a conflation from two sources, both from Ancient Greek: From Ancient Greek καλλίστη, feminine of κάλλιστος, superlative of καλός.

calvin.ety: Latinization of Norman-Picard Cauvin, a nickname for a chauve (“bald”) person.

cambria.ety: Medieval Latin Cambria, from Middle Welsh Kymry, from Proto-Brythonic *kömrüɣ, plural of *kömroɣ. Doublet of Cumberland and Cumbria and Cymru.

cambrie.ety: Variant spelling of Cambree with the suffix -ie.

camelia.ety: From Latin Camellia and Arabic كَامِيلِيَا.

cameron.ety: From Scottish Gaelic Camshròn, from cam (“crooked, bent”) + sròn (“nose”). Compare Campbell, from Scottish Gaelic cam (“crooked”) + beul (“mouth”).

camille.ety: From French Camille (“Camilla”). Doublet of Camilla.

campbell.ety: As a Scottish surname, from Scottish Gaelic Caimbeul, from cam (“crooked”) + beul (“mouth”). Compare Cameron, from Scottish Gaelic cam (“crooked”) + sròn (“nose”).

camélia.ety: From Latin Camellia and Arabic كَامِيلِيَا.

candi.ety: A less common spelling of Candy.

candice.ety: A variant of Candace associated with Late Latin candida (“whiteness”) via.

candida.ety: From Spanish Cándida,Candida, from Latin Candida, from candida, feminine of candidus (“shining white”).

candido.ety: Borrowed from Latin Candidus, name of various saints and others; see Candidus. From candidus (“shining white”).

capucine.ety: From capucine (“nasturtium”). First used as a stage name by a 20th century French actress.

cara.ety: 20th-century English coinage from Italian cara (“dear”) or Irish cara (“friend”).

carey.ety: As a German surname, Americanized from Gehrig, Gehring. As a Welsh surname, variant of Carew.

carina.ety: A spelling variant of Karina, a newer form of Katrina, ultimately from Ancient Greek Αἰκατερίνη (Aikaterínē, “female given name”).

carine.ety: Ultimately from Old Norse Kaðrina (“female given name”), a later form of Katrina (“female given name”), from Ancient Greek Αἰκατερίνη (Aikaterínē, “female given name”).

carita.ety: Latin caritas (“love”). First appeared in the end of the 19th century; possibly inspired by the older names Carina and Marita.

carl.ety: From Germanic, cognate with English Charles. From German and other north European Carl and Karl.

carleigh.ety: A rare spelling variant of Carly.

carlene.ety: A 20th-century coinage from Carl and the ending -ene, -lene, as in Marlene and Charlene.

carles.ety: Inherited from Latin Carolus, from Old High German Karl, from Proto-Germanic *karlaz.

carlisle.ety: From Middle English Carlele, from Middle English Carleol, Carleul, from Cumbric (compare Caer Ligualid in the Historia Brittonum, Middle Welsh Caer Liwelydd, Welsh Caerliwelydd, all suffixed with -ydd).

carly.ety: A feminine form of Carl with -y, taken to use in the latter half of the 20th century; also a pet form of Carla, Carlene and Carlotta.

carol.ety: Shortened from Caroline. Associated by folk etymology with the English noun carol.
carol.m: A round dance accompanied by singing.

carolanne.m: A round dance accompanied by singing.

carole.m: A round dance accompanied by singing.

caroline.ety: Borrowed in the 17th century from French Caroline, from Italian Carolina or its etymon Latin Carolīna, from Latin Carolus (“Charles”), from Middle High German Karl, + -īna. Doublet of Carolina.

carrol.m: A round dance accompanied by singing.

carroll.m: A round dance accompanied by singing.

carson.ety: Could originate from the Gaelic name "Carr" or "Carra", meaning "rock" or "fort," combined with "son", thus "son of Carr.".

carsten.ety: From a Middle Low German variant of Christian.

carter.ety: As an English name, from the occupation carter. As an Irish name, from Irish Mac Artúir, literally “son of Arthur”.

casey.ety: Anglicisation of an Irish surname Ó Cathasaigh, literally “descendant of (a person named) Watchful”.

cash.ety: Variant of Case. In the US adopted by German immigrants named Kirch and Kirsch.

casimir.ety: From a Polish royal name and saint's name Kazimierz, of Slavic origin, meaning "proclamation of peace".

cason.ety: As an English surname, a corruption of the place name Cawston in Norfolk. Also borrowed from Italian Cason, from a Venetan form of casa (“house”).

caspar.ety: An older spelling variant of Kaspar and Kasper, continuing Medieval Latin Caspar.

casper.ety: A spelling variant of Kasper, corresponding to Danish and Swedish Casper and Casper. Ultimately from Medieval Latin Caspar, traditionally the name of one of the Magi in Western Christianity.

cass.ety: As an English surname, from a pet form of Cassandra. As an Irish surname, from Ó Cais (“descendant of the curly-haired one”), from cas (“curly”).

cassandra.ety: From Ancient Greek Κασσάνδρα. The figurative noun sense Named after Cassandra.

cassian.ety: From Latin Cassianus, derivative of Cassius. Name of early saints.

cassidy.ety: From the Irish surname, Anglicized from Ó Caiside (“descendant of Caiside”), from cas (“curly-haired”).

cassie.ety: From Cass + -ie. A of Cassandra or Cassidy.

cassius.ety: Borrowed from Latin Cassius, a Roman name derived from the gens Cassia.

cataleya.ety: Modern coinage form the flower, popularized by a character in a 2011 film.

catalin.ety: Perhaps a masculine equivalent of the feminine given name Cătălina, a Romanian equivalent to Catherine, ultimately of Ancient Greek origin (Αἰκατερίνη). cf. also Ecaterina.

cathal.ety: From Old Irish Cathal, from Proto-Celtic *Katuwalos (“strong in battle”), cognate with Gaulish Katouualos, Old Welsh Catgual, Welsh Cadwal.

catherine.ety: Borrowed from French Catherine, from Ancient Greek Αἰκατερίνη, *Ἑκατερίνη, of debated meaning, possibly from ἑκάτερος (“each of the two”), or from the name of the goddess Hecate.

cato.ety: From Latin Cato. A cognomen made particularly famous by Cato the Elder and Younger, members of the gens Porcia.

cecil.ety: From Latin Caecilius, a Roman family name derived from caecus (“blind”). The surname has absorbed the Old Welsh Seisyllt, from Latin Sextilius, from Sextus.

cecile.ety: From French Cécile, from Anglo-Norman Cecile, from Latin Caecilia.

cedric.ety: Invented by Walter Scott for Ivanhoe, possibly misread for Cerdic, name of a Saxon king, anglicized from Welsh caredig (“beloved”).

celena.ety: Derived from Selene, the Greek goddess of the moon.

celestin.ety: Borrowed from French Célestin, from célestin (“celestine”). Doublet of Celestine.

celina.ety: Variant of Celine, from French Céline, ultimately from Latin.

celinda.ety: Probably a Blend of Celia + Linda.

celine.ety: From French Céline, from Latin Caelīna, derived from the Roman gens name Caelius, from caelum (“heaven”). Also a short form of Marceline, feminine diminutive of Marcel.

celso.ety: From Latin Celsus, from celsus (“high; elevated; noble”). Compare Sicilian Lu Ceusu.

cesar.ety: Anglicized spelling of Spanish César. Doublet of Caesar.

chad.ety: From Middle English Chadde, from Old English Ċeadda, of obscure meaning; name of a seventh-century Anglo-Saxon saint, revived in the 20th century.

chanel.ety: From French Chanel. As a given name, principally after Coco Chanel.

chantal.ety: Borrowed from French Chantal in the 1960s, from the surname of a French saint Jeanne de Chantal, actually a Baroness of Chantal, a place name in France from Old Occitan cantal (“stone, moellon, rubblestone”).

charisma.ety: From the common noun charisma, from Ancient Greek χάρισμα.
charisma.m: A gift or power of leadership or authority.

charity.ety: From charity in the Biblical sense of Christian love; first used by Puritans. In early Christian tradition, Faith, Hope and Charity were the martyred daughters of Saint Sophia.
charity.m: Christian; of those who believe in Christ.

charlene.ety: A feminine form of Charles coined in the nineteenth century. Compare Marlene, Helene and Magdalene for the suffix.

charles.ety: From French Charles, from Old French Charles, Carles, from Latin Carolus, from and also reinfluenced by Frankish and Old High German Karl, from Proto-Germanic *karilaz (“free man”); compare the English word churl and the German Kerl.

charlize.ety: Feminine form of Charles using the popular Afrikaans name suffix -ize. This name was popularized by South African actress Charlize Theron.

charlotte.ety: From French Charlotte in the 17th century, a female diminutive form of Charles, from Middle High German Karl, which came from the Germanic *karlaz.

charlène.ety: Borrowed from English Charlene Borrowed from English Charlene.

charmaine.ety: 20th century variant of Charmian, or coinage from the noun charm with the -aine ending as in Elaine and Germaine.

chauncey.ety: From the Norman name based on several locations in France called Chancé. See Old French chance.

chelsea.ety: From Old English Ċealchȳþ, from cealc (“chalk”) + hȳþ (“landing place”).

cheri.ety: A variant of Sherry or coined from French chéri, chérie (“darling”), not used as a given name in France.

cherif.ety: Borrowed from Arabic شَرِيف Borrowed from Arabic شَرِيف.

cheryl.ety: Coined in the early 20th century, possibly a blend of Cherie or Cherry and Beryl. (See cher for the etymology of Cherie.).

chesney.ety: From Norman place names meaning “oak grove” (cognate to French chênaie), from Picard quesne, from Vulgar Latin *cassanus, probably from Gaulish kassanos (“oak”).

chester.ety: From Middle English Chestre, from Old English Ċeaster, from ċeaster (“a town or city, especially a Roman one”).
chester.m: a town or city, especially a Roman one

chet.m: a town or city, especially a Roman one

cheyenne.ety: Borrowed from French Cheyenne, from Dakota šahíyena, from Dakota šaia (“to speak incoherently”), from Dakota ša (“red”) and Dakota ya (“to speak”).

china.ety: Thumb|240px|Flag of the People's Republic of China.

chloé.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek χλόη (“young green shoot”), an epithet of goddess Demeter.

christ.ety: Inherited from Middle High German Krist From Middle High German and Old High German Krist, from Latin Christus, from Ancient Greek Χριστός, a calque of Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ (māšīaḥ.

christa.ety: Contraction of Christina and Christiana. Rare until the second half of the 20th century, reinforced by the German Christa.

christer.ety: Variant of Christian through a medieval form Christiern.
christer.m: Christian; of those who believe in Christ.

christiana.ety: From Latin Chrīstiāna; a medieval literate form of the female name Christian. Christian + -a.
christiana.m: Christian; of those who believe in Christ.

christiane.m: Christian; of those who believe in Christ.

christianne.ety: Blend of Christian + Anne, coined as a feminine form of Christian.

christiano.m: Christian; of those who believe in Christ.

christina.ety: Name of an early martyr, shortened from Latin Chrīstiāna (“Christian (woman)”). Doublet of Kirsten.

christine.ety: Borrowed from French Christine. Doublet of Christina.

ciaran.ety: From Old Irish Cíarán, originally a byname from ciar (“black”) + -án. Popularized by Irish saints dating back from the 5th century.

cindi.m: Cynthian (of or relating to Mount Cynthus)

cindy.ety: Shortened from Lucinda and Cinderella. In the 20th century adopted as a pet form of Cynthia.
cindy.m: Cynthian (of or relating to Mount Cynthus)

cintia.m: Cynthian (of or relating to Mount Cynthus)

cinzia.ety: Latin Cynthia, from Ancient Greek Κυνθίᾱ; see there for more.
cinzia.m: Cynthian (of or relating to Mount Cynthus)

cirilo.ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin Cȳrillus.

ciro.ety: From Latin Cyrus, from Ancient Greek Κῦρος, from Old Persian 𐎤𐎢𐎽𐎢𐏁.

claes.ety: Variant of Claus, German short form of Nikolaus (“Nicholas”).

clair.ety: A less common spelling of Claire.

claire.ety: Borrowed from French Claire, also a spelling variant of the English Clare.

clarence.ety: Originally a ducal title of the English and British royal family, from Clārensis (“from the town of Clare”), (the town of Clare, Suffolk), although it has also been associated with Italian Chiarenza, Clarentza, &c.

claribel.ety: A fanciful variant of Clara, inspired by names like Annabel, Christabel and Isabel.

clarice.ety: Borrowed from French Clarisse, from Italian Clarissa, from Medieval Latin Clarissa (“Poor Clare”); see there for more. Doublet of Clarissa and Clarisse.

clarissa.ety: From Clara + -issa (“-ess”), from Old Italian Chiara Offreduccio, St. Clare of Assisi, the founder of the order, from Latin clarus (“clear, bright”).

clarisse.ety: Borrowed from French Clarisse, from Italian Clarissa, from Medieval Latin Clarissa (“Poor Clare”); see there for more. Doublet of Clarissa and Clarice.

clark.ety: From Old English clerc (“clergyman; learned man”), whence also clerk.

clarke.ety: From Clark, from Old English clerc (“cleric, clerk”).

claude.ety: In use from the 16th century. Borrowed from French Claude, from Latin Claudius, the name of a Roman gens.

claudius.ety: From Latin Claudius. Doublet of Claude.

claus.ety: From Dutch and German Claus, a contraction of Nicolaus (“Nicholas”). The spelling Klaus is from more modern German Klaus and other Germanic languages.

clay.ety: From a Middle English occupational name for a clay worker, or a habitational name, from Old English clǣġ (“clay”).

clayton.ety: From Middle English Claytone, Cleyton, from Old English clǣġ (“clay”) + Old English tūn (“enclosure, settlement; town”). Analyzable as clay + -ton.

clemence.ety: From clemence, from Latin clēmentia (“mercy; mildness”).

clemens.ety: From Late Latin Clēmēns (genitive Clēmentis), name of early saints and popes, from clēmēns (“merciful”). Doublet of Clement and San Clemente.

clementine.ety: From French Clémentine, from Latin Clēmentīna, from Clēmens (genitive Clēmentis), from clēmens (“merciful”). Clement + -ine.

cleo.ety: Shortened from Cleopatra or a variant of Clio. The rare male name derives from names of Ancient Greek origin such as Cleon and Cleopas.

cleon.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Κλέων, from κλέω (“to recount, celebrate”).

cleopatra.ety: From Middle English Cleopatra, from Latin Cleopatra, from Ancient Greek Κλεοπάτρα, meaning "glory of her father", from κλέος (“glory”) + πατήρ (“father”).

cletus.ety: Borrowed from Latin Clētus, short form of the papal name Anaclētus, from Ancient Greek ἀνάκλητος (“invoked”).

cliff.ety: The given name is from shortenings of the diminutives. The surname is from the noun cliff.
cliff.m: A vertical (or nearly vertical) rock face.

clifford.ety: From Old English clif (“cliff”) + ford (“ford”), a dweller at the ford by the steep bank.

clifton.ety: Literally meaning "town by a cliff." From Old English clif (“cliff”) + tūn (“town”). Analyzable as cliff + -ton.

clinton.ety: A habitational surname, derived from places named Glinton ("town on a hill") or Glympton ("settlement on the River Glyme"), from Old English + tun (“enclosure, homestead, town”), equivalent to the modern -ton.

clotilde.ety: From Spanish Clotilde, from Proto-Germanic *Hlūdahildiz, from *hlūdaz (“famous”) + *hildiz (“battle”).

clovis.ety: Borrowed from French Clovis, from Frankish *Hlōdowig, the same Germanic source as French Louis, Dutch Lodewijk and German Ludwig, see there for further information. Doublet of Louis and Ludwig.

clyde.ety: From Scottish Gaelic Cluaidh, the name of a river in Scotland, of uncertain origin. Possibly influenced by clut (“the cleansing one”).

clélia.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Cloelia Latin Cloelia.

coco.ety: From the Italian Coco, a surname derived from Sicilian cocu (“cook”).

coen.ety: Variant of Cohen. As a modern given name, also a variant of Koen.

colby.ety: From either the Old Norse personal name Koli or kol (“charcoal”) + býr (“settlement”).

cole.ety: The surname is variously from: # A nickname from Old English col (“coal, coal-black”), # A patronymic from Nicholas (see also Coles, Colson.

colin.ety: Coll + -in. diminutive of Coll, a medieval short form of Nicholas. It has also been used to anglicize Irish Coileán and Scottish Gaelic Cailean.

colleen.ety: From the word colleen, from Irish cailín (“girl”), not used as a name in Ireland.

collin.ety: A spelling variant of Colin. From a medieval diminutive of Coll, a diminutive of Nicholas.

collins.ety: As an English surname, variant of Colin. As an Irish and Manx surname, from Ó Coileáin (“descendant of Coileán”), see Cullen, McQuillan, and McCallion.

colt.ety: From colt, as a nickname or occupational name for someone who looked after horses and asses. The given name may also be short for Colton.
colt.m: A juvenile equid or camel; a colt.

columbus.ety: From Latin columbus From Latin columbus (“a dove”). Doublet of Colombo.

come.ety: Compare French Côme and Catalan Cosme.

conan.ety: From Irish Conán, from Middle Irish Conán, from Primitive Irish ᚉᚑᚅᚐᚅᚅ, a derivative of Proto-Celtic *kū (“dog”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwṓ.

conceicao.ety: From (Maria da) Conceição (“Mary of the Conception”), after (Our Lady of the) Immaculate Conception.

concepcion.ety: From concepción (“conception”), shortened from María (de la Inmaculada) Concepción, a Roman Catholic epithet of the Virgin Mary as "Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception".

conley.ety: Anglicization of Irish Ó Conghalaigh and Ó Conghaile, patronyms of Conghalach. Doublet of Connolly.

connor.ety: The first name is from Irish Conchúr, Conchobhar, from Old Irish Conchobar (“lover of hounds”). The surname is from Irish Ó Conchúir (“descendant of Conchúr”).

conor.ety: From Irish Conchúr, from Old Irish Conchobar (“lover of hounds”).

conrad.ety: A variant of German Konrad, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *Kōnirād, from *kōnī (“bold, brave”) + *rād (“counsel”). Cognate of Old English Cēnrēd, Dutch Koenraad and Icelandic Konráð.

consolacion.ety: Consolación (“consolation”), shortened from María (de la) Consolación, a Roman Catholic epithet of the Virgin Mary as "Our Lady of Consolation".

constance.ety: From Latin Cōnstantia Doublet of Constantia.

constantin.ety: From French and Romanian Constantin, from Latin Cōnstantīnus, q.v. Doublet of Constantine and Konstadinos and Kostas and Costas.

constantina.ety: From Latin Cōnstantīna and Greek Κωνσταντίνα.

constantine.ety: From Latin Cōnstantīnus From Latin Cōnstantīnus, from Constans and Constantius + -inus (“-ine: forming adjectives and patronymics”), from Latin cōnstāns (“constant, steadfast”) with and without -ius (“-y: forming adjectives”).

consuela.ety: From Spanish Consuela, a variant of Consuelo.

cora.ety: Apparently brought up in English literature by James Fenimore Cooper in The Last of the Mohicans (1826).

coralie.ety: Coined in France in the end of the 18th century, from Latin corallium (“coral”).

coraline.ety: An elaborate form of Coralie, itself derived from coral. Name of a character in Adolphe Adam's opera Le toréador.

corbin.ety: An Anglo-Norman nickname from corb (“crow”), or shortened from the Corbinian, the name of a Frankish eighth-century saint, probably from Latin corvus (“crow, raven”).

cordelia.ety: Shakespeare's spelling of a historical British name appearing as Cordeilla, etc., possibly derived from the Latin saint's name Cordula.

corentin.ety: Borrowed from Breton Kaourantin Borrowed from Breton Kaourantin.

corinna.ety: From Ancient Greek, probably from κόρη (“girl, maid, daughter”); compare kore.

corinne.ety: From the French equivalent of Corinna, from Ancient Greek κόρη (“girl, maiden, daughter”).

cormac.ety: Borrowed from Irish, from Old Irish Cormac.

cornelia.ety: From Latin Cornēlia, name of a famous Roman matron, feminine form of the gens name Cornelius; in continental Europe, also a feminine form of the saint's name Cornelius.

cornell.ety: From Cornwall, spelling conflated with the Latin family name Cornelius.

corrie.ety: From Scottish Gaelic coire (“cauldron, boiler; corrie”), which denotes a bowl-shaped geographical feature similar to a cirque.

cosma.ety: From Italian and Romanian Cosma, from Latin Cosmas, from Ancient Greek Κοσμᾶς, from κόσμος (“world, cosmos”) + -ᾶς. Doublet of Cosmo and Cosmas.

cosmo.ety: Borrowed by Scotland from Italy in the 18th century.

courtney.ety: Variant of Courtenay, an aristocratic Norman surname derived from place names in Normandy, from Latin Curtenus, a personal name from curtus (“short”).

creed.ety: From the Old English personal name Creoda.

crew.ety: From Crewe in Cheshire, Old Welsh criu (“weir”).

cris.ety: Short form of Christopher, Christian, Christine, and their variants.

crispin.ety: From Latin Crispinus, derivative of the Roman family name Crispus (“curly”).

cristovao.ety: Inherited from Latin Chrīstophanus, variant of Chrīstophorus, from Ancient Greek Χριστόφορος. Doublet of Cristóforo and Christopher.

curtis.ety: From Old French corteis and curteis (Modern French courtois (“polite, courteous”). Doublet of courteous.

cyndi.m: Cynthian (of or relating to Mount Cynthus)

cyndie.m: Cynthian (of or relating to Mount Cynthus)

cynthia.ety: Borrowed from Latin Cynthia, from Ancient Greek Κυνθία, feminine of Κύνθιος (“Cynthian (of or pertaining to Mount Cynthus, a mountain of Delos, celebrated as the birthplace of Apollo and Artemis)”).
cynthia.m: Cynthian (of or relating to Mount Cynthus)

cyriaque.ety: From Latin Cyriacus, from Koine Greek Κυριακός (“Belonging to the Lord”).

cyril.ety: Via Late Latin Cȳrillus, from Ancient Greek Κύριλλος, from κύριος (“lord, master”).

cyrill.ety: From Late Latin Cȳrillus, from Ancient Greek Κύριλλος.

cécilia.ety: Borrowed from Latin Caecilia, female form of Caecilius, a Roman family name derived from the byname caecus (“blind”).

célia.m: heaven (where the stars and the Milky Way is)

césar.ety: Inherited from Middle French Cæsar, borrowed from Latin Caesar. Doublet of tsar.

côme.ety: Compare French Côme and Catalan Cosme.

daenerys.ety: Coined by Q181677. From the name of a character in George R.

dag.ety: From Old Norse Dagr, from dagr (“day”), whence also dag. Cognate with Dagur and Dag.

dagfinn.ety: Old Norse Dagfinnr, from dagr "day" + Finnr "Finn, Sami".

dahlia.ety: From the flower dahlia in the 19th century.

daiana.ety: From the pronunciation of English Diana.

daisy.ety: From the flower daisy, one of the flower names dating from the 19th century. Also a nickname for Margaret, since Marguerite and Margarita are identical with the French and Spanish word for "daisy".

dalila.ety: Borrowed from Latin Dalila, itself ultimately from Biblical Hebrew דְּלִילָה (D'līla).

dallas.ety: # The Texas city was named after George M.
dallas.m: dweller at the house in the dale

dalton.m: A valley, often in an otherwise hilly area.

damian.ety: From the Ancient Greek name Δαμιανός which was derived from δαμάω (“to tame”) (see δαμάζω). Name known in Ancient Greece, later borne by Christian saints.

damon.ety: From Ancient Greek Δάμων, a name famous for the story of Damon and Pythias; derivative of δαμάζω (“to tame, subdue”).

dane.ety: From Middle English Dane, from Old Norse danir or Old English Dene. Both forms ultimately descend from Proto-Germanic *daniz.

danica.ety: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dьnьnica (“morning star”), from *dьnь (“day”) + *-ьnъ (“-ish”) + *-ica. dȃn + -ica.

daniell.ety: Alternative form of Albanian Danjell (“Daniel”); from Latin Dāniēl (from Ancient Greek Δᾱνῑήλ, from Hebrew דָּנִיֵּאל).

danielle.ety: Borrowed from French Danielle, the feminine form of Daniel.

danika.ety: A spelling variant of Danica, a female given name of Slavic origin.

danil.ety: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic Данїилъ.

danna.ety: As a surname from French D'Anna (“of Anna”). The given name is more probably a feminine form coined from Dan or Daniel.

dannie.ety: From Daniel or Daniella; from Hebrew דן, and archaic English -ie.

danny.ety: From Dan (“diminutive of Daniel and Danielle”) + -y, from Hebrew דן.

dany.ety: Short form of Daniel and Danielle.

darby.ety: From the English place name Derby, from Old Norse djúr (“deer”) + býr (“settlement”).

darcy.ety: Originally from Bois-d'Arcy, Yvelines in Northern France. Related to archaic French ardre (“to burn, consume”).

dari.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Dārius Latin Dārius.

daria.ety: Feminine form of Darius, of Old Persian origin. Name of an early Christian saint.

darian.ety: A 20th-century invention, possibly based on Darius or Dorian.

dario.ety: Borrowed from Italian Dario and Spanish Darío.

dariusz.ety: Latin Dārīus, from Ancient Greek Δᾱρεῖος, from Old Persian 𐎭𐎠𐎼𐎹𐎢𐏁, shortened form of 𐎭𐎠𐎼𐎹𐎺𐎢𐏁.

darko.ety: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *darъ (“gift”), from Proto-Indo-European *déh₃rom, and suffix -ko.

darleen.m: : a person who is very dear to one.

darlene.ety: A 20th-century coinage from darling and names like Charlene and Marlene.

darline.m: : a person who is very dear to one.

darling.m: : a person who is very dear to one.

darnell.ety: English surname, from the noun darnel (“type of ryegrass”). Also a variant of Darnall.

darrell.ety: Derived from d'Airel, name of a Norman family that came from a place called Airelle in Calvados.

darren.ety: Of unknown origin. A twentieth-century invention, possibly from a rare Irish surname of obscure meaning, possibly from Dara or Daragh, meaning "oak".

darwin.ety: From Middle English Darwin, Derwin, from Old English Dēorwine, composed of dēore (“dear”) + wine (“friend”). The city in Australia is named after Charles Darwin.

davion.ety: The modern American usage is possibly transferred from the French surname Davion, based on a Provençal diminutive of David. It is not used as a given name in France.

dawid.ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin Dāvīd.

dawn.m: To begin to brighten with daylight.

dawna.m: To begin to brighten with daylight.

dawson.ety: From Daw, a Middle English pet form of David + -son.

daxton.ety: Modern American coinage, rhyming with Axton, Paxton, Jaxton.

daya.ety: Borrowed from Sanskrit दया (“pity, mercy, compassion”).

deacon.ety: English occupational surname for someone working in the household of a deacon. Also as an English surname, variant of Dicken.

dean.ety: The surname or given name is of multiple origins, depending on context.

deane.ety: As an Irish surname, Anglicized from Mac an Deagánaigh (“son of the Deacon”), see Deacon. As an English surname, variant of Dean.

debra.ety: A spelling variant of Deborah first used in the 20th century.

decio.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Decius Latin Decius.

declan.ety: From Old Irish Declán, whence the modern Irish equivalent Deaglán.

deirdre.ety: From Irish Deirdre, from Old Irish Derdriu.

deividas.ety: Borrowed from English David, according to Lithuanian pronunciation respelling.

delaney.ety: From a Norman baronial surname, from a place in France, Old French del aunaie (“from the alder grove”).

della.ety: Possibly a variant of Adela or Delia. First appeared in the 19th century.

delmar.ety: Contraction of Delamare and de la Mare, from places in Normandy named La Mare (“the pond”). In the US, also borrowed from Catalan del Mar (“of the sea”).

delphine.ety: French form of Latin Delphina, meaning woman from Delphi; Delphine of Glandèves was a 14th century nun from Provence.

demetria.m: belonging to Δημήτηρ, the earth goddess

demetrio.ety: Borrowed from Latin Demetrius, from Ancient Greek Δημήτριος.
demetrio.m: belonging to Δημήτηρ, the earth goddess
