demetrios.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Δημήτριος Borrowed from Ancient Greek Δημήτριος.
demetrios.m: belonging to Δημήτηρ, the earth goddess

denise.ety: From French Denise, from Latin Dionȳsia. Dionysus is the mythological Greek god of wine responsible for growth of the vines and the originator of winemaking.

dennis.ety: From Middle English Denis, from Old French saint's name Denis, brought to England by Normans; from Latin Dionysius, a masculine name literally meaning “follower of (the wine god) Dionysus”.

denton.ety: From Old English denu (“valley, den”) + tūn (“enclosure; settlement, town”).

denver.ety: From Old English Dene, from Old English fær, from Old English denu, from Old English ofer Named after James W.

derek.ety: Borrowed in the Middle Ages from a Middle Low German variant of Theodoric, and revived in the 19th century.

dermot.ety: From Irish Diarmaid. Doublet of Jeremy.

desamparados.ety: From desamparados (“defenseless ones”), shortened from María (de los) Desamparados, a Roman Catholic epithet of the Virgin Mary as "Our Lady of the Helpless" in Valencia.

destiny.ety: From the noun destiny since the 1970s.

devon.ety: From Old English Defenas, which meant both "Devonians" and "Devon," exemplifying the common Anglo-Saxon practice of naming a place after the people who inhabit it.

dewey.ety: Possibly from a place name in Northern France, Douai. Welsh origin from Dewi (David) has also been suggested.

dewitt.ety: From Dutch de Witt. The verb sense alludes to the 17th-century assassination by lynching of Dutch politicians Cornelis de Witt and Johan de Witt.

dexter.ety: Variant of Dyster. Also partially from Latin dexter (“right (handed)”).

diamond.ety: As a female given name, from diamond. As a German surname, Anglicized form of Diamant.

diane.ety: An anglicization of French Diane, from Latin Diāna. Doublet of Diana.

didac.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Didacus Latin Didacus.

didier.ety: Inherited from Latin Desiderius, from desiderium (“desire, longing”).

dieter.ety: From Old High German thiot (“people”) + heri (“army”).

dietrich.ety: Inherited from Middle High German Dietrich, from Old High German Diotrih, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *Þeudōrīks.

dilan.ety: Variation of Dylan, originally from Welsh.

dillon.ety: From the Irish surname, from Breton Leon and Norman Léon, named after Sir Henry de Leon of the Viscounty of Léon. Related to the surname Lyon.

dima.ety: From Russian Ди́ма, a diminutive of the male given name Дми́трий (“Demetrius”).
dima.m: belonging to Δημήτηρ, the earth goddess

dimitra.ety: Transliteration of Greek Δήμητρα, a female given name used in modern Greece.

dimitry.ety: From Russian Дмитрий from Ancient Greek Δημήτριος.

dina.ety: Equivalent of the biblical name Dinah in several European languages, ultimately from Hebrew דִּינָה.

dinis.ety: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese Denis, from Old French Denis, from Latin Dionȳsius, from Ancient Greek Διονύσιος. Cognate with Sicilian Dinisi.

diogenes.ety: From Latin Diogenēs, from Ancient Greek Διογένης.

diogo.ety: The Portuguese equivalent of Spanish Diego, from Old Galician-Portuguese Diago, from Latin Didacus.

dion.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Δίων. Also a medieval English and French diminutive of Dionysius (Dennis).

dione.ety: From Latin Diōnē (“of Jupiter”), from Ancient Greek Διώνη (“of Zeus”).

dionisio.ety: From Spanish Dionisio. A reference to Dionysius the Areopagite.

dionne.ety: From French Dionne From Latin Dione, from Ancient Greek Διώνη.

dirk.ety: Borrowed from Dutch and North German Dirk.

dixie.ety: Of unknown origin, but may come from the Mason-Dixon line, the boundary between the northern states and the southern states, or from the slang term dixie for a Louisiana $10 bill (equivalent to English tenner).

dmitry.ety: From Russian Дми́трий, from Medieval Greek Δημήτριος, from Δημήτηρ (“Demeter”) + -ιος (“pertaining to”). Doublet of Demetrius and Dimitri and Dimitris.

dock.ety: As an English surname, possibly from the noun duck. As a Norwegian surname, from Old Norse dǫkk (“pit, depression”), from Proto-Germanic *dankwaz (“dark”).

dominic.ety: From Late Latin Dominicus, derived from Dominus (“Lord”).

dominica.ety: Used for the island of Dominica since it was sighted by Christopher Columbus on a Sunday.

dominique.ety: From French Dominique. Doublet of Dominic.

donna.ety: A 19th-century invention from the Italian noun donna; also interpreted as a feminine form of Donald.

donovan.ety: From Irish Ó Donndubháin (“descendant of (a person named) brown & black”), from donn (“brown”) and dubh (“black”).
donovan.m: descendant of (a person named) brown & black

dora.ety: A diminutive of Dorothy used since early 19th century. Sometimes also short for Theodora or Isidora.

dorcas.ety: From Ancient Greek Δορκάς (“gazelle”), translation of Tabitha in the Bible.

dorian.ety: Constructed like the French Doriens. From the Latin root of Dōres + -ian.

dorinda.ety: An 18th-century coinage from Dora or Dorothy, -inda.

doris.ety: From Ancient Greek Δωρίς. is owing to similarity to Boris.

dorothee.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Δωροθέα Borrowed from Ancient Greek Δωροθέα.

dorothy.ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Δωροθέα.

dorothée.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Δωροθέα Borrowed from Ancient Greek Δωροθέα.

douglas.ety: From a place name, Scottish Gaelic dubh (“black”) + glais (“stream”).

drake.ety: As an English surname, from both senses of the noun drake meaning "male duck" and "dragon." As a German surname, from Low German drake (“dragon”), related to the above.

drew.ety: From Anglo-Norman Drew, Drieu, Drue, from Old French Drogon, Dreus, Drues (made popular by Charlemagne's son Drogo) from Old Dutch Drogo, of uncertain ultimate origin.

duane.ety: Anglicized form of the Irish name Dubhán (from Primitive Irish ᚇᚑᚃᚐᚌᚅᚔ), from dubh (“black, dark”); or transferred from the surname, which is from Irish Ó Dubháin, literally “descendant of Dubhán”.

duarte.ety: An apheresis of earlier Eduarte, from Middle English Edward. Doublet of Eduardo.

dudley.ety: From Old English, literally "wood or clearing of Dudda (a personal name of unknown meaning)".

dulcie.ety: From Latin dulcis (“sweet”) in the 19th century, probably inspired by earlier names like Dowsabel and Spanish Dulcinea.

dulcinea.ety: Miguel de Cervantes coined this name in his satirical quest novel The Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha, giving the name to Don Quixote's mistress.

dumitru.ety: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic Дьмитръ.

duncan.ety: As a Scottish Gaelic and Irish surname, from Donnchadh, a name composed of donn (“brown”) + cath (“battle”). Also spelled as Donagh and Donaghue, Donahue.

dustin.ety: Probably from Old Norse Þorsteinn (“Thor's stone”).

dwight.ety: Probably from a Middle English female name Diot, a pet form of Dionysia, the feminine form of Dionysius.

dzianis.ety: Transliteration of Дзяні́с. Ultimately from Ancient Greek Διονύσιος.

dzmitry.ety: Transliteration of Дзмі́трый. From Latin Demetrius, from Ancient Greek Δημήτριος, from Δημήτηρ (“Demeter”).
dzmitry.m: belonging to Δημήτηρ, the earth goddess

eamon.ety: Borrowed from Irish Éamann (“Edmund”). Doublet of Edmund.

ean.ety: From Manx Ean, an equivalent of John.

eartha.ety: 19th-century coinage from earth + -a. Best known for the American singer Eartha Kitt.

easton.ety: From Old English ēast (“east”) + tūn (“settlement”). Doublet of Aston.

ebba.ety: From a German diminutive of female given names beginning with the Germanic element Eber- "boar". Also interpreted as a feminine form of Ebbe.

eben.ety: Shortened from Ebenezer; equivalent to Hebrew אֶבֶן (éven, “stone”).

ebenezer.ety: From Hebrew אֶבֶן הָעֵזֶר (éven ha`ézer, “stone of help”).

ebony.ety: First used by African Americans in the 1970s.

eda.ety: From Old English ead (“riches”), also short for compound given names beginning thus, particularly Edith.

edgar.ety: From Old English Ēadgār, the name of early English kings, from Old English ēad (“rich”) + gār (“spear”). Compare Icelandic Auðgeir.

edmund.ety: From Old English Ēadmund, from ēad (“prosperity”) + mund (“protection”). Doublet of Eamon.

edna.ety: From Hebrew עֶדְנָה (“pleasure; delight”); a variant of Eden in the Book of Tobit.

ednaldo.ety: From a Germanic language name meaning "he who governs his riches", from Proto-Germanic *audaz (“riches, wealth”) + *waldą (“power, authority”). Related to Edvaldo and Eduardo.

edouard.ety: From Old French Edward, from Old English Ēadweard, from Proto-West Germanic *Audawardu, from Proto-Germanic *Audawarduz.

edric.ety: From Old English Ēadrīc, from Proto-West Germanic *Audarīk, from Proto-Germanic *Audarīks, from *audaz (“wealth, riches”) + *rīks (“king, ruler”).

edrick.ety: From Old English Ēadrīc, from Proto-Germanic *Audarīks, from *audaz (“wealth, riches”) + *rīks (“king, ruler”).

edsel.ety: The automobile marque is Named after Edsel Ford, son of Henry Ford. Compare German Etzel.

edson.ety: From Ed + -son; originally given to the son of a man named Ed.

eduard.ety: From French Édouard, doublet of Edward.

edvaldo.ety: From a Germanic language name meaning "the power of wealth", from Proto-Germanic *audaz (“riches, wealth”) + *waldą (“power, authority”). Cognate with Icelandic Eðvald.

edvard.ety: Borrowed from English Edward, from Old English Ēadweard, from Proto-West Germanic *Audawardu, from Proto-Germanic *Audawarduz, composed of *audaz (“wealth, riches”) and *warduz (“guard, guardian”).

edwin.ety: Inherited from Old English Ēadwine, from Proto-West Germanic *Audawini, from Proto-Germanic *Audawiniz.

edwina.ety: Female form of Edwin from Old English, equivalent to Edwin + -a.

edy.ety: From Middle English Udy, Ude, Latinized as Udo and Odo.

effie.ety: From Euphemia + -ie, or, very rarely, from modern Greek Eftychia or Euthemia (diminutive form).

efrain.ety: Anglicized spelling of Spanish Efraín. Doublet of Ephraim.

efrem.ety: Borrowed from Biblical Hebrew אֶפְרַיִם (Efráyim, “Ephraim”), literally “fruitful”.

egidio.ety: Inherited from Late Latin Aegīdius Inherited from Late Latin Aegīdius.

egil.ety: From Old Norse Egill, from Proto-Germanic *Agilaz. From given names beginning with the element age "awe" or egg "edge, point (of a weapon)".

egon.ety: Variant of Egino, diminutive of Germanic compound names beginning with the element Egin-, from *agi (“awe”), later merged with Old High German ekka (“sharp point”) (from *aggju).

eigil.ety: From Old Danish Eghil, from Old Norse Egill, from Proto-Germanic *Agilaz. Cognate to Norwegian Egil, related to German Egon.

eila.ety: Possibly a variant of Norwegian Eili, a rare form of Eli (“Helen”), or from English Eileen. Popularized by the novel Tuskaa (1907) by Väinö Kataja.

eileen.ety: From Anglicized forms of Irish Eibhlín, Eilín or Aibhilín in Middle English and Modern English, all cognates of Doublet of Evelyn from Old French Aveline.

einar.ety: From Old Norse Einarr, from Proto-Germanic *ainaz (“one”) and *harjaz (“warrior”). Doublet of einherje.

eira.ety: From an Old Norse goddess of medicine, Eir, eir (“relief”).

eirik.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Eiríkr (“male given name”), from Proto-Norse *Aina-rīkijaʀ (“sole ruler”) or *Aiwa-rīkijaʀ (“everlasting ruler”).

eivind.ety: From Old Norse Eivindr, a variant of Eyvindr, from Proto-Norse *ᚨᚢᛃᚨᚹᛁᚾᛞᚢᛉ, from Proto-Germanic *awją (“luck, fortune”) + *winduz (“winner”), or a younger compound of ey (either in the sense of or ) and -vindr (“winner”).

eivor.ety: From Old Norse Eyvǫr, from a first part probably meaning "luck" ( same as in Eivind) + vǫr (“careful”).

elaine.ety: From Old French Elaine, a variant of Elene, cognate to Helen, ultimately from Ancient Greek Ἑλένη. A Celtic origin has also been suggested since the name appears in Arthurian legend.

elbert.ety: A cognate of the more common Albert.

eldbjørg.ety: Newer combination of eld (“fire”) + bjørg (“salvation, help”). Cognate with Faroese Eldbjørg and Eldbjörg.

eleanor.ety: The first known bearer was Eleanor of Aquitaine (1122–1204), Provençal Aliénor, perhaps from Latin alia (“other”) and her mother's name Aenor, its meaning thereby said to be “the other Aenor”.

elenilda.ety: Brazilian creation, a phonetical blend of Helena and the root -ilda (in comparision to names like Matilda, Brunilda, etc., from Proto-Germanic *hildiz).

elenita.ety: Borrowed from Spanish, diminutive of Elena.

eleuterio.ety: From Latin Eleutherius, from Ancient Greek Ἐλευθέριος, literally “liberator”.

eliane.ety: From Latin Aeliana, feminine derivative of the plebeian gens name Aelius.
eliane.m: of pertaining to the gens Aelia.

elie.ety: Variously a form of Elijah used in Romanian, French, and some other languages, or short for names like Eliezer.

elin.ety: Medieval variant of Helene (Helen), comparable to English Ellen.

elis.ety: Short form of Eliisabet or Elisabeth.

elisabeth.ety: The spelling of Elizabeth used in the Authorized Version of the New Testament. Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἐλισάβετ, a transliteration of Hebrew אֱלִישֶׁבַע (Elishéva, “my God is an oath”).

elise.ety: From French Élise or German Elise, both variants of Elisabeth.

elissa.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἔλῐσσᾰ; probably from Phoenician 𐤀𐤋𐤀𐤎𐤕, 𐤀𐤋𐤀𐤎.

elita.ety: Possibly from French élite (“elite”), or a phonetic coinage.

elizabete.ety: Ultimately from Hebrew. Cognate with English Elizabeth.

ella.ety: A 19th-century shortening of Eleanor or Ellen, later also used for any name ending in -ella, such as Gabriella or Daniella.

ellen.ety: Medieval English variant of Helen, from Ancient Greek Ἑλένη; also used as a variant of Eleanor or a feminine counterpart to Elliot.

elli.ety: Diminutive of Elina (“Helen”), later also Eleonoora (“Eleanor”) and likely of Elisabet.

ellinor.ety: A rare spelling variant of Elinor or Eleanor.

elliott.ety: English surname derived from a Middle English diminutive of Elie, Old French form of Elias or Elijah, meaning "my God is Yahweh".

ellis.ety: As an English surname, from the Middle English personal name Elis, an Old French form of Elias. Compare Elijah, Lias, Ely.

elma.ety: A 19th-century creation, usually explained as a form of Wilhelmina or Italian Guglielma. It has also been recorded as a blend of Elizabeth and Mary.

elmer.ety: Medieval variant of the given name Aylmer, from Old English Æþelmǣr, from æþel (“noble”) + mǣre (“famous”).

elmo.ety: From an Italian contraction of Erasmo, cognate with Erasmus. Also a German short form of Elmar.

elodie.ety: From the Spanish saint's name Alodia.

eloi.ety: From French Éloi, from Medieval Latin Eligius, chiefly after Saint Eligius, from Latin ēligere (“to pick, to choose from”) + -ius (“-y: forming adjectives and names”).
eloi.m: to pick, to choose from + -y: forming adjectives and names

elois.ety: From French Éloïse, from the Medieval Latin and French forms that gave rise to its doublet Doublet of Heloise.

eloise.ety: From Éloi + -se (“-ess: feminizing nouns”), from Medieval Latin Eligius, chiefly after Saint Eligius, from Latin ēligere (“to pick, to choose from”) + -ius (“-y: forming adjectives and names”).

elouise.ety: Alternative form of Eloise, influenced by Louise.

eloïse.ety: From Éloi + -se (“-ess: feminizing nouns”), from Medieval Latin Eligius, chiefly after Saint Eligius, from Latin ēligere (“to pick, to choose from”) + -ius (“-y: forming adjectives and names”).

elroy.ety: Derived from Leroy, but with the le in "Leroy" being replaced with its corresponding equivalent in Spanish el.

elsa.ety: Borrowed from German Elsa From German Elsa, contraction of Elisabeth, occasionally used in English after its appearance in Wagner's opera Lohengrin (1847).

else.ety: Contraction of Elisabeth. Cognate with German Elsa.

elsi.ety: From English Elsie, though it may be also be a Finnish diminutive form of Elsa.

elsie.ety: From a Scottish diminutive of Alison/Alice and Elspeth/Elizabeth.

elton.ety: From a number of sources, including: # For the places in Cheshire, County Durham, and Derbyshire, England: from Old English ēl (“eel”) + tūn (“farm, village”) since the village is situated above a small stream.

elvio.ety: From Latin Helvius, name of a plebeian Roman gens.

elvira.ety: A medieval Spanish royal name, of probably Gothic origin, and debated meaning, possibly 𐌲𐌰𐌹𐌻𐌾𐌰𐌽 + *𐍅𐌴𐍂𐌴𐌹, thus "joyful sincerity".

elvis.ety: From the anglicisation of the Irish name of Saint Ailbe (Saint Elvis), also known as Saint Eilfyw or Eilfw. Ultimate origin is.

elwira.ety: From Italian Elvira, from Spanish Elvira.

elwood.ety: From the Middle English personal name Elwald, Elwold, Alwold, which is composed of the Old English elements ælf (“elf”) and weald (“rule”).

ely.ety: Inherited from Middle English Ely, from Old English Ēlīġ, of uncertain origin.

elyse.ety: A rare spelling variant of Elise. By folk etymology, connected to Elysium.

emer.ety: From Old Irish Emer; cognate with Irish Eimhear and Scottish Gaelic Eimhir.

emeric.ety: Taken from Proto-Germanic *haimaz (“home”) + *rīkiją (“ruler”); cf. *Haimarīks. Cognate to French Henri and English Emery or Henry.

emery.ety: From medieval Germanic personal names, either a variant of Amory, from Amalric, Proto-Germanic *amal (“vigor, bravery”) (compare *ammōną) + Old High German rīhhi (“ruler”), or of Henry, from Old High German Heimrich.

emeterio.ety: From Latin Emeterius, name of a Roman legionary and martyr.

emil.ety: From German Emil, from Latin Aemilius, a Roman family name possibly from aemulus (“rival”). Cognate with French Émile.
emil.m: striving to equal or excel, rivaling

emile.m: striving to equal or excel, rivaling

emilee.ety: Modern variant of Emily, influenced by Lee.

emili.m: striving to equal or excel, rivaling

emilie.ety: A Norwegian variant of Emilia, ultimately from Latin Aemilia (“female given name”), the feminine form of the Roman nomen Aemilius.

emilien.ety: From Latin Aemilianus, a derivative of Aemilius.

emilija.ety: Ultimately from Latin Aemilia. Cognate with English Emily.

emily.ety: English form of Latin Aemilia, a gens name from aemulus (“rival, emulator”).

emilyn.ety: Blend of Emy + Lyn, or a similar construct.

emmalyn.ety: From Emma + Lyn or a variant of Emmeline.

emmalynn.ety: From Emma + -lynn or a variant of Emmeline.

emmeline.ety: Medieval English form of Old French Ameline, diminutive form of Amélie, cognate to English Amelia.

emmet.ety: From a Middle English diminutive of the female given name Emma.

emmett.ety: From a Middle English diminutive of the female given name Emma.

emmi.ety: Originally a diminutive of Emilia and Emma.

emmitt.ety: From a Middle English diminutive of the female given name Emma.

emre.ety: From Old Turkic (amran-, “to love, desire”). Also related to Old Turkic (amrıl-, “to be quiet”), (amul, “gentle, quiet”), derived from Proto-Turkic *ăm-.

emrys.ety: From Proto-Brythonic *Ėmrös, from Latin Ambrosius, from Ancient Greek ἀμβρόσιος (“immortal, divine”).

ena.ety: Of unknown origin. Several origins have been proposed..

encarnacion.ety: From encarnación (“incarnation”), shortened from María (de la) Encarnación, a Roman Catholic epithet of the Virgin Mary.

engelbert.ety: From Middle Dutch *Enghelbert, from Old Dutch *Engilberht. Equivalent to engel (“angel, Angle”) + Brecht (“bright - now only found as personal name”).
engelbert.m: angel, Angle + bright - now only found as personal name

enid.ety: From Middle Welsh eneit (“spirit, life; purity”), from Proto-Celtic *anatyom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁- (“to breathe, blow”).

enola.ety: Created for the titular character in the 1886 American novel Enola, derived from alone spelled backwards.

enver.ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish انور (Enver), from Arabic أَنْوَر.

enza.ety: From Enzo + -a, ultimately of Germanic origin.

epifania.ety: Directly borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐπιφάνεια.

erasmo.ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Erasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐράσμιος (“pleasant”); name of an early Christian martyr.

eric.ety: From Middle English Eric, from Old English Eoric, from Old Norse Eirríkr, Eiríkr, or from Proto-Germanic *Aizarīkijaz.

erica.ety: A feminine form of Eric, ultimately from Old Norse. The name has also been associated with the flower genus.

erika.ety: Spelling variant of Erica, the feminine form of Eric, or borrowed directly from modern Scandinavia, ultimately from Old Norse Eiríkr.

eris.ety: From erë (“wind”), probably contaminated with Ancient Greek ἔρις (“strife”).

erland.ety: Old Norse Erlendr, erlendr "foreigner" or "eagle's land"; cognate to Norwegian Erlend.

erle.ety: Short form of Germanic compound names beginning with Erl- (German Erlinde, etc.), also seen as a modern feminine form of Erling and Jarl (“earl”).

erlend.ety: From Old Norse Erlendr, from erlendr (“foreigner”). Cognate with Erlendur and Erland.

erling.ety: Old Norse Erlingr, related to jarl, "son or descendant of an earl".

erna.ety: Borrowed from German Erna, a short form of Ernestine and Ernesta, feminine names derived from Ernst, ultimately from Old High German ernust (“serious, earnest”). in Norway.

ernst.ety: Borrowed from German Ernst, originally a byname based on Ernst (“earnestness, seriousness”), from Middle High German ërnest (“earnestness, seriousness”), from Old High German ernust (“seriousness; vigor, strife”).

errol.ety: Transferred from a rare Scottish surname derived from a place name, of unknown meaning. Later interpreted as a variant of Earl in the U.S.

erwan.ety: Borrowed from Breton Erwan Borrowed from Breton Erwan.

erwin.ety: From Old High German heri (“army”) + wini (“friend”). Taken to regular use from the play Erwin und Elmire (1775) by Goethe.

esa.ety: Medieval vernacular form of Esaias, the old biblical equivalent of English Isaiah. It has also been recorded as a diminutive of Esko and Esau.

esdra.ety: From Latin Esdras, ultimately from Biblical Hebrew עזרא.

eskil.ety: Name of an 11th century Swedish saint, from Old Norse Áskell, ("god") + ("helmet", "cauldron").

esmee.ety: Anglicized spelling of the French Esmée or Esmé.

espen.ety: From Danish Esben, from Old Norse Ásbjǫrn. Cognate with English Osborne.

esta.ety: Variant of Ester, also associated with Estonia, the Latin name of the country.

estefania.ety: From Spanish Estefanía with a stress shift. Alternatively from Portuguese Estefânia, which is stressed as in German, but is nevertheless a less likely origin.

estella.ety: Latinized and Italian variant of the French Estelle.

estevao.ety: From Old Galician-Portuguese Estevão, from Latin Stephanus, from Ancient Greek Στέφανος, from στέφανος (“crown”).

esteve.ety: Inherited from Latin Stephanus, from Ancient Greek Στέφανος.

ethel.ety: Short form of names of Old English origin beginning with Ethel-, æþele (“noble”). First used in the 19th century.

etienne.ety: Inherited from Old French Estiene, from earlier Estiefne, from Latin Stephanus, from Ancient Greek Στέφανος. Doublet of Stéphane, a borrowing from Latin.

eugen.m: good, well + born a certain way

eugene.ety: Borrowed from French Eugène, from Latin Eugenius, from Ancient Greek Εὐγένιος (“well born”), from εὖ (“good, well”) + -γενής (“born a certain way”). Parallel to eugenics.
eugene.m: good, well + born a certain way

eugenie.m: good, well + born a certain way

eugeniusz.m: good, well + born a certain way

eugène.m: good, well + born a certain way

eugénie.m: good, well + born a certain way

eulalie.ety: French from the saints' name Eulalia, from Ancient Greek "sweetly speaking".

evalyn.ety: From Eva + Lyn, or a variant of Evelyn.

evan.ety: Anglicization of Welsh Ifan, ultimately from Latin Jōhannēs, variant of Iōannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (yōḥānān, yokhanán), literally “God is gracious”.

evander.ety: From Latin Euander, from Ancient Greek Εὔανδρος, literally “good man”.

evandro.ety: Latin Evander, from Ancient Greek Εὔανδρος.

evangeline.ety: Invented by the poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow when he began research on his epic poem Evangeline about Acadian lovers deported from French-Canada. From Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (“good news”).

evelyn.ety: From Middle English forms of the Old French female name Aveline, diminutive of the Germanic root *avi-, of uncertain meaning, possibly “desired, wished for“ (compare Latin avēre, "to wish for") or aval “strength”.

evelynn.ety: A rare non-standard spelling of Evelyn with -lynn.

even.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Eyvindr, through a younger Norwegian reduced form, ultimately from Proto-Norse *Auja-winduʀ.

everett.ety: From Dutch Everaert or Everardt (late 16th C.), from Middle Dutch Everarde. Doublet of Everard.

everleigh.ety: From Old English eofor (“wild boar”) + lēah (“woodland clearing”). Compare the Dutch toponym Everlo.

everly.ety: Habitational surname, from a variant of Everleigh.

evert.ety: From a diminutive of Dutch Everard or Everhard, equivalent to English Everett.

everton.ety: From Old English eofor (“wild boar”) + tūn (“settlement”).

evita.ety: From Spanish Evita, a pet form of Eva.

ewald.ety: From the name of two seventh century missionaries, Old High German ewa (“law”) + waltan (“to rule”).

ewan.ety: From Scottish Gaelic Eòghan. Not related to Iwan and Evan.

ezio.ety: From Ancient Greek ᾱ̓ετός (“eagle”), either through the Latin given name Aetius or directly from Ancient Greek.

fabian.ety: From Latin Fabiānus (“belonging to Fabius”), derived from Fabius + -ānus.

fabrice.ety: Borrowed from Latin Fabricius, name of a plebeian Roman gens, of unknown origin, but often explained as from faber (“skillful, one who works with hands”).
fabrice.m: skillful, one who works with hands

faizan.ety: From Arabic فَيْضَان; compare فَيْض (“grace, favor”).

fallon.ety: Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó Fallamhain (“descendant of Fallamhan”), a personal name related to follúnaitheoir (“ruler, governor”).

faouzi.ety: Borrowed from French Faouzi, ultimately from Arabic فوزي (“triumph”).

farley.ety: From Old English fearn (“fern”) + lēah (“woodland”). Equivalent to fern + -ley (“lea”) and doublet of Doublet of Farnley.

farrah.ety: Variant of Farrar, from Middle English ferreor (“iron worker, smith”). The given name was popularized by the American actress Farrah Fawcett (1947-2009).

fatimata.ety: A French spelling of a name ultimately derived from Arabic فَاطِمَة, i.e. Native spellings include Pulaar Faatimata.

faustino.ety: From the Roman cognomen Latin Faustinus, diminutive of faustus (“favorable”).

faycal.ety: Borrowed from Arabic فَيْصَل Borrowed from Arabic فَيْصَل.

faye.ety: Borrowed from French Faye or other languages.

felicia.ety: From Middle English Felicia, from Latin Fēlīcia, from fēlīcia, literally “happy things”, the neuter plural of fēlīx, which often occurred in the phrase tempora fēlīcia (“happy times”).

feliciana.ety: Latin Fēlīciāna, feminine of Fēlīciānus. Felicia + -ana or Felician + -a.

felicita.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Fēlīcitās Latin Fēlīcitātem.

felicity.ety: From the noun felicity, and also the English form of Latin Felicitas, a name borne by early martyrs.

fergal.ety: Fer (“man”) + gal (“valour”); the feminine ā-stem inflection is inherited from the latter noun.

fermin.ety: Fermín and Fermina are derived from the Late Latin proper names Firminus/Firmina, from Latin Firmus/Firma.

fern.ety: From fern; in the case of the surname, it was given to someone who lived in a place where there was an abundance of these plants.

ferris.ety: English surname, from Norman Ferrers, from the toponymic Ferrières, from French fer (“iron”).

fiadh.ety: From fiadh, pre-reform spelling of fia, from Old Irish fíad (“wild; game, deer”).

fiete.ety: Low German short form of Friedrich.

filip.ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Φίλιππος.

filipe.ety: Ultimately from Ancient Greek Φίλιππος (“fond of horses”), from φιλέω (“I like”) + ἵππος (“horse”).

finja.ety: Modern German feminine form of Finn.

finlay.ety: Anglicized from Scottish Gaelic Fionnlagh (“fair warrior/hero”).

finn.m: Sami; member of the Sami people

finnegan.ety: Borrowed from Irish Ó Fionnagáin (“descendant of Fionnagán”). Fionnagán is a given name that descends from Old Irish Finnacán, which is typically anglicised as Finnegan itself.

finnian.ety: From Irish, variant of Fionnán; see fionn (“fair”).

firmin.ety: From Latin Firminus, name of early Christian saints, derivative of firmus (“firm”).

flemming.ety: Old Norse Flæmingr, "a Fleming", originally a medieval byname, used as a given name since the 19th century.

fletcher.ety: English occupational surname from the noun fletcher (“arrow-maker”). Sometimes confused with Flesher.

fleur.ety: French fleur (“flower”), name of a character in Galsworthy's Forsyte Saga.

florence.ety: Borrowed from French Florence, from Latin Flōrentia (as a given name, a feminine form of Flōrentius), from flōrens (“flowering, flourishing”), from flōs (“flower”), connected with English bloom and blossom.

florentin.ety: From the Medieval Latin Flōrentīnus, literally “Florentine, from Florence”, name of a saint (Antoninus of Florence), from Latin Flōrentia (“Florence”), from flōrēns (“flourishing”).

florentina.ety: Borrowed from Late Latin Flōrentīna, name of a Visigothic saint (died c. 612 AD); also the feminine equivalent of Latin Flōrentīnus, literally “Florentine, from Florence”.

florentine.ety: Variant of Florentina, the feminine equivalent of Florentin, from Latin Flōrentīnus.

floriana.ety: Latin Flōriāna, feminine of Flōriānus. Doublet of Florienne.

florinda.ety: Fanciful variant of Flora suffixed with -inda, partly borrowed from the equally rare Spanish Florinda.

floyd.ety: Anglicisation of the Welsh name Lloyd, from Welsh llwyd (“grey, grey-haired”).

flynn.ety: Anglicized from Irish Ó Floinn, "descendant of Flann (red)".

forest.ety: French surname, from Old French forest (“forest”). Compare Laforest and Deforest.

forrest.ety: English surname, from the noun forest. Also adopted and translated from the word for "forest" in various other languages by settlers.

fortune.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Fortunatus Latin Fortunatus. Doublet of Fortunat.

foster.ety: English surname, reduced from Forster; also from the noun foster.

fouad.ety: Borrowed from Arabic فُؤَاد Borrowed from Arabic فُؤَاد.

france.ety: From Middle English France, from Old French France, from Latin Francia, from Francī, the name of a Germanic tribe, of unclear (but Proto-Germanic) origin.

frances.ety: From Old French Franceise, feminine form of Franceis, from Late Latin Franciscus (“Frankish”). Doublet of Francesca and Francisca.

francesc.ety: Borrowed from Latin Franciscus or Italian Francesco.

francois.ety: Borrowed from French François, from Medieval Latin Franciscus.

frank.ety: From Middle High German Franke, from Old High German Franko (“a Frank”). Used in the Middle Ages and revived in the 19th century.

franklin.ety: From Middle English frankelein (“freeholder”), see franklin. The place names are mostly Named after Benjamin Franklin.

franz.ety: From German Franz. Doublet of Francis.

françois.ety: Borrowed from French François, from Medieval Latin Franciscus.

fraser.ety: Scottish surname thought to be from Norman, but not corresponding to any obvious places in France; perhaps a corrupted transcription of a Middle Irish name. More at Fraser.

freda.ety: A feminine form of Frederick and Fred, also a short form of Winifred.

frederica.ety: From Frederick + -a. Compare Danish Frederikke, French Frédérique, German Friederike, and Italian Federica.

frederick.ety: From German Friedrich, Friederich and influenced by Latin Friderīcus, Frederīcus, from Old High German Fridurih, from Frankish *Friþurīk, from Proto-Germanic *Friþurīks, from *friþuz + *rīks, literally “peace king, peaceful ruler”.

frederico.ety: From Latin Frederīcus, Friderīcus, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *Friþurīks (“peace king, peaceful ruler”).

frederik.ety: From Middle Dutch Vrederic, from Old Dutch Frithoric, from Proto-West Germanic *Friþurīk, from Proto-Germanic *Friþurīks, a compound of *friþuz (“peace”) + *rīks (“king”).

fredrik.ety: Of Germanic origin, cognate with the English Frederick.

freeman.ety: Proprialisation of freeman. From originating as a freeman (instead of a serf, indentured, or some other status) free + man.

freja.ety: From Old Norse Freyja, from Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ.

freyja.ety: From Old Norse Freyja, from freyja (“lady”), from Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ.

fridtjof.ety: From Old Norse Friðþjófr. Appears in Old Norse saga and was revived through 19th century literature.

frieda.ety: From Elfriede. From Old English Ælfþrȳþ; later partly merged with æþel (“noble”) + þrȳþ (“strength”) ( =Audrey).

frits.ety: From German Fritz, diminutive of Friedrich (“Frederick”).

fritz.ety: Borrowed from German Fritz, pet form of Friedrich (“Frederick”).

frode.ety: From Old Norse Fróði, a byname from fróðr (“wise”). Cognate with English Frodo.

froilán.ety: Froilán and Froilana are derived from the Spanish proper name Froila.

frøya.ety: From Old Norse Freyja, from freyja (“lady”), from Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ.

frøydis.ety: From Old Norse Frøydís, Freydís, from Freyr + dís (“dis, minor goddess”). Cognate with Faroese Froydis, Icelandic Freydís and Old Swedish Frødīs.

fulton.ety: From Foulden, a village in Norfolk, from Old English fuġol (“bird”) + tūn (“dwelling”).

félix.ety: Borrowed from Latin Fēlīx, literally “fortunate, prosperous”.

gabrielle.ety: Borrowed from French Gabrielle, feminine form of Gabriel (see there for more).

gael.ety: Borrowed from Irish Gael Borrowed from Irish Gael, alt.

gage.ety: An occupational surname from Middle English gage, guage (“measure”) for an assayer, or gage (“pledge”) for a moneylender.

gaja.m: Gaea, the Earth personified as a goddess

galen.ety: Thumb|A 17th-century [[engraving of Galen by Georg P.

galina.ety: Borrowed from Гали́на, from Ancient Greek γαλήνη (“calm”), name of a Nereid and of early martyrs venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church.

galo.ety: Derived from Latin Gallus, from Latin gallus (“rooster”).

galyna.ety: Borrowed from Ukrainian Гали́на, from Ancient Greek γαλήνη (“calm”), name of a Nereid and of early martyrs venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church.

gannon.ety: Derived from Irish Mag Fhionnáin "son of Finan".

gara.ety: Gara is assumed to be derived from the first half of the name of Garajonay peak (the highest point on the island of La Gomera), formerly Garagono(c)he, from Guanche.

gareth.ety: Of Old Welsh origin and cognate with the Welsh name Geraint (from Latin Gerontius (“old man”), from Ancient Greek γέρων (“old man”)) or perhaps the word gwareddawg, gwaredd (“gentleness”); see gwâr (“gentle”).

garfield.ety: Also Garfeld, from Old English gār (“spear”) + feld (“field”).

garland.ety: English surname, from the noun garland. Also derived from Garland in Devon, from an ancestor of the noun gore (“triangular piece of land”) + land.

garrett.ety: A medieval English and Irish form of the Germanic given names Gerard and Gerald. Of Old High German origin.

garrick.ety: From Old English *Gārrīċ, from Proto-Germanic *Gaizarīks. Doublet of Gaiseric.

garth.ety: Welsh garth probably has its influence on Welsh place names.

gary.ety: Medieval short form of Germanic compound names beginning with gari or geri ("spear"), such as Gerard, Garrett, Gerald or Gerbert. Cognate with the Scottish and Irish name Garaidh.

gaute.ety: From Old Norse Gauti, a weak form of Gautr; from gauti, gautr (“Geat”). Originally a byname, and also a short form of names with the element.

gauthier.ety: From a Germanic language (probably Frankish); related to English Walter. For similar development of Germanic w to g in French, see garde and Guillaume.

gavin.ety: Medieval variant of Gawain, the name of an Arthurian knight, first recorded as Old French Gauvain. The form Gavin survived in Scotland and spread to other English-speaking countries in the 1960s.

gaylord.ety: Derived from the Old French surname Gaillard (from gaillard (“strong”)), via Anglo-Norman. Compare Spanish Gallardo (from gallardo (“dashing, strapping, gallant”).

gaël.ety: Possibly a contraction of Gwenaël or Judicaël. By folk etymology interpreted as "a Gael".

gaëtan.ety: Borrowed from Italian Gaetano, from gaetano (“resident or native of Gaeta”), from Latin Caiētānus. Name of a saint.

geir.ety: From Old Norse Geirr, from geirr (“spear”) (whence also geir).

gene.m: good, well + born a certain way

genesio.ety: From Ancient Greek Γενέσιος, related to γένεσις (“source, origin; birth”); the name of several minor saints. Doublet of Ginese.

genesis.ety: From Ancient Greek γένεσις (“creation, beginning, origin”).

geneva.ety: Thumb|canton of Geneva (sense 2) Mentioned in Latin texts as Genava.

genevieve.ety: Borrowed from French Geneviève (patron saint of Paris), from Latin Genovefa, Genoveva, possibly either of Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kunją (“kin, family”) + *wībą (“woman, wife”), or of Celtic origin.

geneviève.ety: From Medieval Latin Genovefa. Possibly from Proto-Germanic *kunją (“kin, family”) + *wībą (“woman, wife”).

genie.m: good, well + born a certain way

genilda.ety: Brazilian creation in comparision to other names ending in the root -ilda (Matilda, Brunilda, etc.), from Proto-Germanic *hildiz.

genildo.ety: Brazilian creation in comparision to other names ending in the root -ildo (Ivanildo, Hildo, etc.), from Proto-Germanic *hildiz.

genna.ety: A variant of Jenna with the spelling possibly influenced by Gina or Gianna.

genowefa.ety: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin Genovefa.

geoffrey.ety: From Middle English Geffrey, from an Old French aristocratic name, Geoffroi (> West, East ), itself from Proto-French forms (latinized in -us) Jotfredus, Jozsfredus, Josfredus (10th century) and Jof[f]redus, Jofridus, Jaufredus.

geoffroy.ety: From Germanic origin, perhaps Frankish *Gardifriþu,*Gaiʀafriþu, or Proto-Germanic *Gautafriþu. See Geoffrey for more.

georg.ety: Borrowed from Latin Georgius, from Ancient Greek Γεώργιος (Geṓrgios), from Ancient Greek γεωργός (geōrgós, “farmer”), from Ancient Greek γῆ (gê, “earth”) + Ancient Greek ἔργον (érgon, “work”).

george.ety: Inherited from Middle English George Name of an early saint, from Middle English George, from Latin Geōrgius, from Ancient Greek Γεώργῐος, from γεωργός (“farmer, earth worker”).

georgia.ety: Latinate feminine form of George, from Ancient Greek Γεώργιος (“farmer”).

georgina.ety: From George + -ina, feminine form of George..

geraldine.ety: From Gerald + -ine. c. 1540 by the Earl of Surrey as a poetic name for Lady Elizabeth Fitzgerald, "one of the Fitzgeralds".

gerard.ety: From Middle English Gerard, from Old French Gerart, from Frankish *Gaiʀahard, from *gaiʀ (“spear”) + *hard(ī) (“hard, brave”).

gerda.ety: Latinate variant of Scandinavian Gerd, from Old Norse Gerðr, garðr (“protection”). The name occurs in nineteenth century Swedish poetry and in Hans Christian Andersen's Snow Queen (1844).

gerhard.ety: Inherited from Old High German Gērhart, from Proto-West Germanic *Gaiʀahard, from *gaiʀ (“spear”) + *hard(ī) (“brave, hard”).

germain.ety: A patronymic from a medieval given name, identical with the French one; or from an ethnic term for a German.

german.ety: From Latin Germānus, Germānī (“the peoples of Germānia”), as distinct from Gauls (in the writings of Caesar and Tacitus), and of uncertain ultimate origin (possibly Celtic/Gaulish).

geronimo.ety: Inherited from Latin Hierōnymus, from Ancient Greek Ἱερώνυμος (“holy name”).

gerrit.ety: A by-form of Gerard, which derives from Middle Dutch Gherart, from Old Dutch *Gērhard, from Proto-West Germanic *Gaiʀahard.

gert.ety: Shortening of Gerard, from Middle Dutch gerart, from older gerhart.

gertrud.ety: From Old High German gēr (“spear”) + Proto-Germanic *þrūþiz (“strength”) or Proto-Germanic *trut (“maiden”).

gertrude.ety: From Old French, from Proto-Germanic *gaizaz (“spear”) + *þrūþiz (“strength”) or *trut- (“maiden, dear”); name of a Belgian seventh century saint.

gheorghe.ety: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic Геѡргеи.

ghislain.ety: From Latin Gislenus (variant Ghislenus), the Latinized name of Saint Ghislain (a seventh-century anchorite in Hainaut), from Proto-West Germanic *Gīslīn, a hypocoristic personal name derived from *gīsl (“hostage.

ghyslaine.ety: Variant of Ghislaine (less common spelling variant); feminine form of Ghislain.

gian.ety: From a contraction of Giovan, shortened form of the given name Giovanni (cognate with English John). Compare Sicilian Giu(v)à.

gianfranco.ety: From Gi(ov)an(ni) (“John”) + Franc(esc)o (“Francis”). Cognate with French Jean-François.

gigi.ety: Borrowed from French Gigi. Sometimes a pet form of English names such as Virginia or Genesis.

gilbert.ety: From Old French Gislebert From Old French Gislebert, from Proto-Germanic *Gīslaberhtaz, from *gīslaz (“pledge”) + *berhtaz (“bright, famous”).

giles.ety: Medieval English form of Old French saints' name Giles, modern Gilles, an altered form of Latin Aegīdius, from Ancient Greek Αἰγίδιος, derivative of αἰγίδιον (“kid, young goat”).

gilmar.ety: Several possibilities are given, including: From the female names Childemara, Cildemara, Quildemara, and Gilmara, which carry the term chile or hile, meaning "combat", and maere, meaning "illustrious, brilliant, famous".

gina.ety: Short form of Georgina. Short form of Regina.

gines.ety: Borrowed from Provençal Genès, from Latin Genesius, from Ancient Greek Γενέσιος, related to γένεσις (“source, origin; birth”).

ginger.ety: A diminutive of Virginia; also a nickname for someone or something with ginger-coloured hair.

gino.ety: Shortened form of several diminutives ending in -gino, such as Luigino (from Luigi (“Louis”)), Giorgino (from Giorgio (“George”)), and so on.

giovana.ety: Borrowed from Italian Giovanna. Doublet of Joana, which was inherited from Latin, of Doublet of Ivana and Jeane, borrowings from Russian and French, respectively.

gisella.ety: Borrowed from Italian Gisella, from French Giselle.

giselle.ety: Inherited from Old French, shortened from Germanic compound names beginning with gisil (“pledge”), from Proto-Germanic *gīslaz (“pledge, hostage”).

gisle.ety: From Old Norse Gísli, short form of compound names containing the word gísl (“hostage”).

gladys.ety: Anglicized from Welsh Gwladus, of uncertain origin, perhaps connected with gwlad (“country”).

glenda.ety: Coined in the twentieth century from Welsh glân (“holy, fair”) and da (“good”).

glenna.ety: From male given name Glen, from Scottish glen (“secluded valley”).

glory.ety: From glory as a variant of the more common Gloria.

godfrey.ety: From Old French Godefrei, from Old High German Godafrid (“peace of God”), from Proto-Germanic *Gudafriþuz. Equivalent to god + frith.

godofredo.ety: From a name composed of Gothic 𐌲𐍉𐌸𐍃 (“good”) + *𐍆𐍂𐌹𐌸𐌿𐍃 (“peace”); respectively from Proto-Germanic *gōdaz and *friþuz. Compare English Godfrey.

golden.ety: As an English surname, from the adjective golden. As an Irish surname, from mag Ualghairg; see McGoldrick.
golden.m: Made of, or relating to, gold.

gordon.ety: The Scottish surname derives from Gordon in Berwickshire.

gorm.ety: Medieval contraction of Old Norse Guðþormr, from guð (“god”) + þyrma (“to spare, respect”).

grady.ety: From the Irish surname, from Ó Grádaigh (see O'Grady) or Mag Bhrádaigh (see McGrady).

graham.ety: The surname derives from Gra(nt)ham, the name of a place in Lincolnshire, from Old English *grand (“gravel”) + hām (“homestead”).

grainne.ety: Possibly a derivative of Old Irish grán (“grain”) if originally the name of an agricultural goddess or a derivative of Middle Irish gráin (“awfulness, horror”) if the original sense was.

grant.ety: From Scottish Gaelic Grannd, from Anglo-Norman graunt (“big, large”), from Old French grant, from Latin grandis. Doublet of grand.

granville.ety: The commune of France is from Old French Granville, Grandvilla, Grande Villa, Grandivilla, from grant (“grand”) + ville (“settlement”).

gray.ety: As an English, Irish, Scottish, and Norman surname, from the placename Graye-sur-Mer in Calvados, from Late Latin Graecus (“Greek”). Also as an English surname, from the adjective gray.

graziele.ety: Alteration of Graziela, under influence of other languages.

grazielle.ety: Alteration of Graziela, under influence of other languages.

grazyna.ety: Coined by Adam Mickiewicz in his 1823 poem Grażyna. From lt:gražus + -yna.

grecia.ety: Borrowed from Latin Graecia, from Ancient Greek Γραικός.

gregoria.ety: A feminine form of Latin Gregorius.

gregory.ety: Via Latin Grēgorius, from post-classical Ancient Greek Γρηγόριος (“watchful, vigilant”), from Ancient Greek ἐγείρω (“awaken, arouse”).

grethe.ety: Originally a German diminutive of Margarete, first recorded in Norway in the 18th century.

grigory.ety: From Russian Григо́рий, from Medieval Greek Γρηγόριος. Doublet of Gregory.

gro.ety: Old Norse Gróa from the verb gróa ("to grow").

grégoire.ety: Inherited from Old French Gregoire From Old French Gregoire.

gudrun.ety: From Old Norse Guðrún, revived as a historical-literary name during the Nordic name renaissance of the 19th century. The Old Norse name is from guð (“god”) + rún (“secret knowledge, rune”).

guilhem.ety: Borrowed from Occitan Guilhèm Borrowed from Occitan Guilhèm.

guillaume.ety: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French Guillaume, Willame, from Frankish *Willahelm (“William”), literally “will-helmet”, from Proto-Germanic *Wiljahelmaz.

guinevere.ety: From Middle English Gwenyver, from Welsh Gwenhwyfar. Doublet of Jennifer.

gumersindo.ety: Alteration of Latin Gumesindus, from Gothic, from Proto-Germanic *Gumasinþaz, from *gumô (“man”) + *sinþaz (“journey; companion”). Compare Galician Gomesende.

gun.ety: From Old Norse Gunnr, short form of female compound names with the element gunnr (“battle”). Name of a Valkyrie in Norse mythology.

gunda.ety: Short form of compound given names containing the Old High German element gund (“battle”).

gunn.ety: From Old Norse Gunnr, from gunnr (“battle”). Also a short form of compound names containing the element.

gunnar.ety: From Old Norse Gunnarr, from Proto-Germanic *Gunþiharjaz, from *gunþiz (“battle”) + *harjaz (“warrior”). Cognate with Gunnar, Danish Gunder and German Gunther.

gunnbjørg.ety: From Old Norse Gunnbjǫrg, from gunnr (“battle”) + bjǫrg (“salvation”).

gunnhild.ety: From Old Norse Gunnhildr, from gunnr (“battle”) + hildr (“battle (maid)”).

gunther.ety: From Old High German gund (“battle”) + heri (“army”), from Proto-Germanic *Gunþiharjaz. Name of a king in the Nibelungenlied, and of a medieval German saint.

guri.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Guðríðr, from Guðfríðr, from guð (“god”) + fríðr (“beautiful”).

guro.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Guðrún, through a younger Norwegian form in which the final was lost after nasalising the preceding vowel.

gus.ety: Short form of Augustus. From the Latin name Augustus.

gustav.ety: From Old Swedish Gøtstaf, from Old Norse Gautr (“Geats”) + stafr (“staff”).

gustave.ety: From French Gustave. French form of Swedish royal name Gustav; see Gustav for more.

guttorm.ety: From Old Norse Guðþormr, from guð (“god”) + þormr, from þyrma (“to spare, respect”).

guy.ety: From the Hebrew name גַּיְא (gáy), literally “valley”, with the spelling influenced by the existing English name.

gwen.ety: A female given name from Welsh. Borrowed from Welsh Gwen. short form of Gwendolen.
gwen.m: white, fair, blessed + ring, bow, hair, brow

gwenael.ety: Name of a sixth century Breton saint, from gwenn "white" + hael "generous".

gwendoline.m: white, fair, blessed + ring, bow, hair, brow

gwendolyn.ety: A variant of Gwendolen, Gwendoline with -lyn.
gwendolyn.m: white, fair, blessed + ring, bow, hair, brow

gwenn.ety: From Old Breton gwenn. Compare Welsh gwyn.

gøril.ety: From Danish Gerhild, from Old Norse geirr (“spear”) + hildr (“battle”).

günter.ety: From Old High German gund (“battle”) + heri (“army”), from Proto-West Germanic *Gunþihari, from Proto-Germanic *Gunþiharjaz.

hadassah.ety: Borrowed from Hebrew הֲדַסָּה (“myrtle”), the Hebrew name of Esther in the Hebrew Bible.

hadley.ety: From Old English hǣþ (“heath”) + Old English leah (“woodland clearing”). Equivalent to heath + -ley.

hakan.ety: From Persian خاقان (xâqân), a Persianized variant of Old Turkic 𐰴𐰍𐰣 (qaɣan). Cognate with Turkish Kaan, kağan.

hal.ety: A diminutive lambdacism of Harry (compare Sally from Sarah and Moll from Mary).

haldis.ety: Old Norse Halldís, from hallr (“flat stone”) + dís (“minor goddess”).

haleigh.ety: Variant spelling of Haley with the suffix -leigh.

haley.ety: Variant of Hayley, from Old English.

halil.ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish خلیل (Halîl), from Arabic خَلِيل (“friend”).

halina.ety: Borrowed from Belarusian Галі́на, from Ancient Greek γαλήνη (“calm”), name of a Nereid and of early martyrs venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church.

halle.ety: As a German surname, variant of Hall. As a French surname, from the noun halle (“covered room”).

hallgeir.ety: From Old Norse Hallgeirr, from hallr (“stone”) + geirr (“spear”). Cognate with Faroese Halgeir, Halgir and Icelandic Hallgeir.

hallvard.ety: Hall + -vard; from Old Norse Hallvarðr, from hallr (“stone”) + -varðr, cf. vǫrðr (“guardian”). Cognate with Hallvarður.

halyna.ety: From Slavic (Ukrainian Галина, etc), from Ancient Greek; doublet of Halina and Galina and Galyna.

hamilton.ety: From Old English *Hameldūne, from hamel (“blunt, flat-topped”) + dūne (“hill”). The Scottish surname is from the place in Leicestershire.

hamish.ety: Anglicized spelling of Scottish Gaelic Sheumais, vocative case of Seumas, from English James (see for more). Doublet of James etc.

hampton.ety: Variously from: Old English Hāmtūn, from hām and tūn (equivalent to home + town); Old English hēantūn, from hēah and tūn (equivalent to high + town).

hania.ety: From Ottoman Turkish خانیه (Hanya) and irregular romanization of Greek Χανιά, q.v.

hanne.ety: Either a short form of Johanne, a feminine form derived from Johannes, or an e-form of Hanna.

hannes.ety: Borrowed from German Hannes, a short form of Johannes (“John”), ultimately from Late Latin Iōhannēs, a variant of Latin Iōannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yôḥānān, “Yahweh is gracious”).

hans.ety: Borrowed from German Hans, a medieval short form of Johannes (“John”), ultimately from Latin Iōhannēs, a variant of Latin Iōannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yôḥānān, “Yahweh is gracious”). in Norway.

hardy.ety: As an English, Scottish, and French surname, from Middle English hardy, hardi, from Old French hardi (“hardy, daring, stout, bold”).

harlan.ety: American contraction of Harland, from Old English har (“grey”) / hara (“hare”) + land (“land”).

harlee.ety: A fanciful spelling variant of Harley.

harley.ety: From Old English hær (“rock”) or hara (“hare”) + lēah (“wood, clearing”). Equivalent to hare + -ley (“lea”).

harlow.ety: From Old English hær (“rock”) or here (“army”) + hlæw (“hill”).

harold.ety: From a merger of Old English Hereweald and Old English Harold (itself from Old Norse Haraldr), both from Proto-Germanic *Harjawaldaz, from *harjaz (“army”) + *waldaz (“ruler, authority”).

harri.ety: From English Harry, and also used as a diminutive form of Swedish Harald.

harriet.ety: Anglicized form of French Henriette, feminine form of Henri (“Henry”), popular in England in the 18th and 19th centuries.

harris.ety: From Harry + -s (“patronymic suffix”). From Harry, a male given name derived from a Middle English pronunciation of Old French Henri.

harry.ety: Medieval English spoken form of Old French Henri.

harun.ety: From Arabic هَارُون. Doublet of Aaron.

harvey.ety: From Haerviu, name of a Breton saint, from Old Breton hoiarn (“iron”) + viu (“blazing”). Cognate with modern Breton Haerviu.

haskell.ety: The programming language is Named after Haskell Curry. As an English surname, from the Middle English personal name Askell, from Old Norse Áskell.

hayden.ety: Originally a place name, from Old English heg (“hay”) + denu (“valley”). Alternatively, from Middle Dutch heiden (“heathen”).

hayes.ety: As an English locational surname, from Old English hæs (“brushwood”) (see hris) and Middle English hay (“enclosure”), heye. As an Irish surname, from Ó hAodha (“descendant of Aodh”).

hayley.ety: Localities in England, from Old English hēg (“hay”) + lēah (“wood, clearing”). Equivalent to hay + -ley (“lea”).

heath.ety: English surname, from the noun heath.

heather.ety: From heather; the given name is one of the plant names taken up in the 19th century. The surname is habitational, also meaning someone living on a heath.

hebe.ety: From Ancient Greek Ἥβη, literally “Youth, Prime of Life”.

hedda.ety: Diminutive of Hedvig, made famous by Henrik Ibsen's play Hedda Gabler ( 1890).

hedwig.ety: From German Hedwig, from Old High German Haduwig, Hadwig, from Proto-Germanic *Haþuwīgą.

heine.ety: Shortened from German Heinrich, the German cognate of English Henry, originally from Proto-Germanic *Haimarīks (“ruler of the home”), from *haimaz (“home”) and *rīks (“ruler, king”).

heinrich.ety: From Old High German Heimrih, Haimirich (8th century), composed of heim (“home”) + -rih (“suffix for male names, originally a noun meaning king”); corresponds to Proto-West Germanic *Haimarīk, from Proto-Germanic *Haimarīks.

helder.ety: Unclear origin, possibly from Dutch helder.

helen.ety: From French Hélène, from Latin Helena, from Ancient Greek Ἑλένη. Doublet of Elaine.

helena.ety: A Latinate form of Helen, borrowed from Latin Helena.

helene.ety: From French Hélène and from German Helene. Doublet of Helen and Helena and Elaine.

helga.ety: From Old Norse Helga (“holy”), a pre-Christian term, feminine form of Helgi. Doublet of Olga.

helio.ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Ἥλῐος.

helmer.ety: German equivalent of Hjalmar or from Germanic heil "hale" + mar "famous".

helmut.ety: Probably from Proto-Germanic *helmaz and *mōdaz, but derivations from MHG heil/helm + muot have also been suggested. The name is shaped similar to modern German hell + Mut ("clear courage").

heloise.ety: From Medieval Latin Heloisa under influence from French Héloïse, probably from French Éloi + -se (“-ess: feminizing nouns”), from Medieval Latin Eligius, chiefly after Saint Eligius, from Latin ēligere (“to pick.

hendrick.ety: From Low German Hendrick and Dutch Hendrik, equivalent to Henry.

hendrik.ety: From Middle Dutch Hendric, Henric, from Old Dutch *Hēmrīk, *Heimrīk, from Proto-West Germanic *Haimarīk, from Proto-Germanic *Haimarīks.

henna.ety: A pet form of Henriikka, Henrietta.

henning.ety: From a Middle Low German pet form of Johannes ( =John) and Heinrich ( =Henry) borrowed into Scandinavia in the Middle Ages; partly confused with Hemming, a saint's name of Old Norse origin.

henrietta.ety: Latinate form of French Henriette, derived from the male given name Henry.

henriette.ety: From French Henriette, feminine form of Henri (“Henry”) coined in the seventeenth century; in English more popular as Harriet and Henrietta.

henrik.ety: Cognate with Swedish Henrik, German Heinrich and English Henry.

henry.ety: From Middle English Henry, from Old French (and Anglo-Norman) Henri, from Frankish, from Proto-Germanic *Haimarīks.

heorhii.ety: Transliteration of Гео́ргій. Borrowed from Ancient Greek Γεώργιος.

herbert.ety: From Old French Herbert, from Frankish *Hariberht.

herborg.ety: From Old Norse Herborg, from herr (“army”) + borg.

hercules.ety: From Latin Herculēs, from Etruscan 𐌇𐌄𐌓𐌂𐌋𐌄, from Ancient Greek Ἡρακλῆς, apparently cognate of Ἥρα (“Hera”) and, according to Haudry, from Proto-Indo-European *yóh₁r̥ (“year, season”) + κλέος (“glory”).

herdis.ety: Old Norse Herdís, from herr (“army”) + dís (“minor goddess”).

herman.ety: From Old English here (“army”) + man (“man”) It was revived in the 19th century, partly due to American immigrants from continental Europe where the name has been more popular.

hermann.ety: Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *harjaz + *mann- and corresponding to the common noun *harjamann- (“warrior”); equivalent to Heer (“army”) + Mann (“man”).

hermine.ety: Partially from German Hermine and partially from hermine (“ermine”).

hermione.ety: From the Ancient Greek Ἑρμῐόνη. Not related to German Hermine.

hernani.ety: Doublet of Fernando. Of Spanish origin.

hershel.ety: Borrowed from Yiddish הירשעל, a diminutive of הירש (“deer, buck”).

hester.ety: From the Latin form of Esther.

hilaire.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Hilarius Latin Hilarius.

hilary.ety: From Latin Hilarius (“cheerful, happy”), name of a fourth-century saint, and from its feminine form Hilaria.

hilbert.ety: From a Middle English given name of Proto-Germanic origin, from Old English hild (“battle”) + beorht (“bright”) (Proto-Germanic *Hildiberhtaz).

hilda.ety: Short form of Germanic names beginning or ending in hild (“battle”).

hildegard.ety: Ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *Hildigardu, from Proto-Germanic *hildiz (“battle”) + *gardaz (“enclosure”), with the approximate meaning “battle protector”.

hildegunn.ety: Old Norse Hildigunnr, from hildr (“battle”) + gunnr (“battle”).

hillary.ety: From Latin Hilarius or Hilaria, from hilare (“cheerfully”) (compare English hilarious).

hilma.ety: Used in early 19th-century Scandinavian literature, probably as a variant of Wilhelmina.

hjalmar.ety: From Old Norse Hjalmarr, from hjalmr (“helmet”) + herr (“army”).

hjørdis.ety: Hjør (“sword”) + dis (“goddess”); from Old Norse Hjǫrdís. Cognate with Icelandic Hjördís and Swedish Hjördis.

hoang.ety: The Northern reading of the character. Doublet of Huỳnh, the Southern form.

holger.ety: From Old Danish Holmger, from Old Norse Hólmgeirr, from hólmr (“island”) (see holm) + geirr (“spear”).

holley.ety: As an English surname, spelling variant of Holly.

holli.ety: A rare spelling variant of Holly.

holly.ety: As an Irish surname, calque of mac cuilinn (“holly”) (see McCullen) and sometimes McQuillan. As an English surname, variant of Holley.

homer.ety: From Latin Homērus, from Ancient Greek Ὅμηρος.

homero.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ὅμηρος, from ὅμηρος (“hostage”). Compare Latin Homērus.

hong.ety: 洪, 鴻 and so on. Doublet of Hường.

honor.ety: Shortened from Honoria and Honora; later also interpreted as a virtue name by Puritans.

honore.ety: From Late Latin Honorātus, from honōrātus. Cognate with Italian Onorato.

honorine.ety: From Late Latin Honorina, name of an early Christian martyr, feminine of Honorinus, derivative of Honorius.

horace.ety: From Latin Horatius, a Roman family name of obscure origin, possibly from Etruscan. Doublet of Horatio.

horacio.ety: From English Horatio, in L. Zamenhof's translation of Hamlet.

horst.ety: Possibly related to the common noun (etymology 1). First used in an 18th-century play, taken into regular use in the 19th century, popular after 1920, now rare for a child.

hortense.ety: From the French form of the Latin Hortēnsia, feminine form of Hortēnsius (“name of a Roman gens”), probably derived from hortēnsis (“having to do with gardens”) on the basis that the first to bear the name was a gardener.

houston.ety: Originally from a place near Glasgow, from the Middle English equivalent of "Hugh's town". Analyzable as Hugh + -s- + -ton.

howard.ety: Medieval personal name from Middle English Howard, Howarde, from Old Norse Hávarðr, from hár (“high”) + varðr (“guard”). In some cases a variant of Heward, from Old French Huard.

howell.ety: From Welsh Hywel. Doublet of Huell and Powell.

hryhorii.ety: Transliteration of Григо́рій. From Ancient Greek Γρηγόριος.

hubert.ety: From Old French Hubert, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hugiz (“mind”) + *berhtaz (“bright, famous”). See Saint Hubert.

hugh.ety: From the Old French aristocratic and saint's name Hughe, brought to England by Normans, from a short form of Germanic names beginning with Proto-Germanic *hugiz (“heart, mind”), such as Hubert.

hughie.ety: From Hugh + -ie. Regarding rain, various etymologies have been proposed; see Send 'er down, Hughie!.

hugues.ety: From Old French Huges, nominative singular of Hugon, from a Frankish name *hugi (“heart, mind”), from Proto-Germanic *hugiz (“thought, understanding”).

humza.ety: From Urdu حمزہ (hamza), from Arabic حمزة (hamza).

huxley.ety: From the Old English personal name *Hucc + -s- + lēah (“woodland clearing, glade”). The first element could also be husc (“insult, scorn, mockery”).

hyman.ety: Anglicisation of Hyam, from Hebrew חַיִּים (ḥayím, “life”).

håkon.ety: From Old Norse Hákon. Cognate with Swedish Håkan.

håvar.ety: Of uncertain exact origin. Either a younger form of Old Norse Hávarr, or a variant of Håvard, from Old Norse Hávarðr.

håvard.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Hávarðr, a compound name whose first element is traditionally interpreted in two ways.

iain.ety: From Scottish Gaelic. Cognate of John; see there for more.

iara.ety: Borrowed from Nheengatu iiyara (“mistress of water”), from ií + yara.

iben.ety: The name first appears as a male name, possibly shortened from some Germanic compound name. The modern female name is associated with ibenholt (“ebony wood”).

icaro.ety: From Latin Icarus, from Ancient Greek Ἴκαρος.

idar.ety: 19th century invention based on the female name Ida and the -ar ending of Old Norse names, from herr (“army”) or geirr (“spear”).

ide.ety: From the medieval male (and less often female) given name Ida.

idunn.ety: From Old Norse Iðunnr, Iðuðr, from ið + unnr, uðr (“wave”). Cognate with Faroese Íðunn and Iðunn.

ieva.ety: From Latin Eva, ultimately from Hebrew. Also a plant name from ieva (“bird cherry”).

ignasi.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Ignātius Latin Ignātius.

ignatius.ety: From Latin Ignātius, variant of gens name Egnātius, altered to resemble ignis (“fire”), establishing a folk etymology meaning akin to “Fiery One”.

igor.ety: Transliterated from Russian И́горь, a Varangian name derived from Old Norse Yngvarr, Ingvarr, from Yngvi (name of a god) + herr (“army”). Doublet of Ivor and Ihar and Ihor.

ihar.ety: Transliteration of І́гар. Inherited from Old East Slavic Игорь.

ihor.ety: Transliteration of І́гор. Inherited from Old East Slavic Игорь.

ilario.ety: Inherited from Latin Hilarius Inherited from Latin Hilarius.

ilda.ety: Originating as a diminutive of names bearing the Proto-Germanic element *hildiz (“battle, fight”).

ilias.ety: Borrowed from Arabic إِلْيَاس, from Ancient Greek Ἠλίας, from Hebrew אֵלִיָּהוּ (eliyáhu), whence also Elia, Elias.

illia.ety: From Ukrainian Ілля́. Compare Russian Илья́ and Belarusian Ілья́.

ilma.ety: From in the 19th century. Also shortened from Ilmatar, ilman impi, spirits of air in Finnish mythology.

ilona.ety: From Hungarian Ilona. A rare variant of Helen or Helena.

ilva.ety: Of unknown origin etymology, possibly a phonetic coinage.

ilya.ety: From Russian Илья́. Doublet of Elijah.

ilyas.ety: Borrowed from Arabic إِلْيَاس, from Hebrew אליהו.

imanol.ety: Coined by Sabino Arana from Hebrew עִמָּנוּאֵל ('imánuel).

imelda.ety: From Spanish Imelda, from Imelda Lambertini, from Proto-Germanic *ermunaz (“all, whole”) + *hildiz (“battle”).

imogen.ety: First used by William Shakespeare in Cymbeline, a misprint for Innogen, from Scottish Gaelic inghean (“girl, maiden”).

imre.ety: From Germanic Amalrich or Emmerich, Proto-Germanic *amal (“vigor, bravery”) + rīhhi (“ruler”) The old Hungarian variants of the Latin names Emericus, Emmeric are: Emrik, Emrih, Imreh.

ina.ety: Short form of given names ending in -ina, e.g. Georgina, Christina, Wilhelmina.

inaki.ety: Coined by Sabino Arana, from Latin Ignatius.

indiana.ety: From Indiana Territory<ety from From Indian + -a. From Indiana Territory, dating from 1800, noting the territory's large Native American Indian population.

indra.ety: From Sanskrit इन्द्र. Doublet of indra.

ines.ety: From Latin Agnes, from Ancient Greek Ἁγνή, from Ancient Greek ἁγνός (“pure, chaste”), Ancient Greek ἁγνεία (“purity, chastity”).

inez.ety: Anglicised form of Spanish Inés and Portuguese Inês, both from Latin Agnes, from Ancient Greek Ἁγνή. First used in 18th century English poetry and plays referring to Inês de Castro.

inga.ety: From Danish, Norwegian, Swedish Inga etc., all from Old Norse Inga.

ingar.ety: A new coinage from the Old Norse elements Ing- "god Ing or Yngvi" + -ar, either herr "army" or geirr "spear".

inge.ety: Short form of female given names beginning with Ing-, Inge-, Ingi- Old Norse ("the god Ing or Yngvi").

ingelin.ety: 18th century coinage from names beginning with Ing-, Inge-, such as Inger + the ending -lin(e), as in Malin, Elin, Karoline, etc.

ingerid.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Ingiríðr, a variant of the fuller Ingifríðr. The first element is the divine name Ing, another name of Yngvi, while the second ultimately continues fríðr (“beautiful, fair”).

ingo.ety: Pet form of names in Ing-, chiefly Ingolf.

ingolf.ety: Old Norse Ingólfr, from the god Ing or Yngvi, and ulfr ("wolf").

ingunn.ety: Old Norse Ingunnr, from Ing (“the god Ing/Yngvi”) and unna (“to love”).

ingvald.ety: Old Norse Ingivaldr, from Ingi ("the god Ing/Yngvi") and valdr ("ruler").

ingvild.ety: Old Norse Yngvildr, from Yngvi ("the god Ing/Yngvi") and hildr ("battle").

inna.ety: Transliteration of Russian И́нна, of uncertain origin. (One suggestion is Ancient Greek ἴννα, from ἴννην (“little girl”).).

inès.ety: From Latin Agnes, from Ancient Greek Ἁγνή, from Ancient Greek ἁγνός (“pure, chaste”), Ancient Greek ἁγνεία (“purity, chastity”).

inês.ety: From Latin Agnes, from Ancient Greek ἁγνός (“chaste”).

ioan.ety: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic Іѡаннъ, from Ancient Greek Ἰωάννης, a contraction of the Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yôḥānān); see John for more.

ioannis.ety: Transliteration of Greek Ιωάννης, a male given name used in (modern) Greece. Doublet of Giannis.

iola.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἴον (“violet”), evoking the flower's symbolism of modesty and beauty.

iolanda.ety: Either a variant of Violante, from Late Latin Violantes, from Latin viola (“violet”), through Old French Yolande; or from Ancient Greek ἴον ἄνθος (“violet flower”).

ion.ety: A non-standard spelling of Jon, the sequence io stands for.

iona.ety: Probably a misreading of Latin Ioua, an attempt to Latinize Old Irish Í.

iracema.ety: Coined by Q455703 as the name of the title character in the novel Iracema. According to the author, it means “honey lips”, although honey is eíra and lip is apûã//embé.

iraci.ety: From Old Tupi eíra, from Old Tupi sy Navarro considers it a doublet of Araci.

iratxe.ety: The given name comes from the name of the monastery.

irenee.ety: From Latin Irenaeus, from Ancient Greek Εἰρηναῖος, from εἰρήνη (“peace”).

ireneusz.ety: Latin Irenaeus, from Ancient Greek Εἰρηναῖος, from εἰρηναῖος, from εἰρήνη.

irina.ety: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic Ирина, from Ancient Greek Εἰρήνη, from εἰρήνη (“peace”).

irineu.ety: From Latin Īrēnaeus, from Ancient Greek Εἰρηναῖος, from εἰρήνη (“peace”).

irma.ety: From German Irma in the nineteenth century. Short form of Germanic names beginning with irm(en)-, erm(en) "whole, entire", from Proto-Germanic *ermunaz.

irmgard.ety: Name of an 11th century German saint, from Old High German *irmin + gard (“enclosure, protection”).

irving.ety: Variant of the Scottish habitational surname Irvine, probably from a Celtic word cognate with Welsh ir, yr (“fresh”) + afon (“river”).

irwin.ety: From a medieval given name Erwin, from Eoforwine, from Old English eofor (“boar”) + wine (“friend”), the latter of which is from Proto-West Germanic *wini.

iryna.ety: From Іри́на, akin to English Irene.

isaak.ety: Borrowed from Latin Isaāc, from Ancient Greek Ἰσαᾱ́κ, from Biblical Hebrew יִצְחָק (Yiṣḥāq), literally “he laughs”.

isabela.ety: Borrowed from Spanish Isabela. The province is named after Isabella II of Spain.

isabell.ety: From Isabel. From Spanish Isabel, Portuguese Isabel.

isabelle.ety: From Old Spanish Isabel in the 12th century, ultimately from Hebrew אֱלִישֶׁבַע (Elishéva, “my God is an oath”).

isac.ety: A less common spelling of Isak.

isadora.ety: A variant of Isidora, from Latin Isidōra, equivalent of Īsidōrus, from Ancient Greek Ῑ̓σῐ́δωρος (“gift of Isis”).

isadore.ety: A non-standard variant of Isidore, possibly inspired by the well-known feminine variant Isadora of Isidora.

isaias.ety: From Old Galician-Portuguese Ysayas, borrowed from Latin Īsaias, Ēsaias, from Ancient Greek Ἠσαΐας, from Hebrew יְשַׁעְיָהוּ (yəšaʿyā́hū).

isaura.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Isaura Latin Isaura.

isaías.ety: From Old Galician-Portuguese Ysayas, borrowed from Latin Īsaias, Ēsaias, from Ancient Greek Ἠσαΐας, from Hebrew יְשַׁעְיָהוּ (yəšaʿyā́hū).

isela.ety: Probably a variant of Isabel or Isabella.

isidora.ety: Name of a fourth-century saint. The feminine equivalent of Isidore, from Ancient Greek Ἰσιδώρα (“gift of Isis”).

isidore.ety: French form of the name of early Spanish saints, from Ancient Greek Ἰσίδωρος, meaning "gift of (the goddess) Isis".

isis.ety: Latin Īsis from Ancient Greek Ἶσις, from Egyptian ꜣst (ꜣst).

isolde.ety: Borrowed from the German Isolde, German form of Iseult.

itziar.ety: Perhaps from ihintz + ihar. The given name comes from the name of the shrine.

iuliia.m: Of the gens Julia, a patrician Roman family.

iva.ety: From Ivo. A hypocoristic form of Ivan.

ivana.ety: Borrowed from Slavic - From various Slavic languages, such as Ивана.

ivanna.ety: Transliteration of Ukrainian Іва́нна. Doublet of Jane.

ivar.ety: From Old Norse Ívarr, from Proto-Norse *ᛁᚹᚨᚺᚨᚱᛃᚨᛉ, from Proto-Germanic *īwaz (“yew tree, bow”) + *harjaz (“warrior, army”); also partly merged with Old Norse Yngvarr.

ivete.ety: Borrowed from French Yvette, from Yves + -ette, with Yves deriving from a Germanic name and -ette being a French suffix. Doublet of Ivone and female equivalent of Ivo.

ivone.ety: Borrowed from French Yvonne, a suffix deriving from the name Yves, of Germanic origin. Doublet of Ivete and female equivalent of Ivo.

ivor.ety: Medieval form of Old Norse Ívarr. Doublet of Igor.

ivory.ety: The surname is habitational from Ivry in Normandy, and in some cases patronymic from a diminutive of Ivor. The modern given name is associated with ivory.

ivy.ety: From ivy, the name of a plant.

izabella.ety: Either from Spanish Isabel or Hebrew אִיזֶבֶל (Jezebel).

izaro.ety: The given name comes from the name of the island.

izzy.ety: From the root of the names + -y.

jacenty.ety: Medieval Latin Jacintus, from Classical Hyacinthus, from Ancient Greek Ὑάκινθος. Doublet of Hiacynt.

jacinda.ety: Probably an alteration of Spanish Jacinta under the influence of the female given name suffix -inda.

jacinta.ety: Borrowed from Jacinta, transferred into English by the Australian and New Zealand Catholic community in honour of Portuguese saint Jacinta Marto. Variant of Jacinda and Jacintha.

jack.ety: From Middle English Jak, Jakke (also Jackin, Jankyn, etc.), from Anglo-Norman Jakke, *Janke, from Middle Dutch Janke, diminutive of Jan (“John”); equivalent to John + -kin. Doublet of Yankee.

jacqueline.ety: From French Jacqueline, a feminine diminutive form of Jacques (“James”), from Hebrew יעקב (ya'akóv, “Jacob”), from the root עקב (‘akev, “heel”), because the biblical patriarch Jacob was born just behind Esau.

jade.ety: From jade (“jade”), in imitation of English usage.

jagger.ety: Occupational surname from Yorkshire, jagger (“peddler”). The modern given name use is partly after Mick Jagger.

jake.ety: Originally a medieval variant of Jack; today also used as a diminutive form of Jacob and James.

jalen.root: a combination of James and Len

jalisa.ety: Ja- (possibly from Jane) + -lisa (possibly form Lisa; diminutive of Elizabeth), styled similar to names like Alyssa or Melissa; predominantly an African American name in the United States during the latter half of the 20th century.

jami.ety: Diminutive of Viljami, Jalmari and Benjamin.

janae.ety: 20th-century coinage from Jane, possibly influenced by Renée.

janaina.ety: Of unknown origin. Some theories include: From Guarany îanã + îna literally "river mother" From an alternative name to the orisha Iemanjá, of Yoruba origin.

jandira.ety: From Old Tupi jurandira (“she who says sweet words”), from jura (“mouth”) + ndieira (“honey bee”). The male name Jurandir comes from the same origin.

jane.ety: A contracted Norwegian form of Johane, a variant of Johanne.

janet.ety: From Jane + -et, q.v. Chiefly Scottish until the 19th century.

jani.ety: From Swedish Jan, a diminutive of (a cognate of) Johannes.

janice.ety: Variant of Jane under apparent influence from Alice, Bernice, Eunice, etc., from French Jeanne, from Middle French Jehanne, from Medieval Latin Johanna, variant of Latin Ioanna under influence from Latin Iōhannēs.

janina.ety: From Polish Janina and possibly other Slavic languages as well.

janine.ety: From French Janine and Jeannine under influence from Jane, from Jeanne + -ine, q.v.

janita.ety: 20th century variant of Johanna (like Janika and Janina), in the fashion of names like Anita and Marita. Analyzable as a feminine form of Jani.

janna.ety: Either a feminine derivative of Jan or a contracted form of Johanna. Both source names belong to the Johannes name family.

janne.ety: A Norwegian female given name, either derived from the male given name Jan or contracted from Johanne.

january.ety: From Middle English Januarie, januari, re-latinised forms of Middle English Janevere, Ieneuer, from Anglo-Norman genever, from Latin Iānuārius (“(month) of Janus”), a compound of Iānus + -ārius.

jaouad.ety: Borrowed from Arabic جَوَاد Borrowed from Arabic جَوَاد.

jari.ety: Originally a pet form of Jalmar, Jalmari. Generally credited to Coined by Jalmari Finne, whose godson (born in 1937) was likely the first to bear the name.

jarl.ety: From the title of jarl (earl), used as a given name since the 19th century.

jaromir.ety: Of Slavic origin, in which the first element could be Proto-Slavic *jaro (“spring”) and the second element *mirъ (“peace, world”).

jarosław.ety: Inherited from Old Polish Jarosław, Jerosław, from Proto-Slavic *Jaroslavъ, from *jarъ + *slava.

jarrett.ety: Variant of Garrett, a medieval form of Gerard and Gerald.

jarvis.ety: A surname derived from a Middle English form of Gervase.

jasmine.ety: From French jasmin, from Arabic يَاسَمِين, from Classical Persian یاسمین (yāsamīn), from earlier یاسمن (yāsaman), from Middle Persian yʾsmn' (yāsaman).

jasper.ety: A name given to one of the Magi in a medieval European cult, from Biblical Hebrew גִּזְבָּר (gizbar), ultimately from Old Median *ganǰabarah; see it for more.

javion.ety: African-American coinage from the second half of the 20th century. Compare Javon, Jayvion.

javon.ety: African-American coinage from the second half of the 20th century. Compare Javion, Jayvion.

javonte.ety: African-American coinage from the second half of the 20th century. Compare Javon, Javion.

jax.ety: Shortened from Jackson, Jaxon or fanciful spelling of the surname Jacks.

jaxton.ety: Modern American coinage from Jax, Jaxon, rhyming with Axton, Paxton, Daxton.

jayceon.ety: Fanciful variant of Jason, influenced by Jay and Jayce.

jayde.ety: Variant of Jade, perhaps influenced by Jay.

jayden.ety: Invented at the end of the 20th century by American parents who wanted to combine the initial "J" with the fashionable sound of Aidan, Braden, Caden and Hayden.

jayla.ety: 1990s coinage similar to Jaylen and Kayla.

jaylee.ety: 20th-century coinage from Jay + Lee. Compare Jaylynn, Kaylee.

jaylene.ety: 20th-century coinage from Jay + -lene ending as in Charlene, Jolene, etc.

jaylin.ety: 20th-century coinage, variant of Jaylen and Jaylynn.

jayse.ety: Non-standard spelling of Jase or Jace.

jayson.ety: Modern variant of Jason, perhaps influenced by Jay.

jayvion.ety: African-American coinage from the second half of the 20th century. Compare Javion, Javon.

jazlyn.ety: Modern invention, from Jasmine and Lyn, or variation of Jocelyn.

jazz.ety: A fanciful spelling variant of Jaz and Jas.

jean.ety: From French Jean, from Old French Jehan, from Latin Iōhannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης, from Hebrew יוחנן (Yôḥānān), literally “God is gracious”.

jeanette.ety: From Jean + -ette or misspelling of French Jeannette, from Jeanne + -ette, q.v. Originally chiefly Scottish.

jeanne.ety: From French Jeanne, from Middle French Jehanne, from Medieval Latin Johanna, variant of Latin Ioanna under influence from Latin Iōhannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννα, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָה (Yôḥānāh), literally “God is gracious”.

jeannette.ety: From French Jeannette, from Jeanne + -ette, q.v.

jeannine.ety: From French Jeannine, from Jeanne + -ine, q.v. Sometimes also parsed as a diminutive of English Jean, Jeanne, etc.

jedidiah.ety: Borrowed from Hebrew יְדִידְיָה (“beloved of Yahweh”).

jeff.ety: From Jeffrey, a variant of Geoffrey, from Middle English Geffrey, from an Old French aristocratic name, Geoffroi (> West, East ), itself from Proto-French forms (latinized in -us) Jotfredus, Jozsfredus.

jefferson.ety: From Jeffrey + -son. The placenames in the United States are named for Thomas Jefferson.

jelena.ety: Borrowed from Еле́на and Pannonian Rusyn Єлена, from Latin Helena, from Ancient Greek Ἑλένη. Doublet of Helen and Ellen.

jemima.ety: From the name of a minor biblical character, from Hebrew יְמִימָה (“dove”). By folk etymology also used as a feminine form of James.

jenessa.ety: Most likely a Blend of Jennifer + Vanessa.

jenna.ety: A Cornish name, usually as a diminutive form of Jennifer.

jennica.ety: Blend of Jennifer + Jessica, a 20th-century coinage.

jennifer.ety: From Cornish Gweniver, from Middle Cornish Gwynnever (cognate with Welsh Gwenhwyfar), from Proto-Brythonic *Gwɨnnohuɨβar. Doublet of Guinevere.

jenny.ety: From Jen + -y, historically as a hypocoristic form of Janet, Jane, etc. but now more often used as a diminutive of Jennifer.

jens.ety: Medieval vernacular form of Johannes (“John”). Recorded in Denmark since the 14th century.

jere.ety: Short form of Jeremias. Comparable to English Jerry.

jeremie.ety: From Latin Jeremias From Latin Jeremias, from Ancient Greek Ἰερεμίας, from Biblical Hebrew יִרְמְיָה (Yirməyâ, “Jeremiah”), literally “the will raise”.

jericho.ety: From Middle English Iericho, from Old English Iericho, from Latin Ierīchō, from Ancient Greek Ἰερῑχώ, from Biblical Hebrew יְרִיחוֹ (yərīḥō), recorded early as Ugaritic 𐎊𐎗𐎃 (yrḫ).

jerilyn.ety: From Jerry. From Middle English Gerard, from Old French Gerart, from Frankish *Gaiʀahard, from *gaiʀ (“spear”) + *hard(ī) (“hard, brave”).

jerome.ety: From the Old French vernacular form of the saint's name Hieronymus, from Ancient Greek Ἱερώνυμος. Doublet of Geronimo and Hieronymus.

jeronimo.ety: Inherited from Old Spanish, from Latin Hierōnymus, from Ancient Greek Ῑ̔ερώνυμος, from ἱερός (“sacred”) + ὄνομα (“name”).

jerzy.ety: Inherited from Old Polish Jirzy, Jurzy, from Old Czech Jiří, Juří, from Latin Geōrgius, from Ancient Greek Γεώργιος.

jesenia.ety: Variant of Gjesenia, first recorded in the 19th century, possibly cognate with German Gesine.

jesper.ety: Medieval Danish variant of Kasper (same as Caspar), with possible confusion with Esbern, Espen, from Old Norse Ásbjǫrn.

jessa.ety: 20th-century coinage from Jessie + feminine suffix -a; compare Jenna from Jenny.

jessica.ety: First used by William Shakespeare in Merchant of Venice in the early 17th century, probably from Hebrew 5=Iscah in Genesis 11:29, Jescha in the Wycliffe version (yiská), a proper name meaning "he will see/behold/look for".

jewel.m: A precious or semi-precious stone; gem, gemstone.
