jewell.ety: From Middle English - Medieval/Middle English form of a Breton saint's name, from Old Breton Judicaël "lord" + "generous." The second element is from hael (“generous.

jibril.ety: Borrowed from Arabic جِبْرِيل Doublet of Gabriel.

jill.ety: A variant of Gill, diminutive of Gillian, a medieval form of Juliana, ultimately from Latin.

jimena.ety: From Old Spanish Ximena, from Basque Ximena.

jo.ety: Short form of names with the element jo (such as Jostein and Jorid), from jór (“horse”).

joachim.ety: From Latin Iōākīm, from Ancient Greek Ἰωακείμ, Ἰωακίμ (2 Kings 24:1), from Biblical Hebrew יְהוֹיָקִים (yəhôyâqîm), literally “may Yahweh raise up”.

joane.ety: Coined by Sabino Arana, based on Ancient Greek Ἰωάννα.

joanne.ety: From Old French Joanne, from Latin Joanna, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννα, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָה (Yôḥānāh), literally “God is gracious”, the feminized form of יְהוֹחָנָן (Yəhōḥānān) which produced John and its many doublets.

joao.ety: From Old Galician-Portuguese Joan, from Latin Iōhannēs, a variant of Iōannēs, from New Testament Ancient Greek Ἰωάννης, contraction from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (yôḥānān), literally “God is gracious”.

joar.ety: Jo + -ar; from Old Norse Jóarr, from jór (“horse”) + herr (“army”), or a variant of Jógeirr, from geirr (“spear”). Cognate with Old Swedish Iōar.

jocelyn.ety: From the Middle English male given name from Old French Joscelin, German Gautzelin, diminutive of names beginning with the tribal name Gaut (“a Geat, a Goth”).

jocelynn.ety: A rare non-standard spelling of Jocelyn with -lynn.

jody.ety: Variant of Judy, diminutive of Judith, q.v.

joe.ety: (diminutive form) of various names beginning with Jo..., particularly the male names Joseph and, less often, Joel, Josiah and Josias.

johann.ety: Borrowed from German Johann (“male given name”), a short form of Johannes (“male given name”), ultimately from Latin Iōhannēs (“male given name”), from Ancient Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs, “male given name”).

johanne.ety: A younger form of Johanna, ultimately from Latin Iōhanna, a variant of Joanna, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννα (Iōánna), from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָה (Yôḥānāh, “Yahweh is gracious”).

johnna.ety: A rare feminine form of John recorded since the 18th century.

johnny.ety: From John + -y. In the sense of an Englishman, compare John Bull.

johnson.ety: A patronymic surname from John + -son, literally “son of John”.

jokin.ety: Coined by Sabino Arana, based on Spanish Joaquín.

jolanta.ety: Cognate with French Yolande, Italian Iolanda, and Spanish Yolanda.

jolene.ety: A blend of the element Jo... in common anglicized forms of various Hebrew names and the ending...lene shared by the German names Helene and Magdalene.

jona.ety: From Biblical Hebrew יוֹנָה (Yōnā, “dove”), through biblical tradition. The form corresponds more closely to the Hebrew name than Jonas, whose final ⟨s⟩ reflects the Greek and Latin nominative forms.

jonas.ety: From Latin Iōnās, from Koine Greek Ἰωνᾶς, from Biblical Hebrew יוֹנָה (yônâh, “dove”). Doublet of Jonah.

jonay.ety: Jonay is assumed to be derived from the second half of the name of Garajonay peak (the highest point on the island of La Gomera), formerly Garagono(c)he, from Guanche.

joni.ety: Commonly used as a diminutive of Joan.

jonn.ety: A spelling variant of Jon and John, with doubled ⟨n⟩ representing a short vowel followed by long.

jordan.ety: From Latin Iordanēs, from Ancient Greek Ἰορδάνης, from Biblical Hebrew יַרְדֵּן (yardén, “Jordan (river)”). Doublet of Yarden.

jordy.ety: Shortened from Jordan + -y, and a modern spelling variant of Geordie.

jorgelina.ety: From Jorge + -ina, with an l to separate the vowels e and i.

jori.ety: Phonetic rendering of Swedish Georg (“George”). Also recorded as a pet form of Jorma.

jorid.ety: Old Norse Jóríðr, from jór (“horse”) and fríðr (“beautiful”).

jorunn.ety: From jǫfurr (“wild boar”) (cognate to Old English eofor), and unna (“to love”).

jose.ety: From Spanish/Portuguese José, from Hebrew. Doublet of Joseph.

josef.ety: From Latin Iōsēphus, from Ancient Greek Ἰωσήφ, from Hebrew יוֹסֵף (“(God) shall add”). Doublet of Albanian Jozef (“Joseph”).

josephine.ety: From French Joséphine, diminutive of Josèphe, feminine form of Joseph. Popularized in English by Josephine Bonaparte, the empress of Napoleonic France.

jostein.ety: Old Norse Jósteinn, from jór (“horse”) and steinn (“stone”).

journey.ety: From journey at the end of the 20th century.

jovanni.ety: From Spanish Jovanni, from Italian Giovanni.

joy.ety: From the noun joy, first used by Puritans in the 17th century.

joyce.ety: Medieval (Middle English) given name from Old French Josse, name of a seventh century saint Latinized as Iodocus, from Breton Iodoc, diminutive of iudh (“lord”), from Proto-Celtic *yowdos.

jozef.ety: From Latin Iōsēphus, from Ancient Greek Ἰωσήφ, from Hebrew יוֹסֵף.

joziah.ety: Rare non-standard spelling variant of Josiah.

joão.ety: From Old Galician-Portuguese Joan, from Latin Iōhannēs, a variant of Iōannēs, from New Testament Ancient Greek Ἰωάννης, contraction from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (yôḥānān), literally “God is gracious”.

juanita.ety: From Spanish Juanita, from Juana + -ita (“-ette”), from Old Spanish Johanna, from Medieval Latin Johanna, variant of Joanna, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννα, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָה (Yôḥānāh), literally “God is gracious”.

juanito.ety: From Juan, equivalent to the English John.

judd.ety: From a Middle English short form of the given name Jordan.

jude.ety: Short form of Judas, used in an attempt to distinguish the Apostle Judas Thaddaeus from Judas Iscariot. From Old Testament Judah, Hebrew יְהוּדָה (yehudá), said to mean “praised”.

judicael.ety: English form of Judicaël, itself the French form of the Old Breton name Iudicael, derived from Old Breton iudd (“lord, ruler, prince”) + Old Breton cael (“generous, noble”).

judson.ety: From a Middle English short form of the given name Jordan + son.

jule.m: Of the gens Julia, a patrician Roman family.

jules.m: Of the gens Julia, a patrician Roman family.

juli.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Iūlius Latin Iūlius.
juli.m: Of the gens Julia, a patrician Roman family.

julian.ety: Latin Iūliānus (“Roman personal name”), shortened by the loss of the Latin nominative ending -us.

juliane.ety: Borrowed from German Juliane Borrowed from German Juliane.

juliann.ety: A variant of Julian, Juliana or Julianne. Can also be interpreted as a combination of Julia + Ann.
juliann.m: Of the gens Julia, a patrician Roman family.

julianna.ety: Modern combination of Julie + Anna, perhaps sometimes intended as a form of Juliana.

julianne.ety: A 19th/20th century variant of Juliana. Can also be interpreted as a combination of Julia + Anne.
julianne.m: Of the gens Julia, a patrician Roman family.

juliano.ety: Latin Iūliānus; doublet of Julião, from an Old Galician-Portuguese borrowing. These two forms displaced Old Galician-Portuguese Juião, which was inherited from Latin.

julie.m: Of the gens Julia, a patrician Roman family.

juliet.ety: Borrowed from Italian Giulietta, diminutive of Giulia, from Latin Iūlia, feminine of Iūlius, a Roman family name. Cognate with French Juliette.
juliet.m: Of the gens Julia, a patrician Roman family.

juline.ety: Of unknown origin. in Norway. Several origins have been proposed.

julita.m: Of the gens Julia, a patrician Roman family.

juliusz.m: Of the gens Julia, a patrician Roman family.

july.ety: From Middle English Julie,julius,julye, from Anglo-Norman julie, from Old French jule, juil, from Latin iūlius (Gaius Julius Caesar's month), perhaps a contraction of *Iovilios, "descended from Jove".

june.ety: From Middle English June, june, re-Latinised variants of earlier Middle English Juyn, juyng, from Old French juing, juin, from Latin iūnius, the month of the goddess Iuno (“Juno”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yéwHō.

juni.ety: From juni (“June”), partly as a translation of the English given name June.

juniper.ety: A topographic surname from juniper. In some cases matronymic from an equivalent of Jennifer influenced by folk etymology.

jurandir.ety: From Old Tupi îurandira (“he who says sweet words”), from îura (“mouth”) + ndieira (“honey bee”). The female name Jandira comes from the same origin.

jurema.ety: From Old Tupi îurema (“stinky thorn tree”), from îu (“thorn”) + rema (“bad odor”).

justin.ety: Name of early saints, Latin Iūstīnus, from Iūstus + -īnus, from iūstus (“just”).

justine.ety: From French Justine, from Latin Iūstīna, name of early saints, feminine of Iūstīnus, derivative of Iūstus, from iūstus (“just”). The feminine equivalent of Justin.

jérome.ety: From Latin Hierōnymus, from Ancient Greek Ἱερώνυμος. Doublet of Hiéronyme.

jérémie.ety: From Latin Jeremias From Latin Jeremias, from Ancient Greek Ἰερεμίας, from Biblical Hebrew יִרְמְיָה (Yirməyâ, “Jeremiah”), literally “the will raise”.

jérôme.ety: From Latin Hierōnymus, from Ancient Greek Ἱερώνυμος. Doublet of Hiéronyme.

jørgen.ety: Borrowed from Middle Low German Jurian, a Low German form of Georg, from Latin Georgius, from Ancient Greek Γεώργιος (Geṓrgios), from Ancient Greek γεωργός (geōrgós, “farmer”), from Ancient Greek γῆ (gê.

kadence.m: The act or state of declining or sinking.

kahina.ety: Borrowed from Arabic كَاهِنَة Borrowed from Arabic كَاهِنَة.

kaidence.m: The act or state of declining or sinking.

kaila.ety: Kaila (“style”),a loan word from English style; can also be construed as ka (“the”) + ila (“dark birthmark; darkness; seedling”).

kaili.ety: Modern combination of Kai (“Catherine”) and Lii (“Elizabeth”).

kairi.ety: Modern coinage, possibly a combination of Kai (“Catherine”) and Maria.

kaisa.ety: Medieval diminutive of Katariina (compare Maisa), cognate to Swedish Kajsa.

kaiser.ety: From English Kaiser, from German Kaiser, which see.

kaj.ety: Used in Denmark since the 15th century and Latinised as Caius, possibly originating from the Roman name. Related to modern English and German Kai.

kaja.ety: 20th century creation from kaja (“echo”). Also interpreted as a variant of Kaia, from Katariina (“Catherine”).

kajetan.ety: From the Latin Caiētānus (“inhabitant of Gaeta”), re-Latinized from Italian Gaetano, name of a saint.

kaleb.ety: From Hebrew כלב (“dog”), possibly referring to a dog’s unconditional devotion to its master.

kalena.ety: Ka (“the”) + lena (“yellow”).(Yellow was a royal color.) Later also used as a phonetic rendering of the English Karen.

kalia.ety: Kalia (“waited for”), also the name of a native tree of the linden family.

kamil.ety: Borrowed from a Romance language, ultimately from the Roman cognomen, Latin Camillus, probably of Etruscan origin, but of unknown meaning.

karen.ety: From Danish Karen, a vernacular form of Catherine that emerged in medieval Denmark. The term later acquired a distinct contemporary social meaning.

karin.ety: From Swedish Karin or Danish Karin, a medieval form of Katarina, ultimately from Ancient Greek Αἰκατερῑ́νη. See also Karen.

karleigh.ety: A rare spelling variant of Carly.

kasandra.ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Κασσάνδρα.

kase.ety: Modern spelling variant of Case. The surname derives from German Käse.

kaspar.ety: A variant of Kasper, reflecting the older continental European form Caspar or Kaspar.

kasper.ety: Variant of Kaspar, from Medieval Latin Caspar (“male given name”), traditionally the name of one of the Magi in Western Christianity.

katarina.ety: From the Ancient Greek Αἰκατερίνη, name of a saint.

katarzyna.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Catharina, Catherina.

katell.ety: Borrowed from Breton Katell Borrowed from Breton Katell.

katharine.ety: A variant spelling of Catherine, based on the folk etymology that it would derive from Greek καθαρός (katharos "pure").

kathleen.ety: Anglicization of Caitlín, an Irish equivalent of the English Catherine.

katja.ety: From Russian Катя. Cognate with English Katya.

katrin.ety: From Ancient Greek Αἰκατερίνη, *Ἑκατερίνη, of debated meaning, possibly from ἑκάτερος (“each of the two”), or from the name of the goddess Hecate.

katya.ety: Transliteration of Ка́тя, diminutive of Екатери́на, Катери́на.

kaue.ety: Borrowed from Old Tupi kaûã, meaning "falcon".

kaydence.m: The act or state of declining or sinking.

kayla.ety: A modern invention possibly based on Kay or Michaela; possibly formed on the pattern of Layla.

kaylee.ety: Coined toward the end of the 20th century A combination of Kay + Lee. A variant of the surname Cayley or Keeley.

keaton.ety: A variant of Caton or Keeton, or a habitational name from Keaton in Ermington, Devon, possibly derived from Welsh cae (“hedge, enclosure”) + Middle English toun (“farmstead, settlement”).

keegan.ety: Borrowed from Irish Mac Aodhagáin (“son of Aidan”).

keeley.ety: Reduced Anglicized from Irish Ó Caollaidhe (“descendant of Caollaidhe”), a personal name based on the adjective caol (“slender, graceful”).

keelin.ety: Borrowed from Irish Caoilfhionn, from caol (“thin, slender”) + fionn (“light, fair”).

keenan.ety: From Irish Cianán, a diminutive of Cian.

keira.ety: A modern feminine form of Kieran, from Irish ciar (“black, dark, little dark one”).

keith.ety: As a Scottish surname, from the placename in Moray, Scotland, from Scottish Gaelic Cèith, meaning "wood" or "from the battleground," which is probably borrowed from Pictish *ᚉᚓᚈ (cēt) meaning "wood", or a forest, from Proto-Brythonic *koɨd.

kelli.ety: From Kerli. Combination of Kertu (“Gertrude”) and Lii (“Elizabeth”).

kelly.ety: Borrowed from Irish Ó Ceallaigh. Doublet of Kellogg and Callahan.

kelsea.ety: Variant of Kelsey, presumably influenced by Chelsea.

kelvin.ety: Of Celtic/Scottish Gaelic origin, possibly from caol (“narrow”) or coille (“wooded”) + abhainn (“river”). The surname is derived from the river.

kendal.ety: From Old English Cent + dæl = "valley of the river Kent".

kendall.ety: From the placename Kendal in Cumbria, "valley of the river Kent", and Kendale in Humberside, from Old Norse kelda (“spring”) + dalr (“valley”).

kendra.ety: Coined in the latter half of the twentieth century, presumably a Blend of Kenneth + Sandra.

kenley.ety: Shortened from McKenley, variant of McKinley Habitational from Old English Cena (“a man's name”) + lēah (“woodland clearing”).

kenna.ety: As a Scottish surname, shortened from McKenna. As a Manx and Irish surname, from Ó Cionaodha//Ó Cionaoith (“descendant of Cionaodh”), a name usually Anglicized as Kenneth.

kennedy.ety: Borrowed from Irish Ó Cinnéidigh (ceann (“head”) + éidigh (“ugly”)) or Scottish Gaelic Ceannaideach (ceann (“head”) + aideach (“ugly”). Compare Kenneth and Irish eitigh (“refuse, reject”).

kenneth.ety: Anglicized form of two Goidelic names, Old Irish Cináed, the name of Scottish kings derived from Pictish *ᚉᚔᚅᚔᚑᚇ (Ciniod), and the saint's name Cainnech, literally “handsome” (modern Scottish Gaelic Coinneach), as in the surname Mackenzie.

kent.ety: Inherited from Middle English Kent, from Old English Cent, from Latin Cantium, from Brythonic *Cantio (compare Old Irish céite (“gathering, folkmoot, hillock”)), from Proto-Celtic *kantos (“corner, rim”).

kenton.ety: From either the Old English personal name Cena or cyne- (“royal”) + tūn (“enclosure; settlement, town”).

kenya.ety: Borrowed from English Kenya, from the name of Mount Kenya. The modern form was recorded in the 19th century by the German missionary and explorer Johann Ludwig Krapf as Kenia and Kegnia.
kenya.m: mountain of brightness; mountain of whiteness

kenzo.ety: Borrowed from Japanese けんぞう (Kenzō).

keona.ety: Ke (“the”) + ona (“attractive”). Also a short form of compound given names beginning thus.

kermit.ety: Variant of English and Manx Kermode, cognate with Irish Mac Diarmata and Scots Gaelic McDiarmid (“son of Dermot”). Popularized in the US by the naming of Kermit Roosevelt (after a Manx ancestor).

kerrigan.ety: Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó Ciaragáin (“grandson/descendant of Ciaragán”), a byname from a double diminutive of ciar (“black”).

kerry.ety: As an English surname, from a personal name derived from Old Norse Kári. As an Irish surname, from Ó Ciardha (“descendant of Ciardha”), from ciar (“black”).

kevin.ety: Name of a seventh-century Irish saint, from Irish Caoimhghin or Caoimhín, from Old Irish Cóemgen, literally “dear birth/person”. It first became popular outside Ireland in the mid-twentieth century.

kezia.ety: From Hebrew קְצִיעָה (“cassia tree”). Compare cassia.

khaleesi.ety: Borrowed from Dothraki khaleesi (“queen”), feminine of khal (“king”). Coined by Q181677 for the title of the character Daenerys Targaryen in his book A Song of Ice and Fire (1996) novels.

khloe.ety: Variant of Khloé, a fanciful spelling variant of Chloe, made known in the 2000s by American TV personality Khloé Kardashian.

khrystyna.ety: Transliteration of Христи́на. Name of an early martyr, shortened from Latin Chrīstiāna (“Christian (woman)”).

kiana.ety: Borrowed from Hawaiian Kiana, itself from English Diana. Also used as a modern feminine form of Kian.

killian.ety: An anglicized spelling of Irish Cillian.

kim.ety: Short form of Kimball and Kimberley as a male name, and of Kimberley and Kimberly as a female name.

kimball.ety: From Old Welsh Cynbel, from cyn (“chief”) + bel (“war”). Possibly also from Old English Cynebeald.

kimber.ety: From the name of a 7th-century English female saint, Kyneburga or Cyneburg, from Old English cyne- (“royal”) + burh (“fortress”).

kimberley.ety: English place name "wood or clearing of Kyneburga (a seventh century female saint)", from Old English cyne- (“royal”) + burh (“fortress”) + lēah (“leigh, clearing”).

kinsley.ety: From Old English Cyne (“Royal (a man's name)”) + -s (“'s”) + lēah (“woodland clearing”).

kira.ety: Variant of Kyra or Borrowed from Russian Ки́ра, ultimately from Persian کوروش (Kūrūš). Also used as a respelling of Ciara, from Irish.

kirby.ety: Originally Kirkby, from kirk (“church”) + -by (“habitation”), "village with a church".

kirill.ety: From Russian Кири́лл, from Ancient Greek Κύριλλος. Doublet of Cyril.

kirsten.ety: From North Germanic (Danish Kirsten and Norwegian Kirsten). Doublet of Christina.

kirsti.ety: Medieval pet form of Kristiina, perhaps via Danish Kirsten.

kirstie.ety: A 20th-century variant of Kirsty, a form of Christina.

kiryl.ety: Transliteration of Кіры́л. Borrowed from Ancient Greek Κύριλλος.

kitty.ety: Short form of Katherine and related names -y.

kizzy.ety: From a pet form of Kezia. Explained as a Mandinka name by Alex Haley in Roots (1976).

kjell.ety: Variant of Kjetil and Ketil; also a short form of given names with the Old Norse element ketill (“cauldron", "helmet”). Cognate with Danish Keld and Kjeld.

kjerstin.ety: A variant of Kristine (“Christina”), cognate to Swedish Kerstin.

kjetil.ety: From Old Norse Ketill, from ketill (“(sacrificial) cauldron", "helmet”).

klara.ety: Borrowed from Latin clāra, feminine of clārvs (“bright, shining, clear”), a post-classical name made famous by the 13th century Saint Clara (Clare) of Assisi.

klemens.ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin Clēmens.

knox.ety: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic cnoc (“round hill”).

knut.ety: From Old Norse Knútr, originally a byname; from knútr (“knot”). Cognate with Knútur, Danish Knud and English Canute.

kolbjørn.ety: From Old Norse Kolbjǫrn, from kol (“coal”) + bjǫrn (“bear”).

koldo.ety: Short form of Koldobika, Coined by Sabino Arana from Latin Clodovicus, itself from Frankish *Hlōdowig.

kole.ety: The surname is an anglicization of German Kohl. The given name is a modern spelling variant of Cole.

konrad.ety: From Middle High German Kuonrāt, from Old High German Kuonrad, Chuonrad, from Proto-West Germanic *Kōnirād; equivalent to Proto-West Germanic *kōnī (“bold, brave”) + *rād (“counsel”).

koran.ety: Borrowed from Spanish Corán, from Arabic قُرْآن. Doublet of Alkoran and Qur'an.

kostiantyn.ety: Transliteration of Костянти́н. From Latin Constantinus.

krish.ety: Borrowed from Hindi कृष, from Hindi कृष्णा.

krista.ety: A spelling variant of Christa, a modern short form of Christina, partly borrowed from German Christa.

kristel.ety: Variant of Kristiina (“Christina”). Cognate with German Christel.

kristen.ety: A spelling variant of Kristin, from Christina, fairly popular in the latter half of the twentieth century.

krister.m: Christian; of those who believe in Christ.

kristian.ety: A Nordic spelling of Christian (“male given name”), from Latin Latin Christianus (“Christian; follower of Christ”), from Ancient Greek Χριστιανός (Khristianós, “Christian; follower of Christ”).

kristiana.ety: From Latin Christiana. Feminine form of Kristiāns (“Christian”).

kristin.ety: Borrowed in the 20th century from Norwegian Kristin, a variant of Christina.

kristina.ety: From Latin Christina (“female given name”), a feminine derivative of Christianus (“Christian; male given name”), from Latin Christus (“Christ”), from Ancient Greek Χριστός (Khristós, “anointed”), from χρίω (khríō, “to anoint”).

kristoffer.ety: Saint's name of Ancient Greek origin, cognate with English Christopher.

krystian.m: Christian; of those who believe in Christ.

krzysztof.ety: Contraction of archaic Krzysztofor, from Ancient Greek Χριστόφορος, from Χριστός (“messiah”) + φέρω (“I carry, I bear”).

ksenia.ety: Transliteration of Ксения. Borrowed from Carpathian Rusyn Ксенія and/or Serbo-Croatian Ксенијa//Ksenija, ultimately from Ancient Greek ξενία.

kurt.ety: From kurt (“wolf”), from Ottoman Turkish قورت (Kurt).

kye.ety: Possibly a modern phonetic rendering of Kai, or a short form of Kyle and Kyler.

kyla.ety: Modern invention that can be explained as a feminine form of Kyle with -a.

kylan.ety: Modern coinage; compare Kyle. Variant: Kylen.

kylen.ety: Modern coinage, compare Kyle. Variant: Kylan.

kyler.ety: An American anglicization of Dutch Cuyler "archer" and German Keiler "wild boar". The surname is quite rare.

kylie.ety: Possibly from kylie (“boomerang”). Originally popular in Australia, the name has gained popularity elsewhere in the English-speaking world due to the fame of Kylie Minogue.

kyra.ety: Name of a Greek Orthodox saint, from Medieval Greek κυρά (“lady”), or from Cyra, feminine form of Cyrus. The English name may also be a variant of Keira.

kyree.ety: From a biblical reference Kyree comes from The name Kyria which is Greek in origin & its meaning is "noble lady" 2 John 1:1.

kyrre.ety: A modern revival of Old Norse kyrri (“the peaceful one”), the weak form of kyrr (“calm, peaceful”). The byname is particularly associated with Olav Kyrre, King Olav III of Norway.

kyrylo.ety: From Ukrainian Кири́ло, from Ancient Greek Κύριλλος. Cognate with English Cyril.

kyson.ety: Modern coinage; compare Kyle and Tyson, Bryson.

kåre.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Kári (“male given name”), originally a byname meaning “curly-haired”, related to kárr (“curly-haired; curly, curved”). Thus, the name originally meant “the curly-haired one”.

lachlan.ety: From Scottish Gaelic Lachlann, Lochlann (“land of the lochs, loch or fjord land, i.e. Scandinavia”), said to refer to an immigrant from Norway, a Norseman.
lachlan.m: land of the lochs, loch or fjord land, i.e. Scandinavia

laerte.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Lāertēs Latin Lāertēs, from Ancient Greek Λαέρτης.

lafayette.ety: French surname from Occitan, "the little beech tree".

laina.ety: Proposed as a new given name in the 19th century. Perhaps from laina (“loan”), with the philosophy that children are but a loan to their parents.

lakeisha.ety: An African-American creation from the 1970s, possibly La + Keisha.

lamar.ety: From a placename in Normandy, which was derived from Old French la mare (“the pool”).

lambert.ety: From Middle English Lambert, from Old French Lambert, a saint's name (of a Bishop of Maastricht) brought to England by the Normans, from Proto-West Germanic *Landaberht, from *land (“land”) + *berht (“bright”).

lamia.ety: Borrowed from Arabic لَمْيَاء Borrowed from Arabic لَمْيَاء.

lana.ety: Short form of Alana, or from Russian Ла́на, diminutive of several names including Светла́на.

lance.ety: The surname is derived from a medieval given name Lanzo, short form of names beginning with the Germanic element *land; see land. Doublet of Lanzo.

lancelot.ety: From Middle English Launcelot, from Old French Lancelot, from Frankish *Lanzo, hypocoristic form of names beginning in *Land-, from Proto-Germanic *landą (“land”), and diminutive Old French endings -el and -ot.

landon.ety: Place names in England, from Old English lang (“long”) + dūn (“hill”).

lane.ety: As an English surname, from lane; as an Irish surname, from several origins, including Laighin.
lane.m: A road, street, or similar thoroughfare.

langston.ety: From Old English lang (“long, tall”) + stan (“stone”).

lara.ety: Borrowed from Latin Laura, from the feminine form of laurus (“laurel tree”).

lars.ety: Borrowed from North Germanic, from Latin Laurentius.

lasse.ety: Diminutive of Lars, taken to regular use as a formal given name in the 20th century.

lastenia.ety: From Ancient Greek Λασθένεια, one of Plato's female students, Lastheneia of Mantinea.

laszlo.ety: Borrowed from Hungarian László, from the Slavic given name Ladislav, a variant of Vladislav. Doublet of Ladislaus.

latoya.ety: Possibly La + Toya (“a Spanish pet form of Victoria”).

lauren.ety: Latin Short form of Laurentius. Doublet of Laurence.

laurence.ety: From the name of a third century Roman martyr, Latin Laurentius, "a person from Laurentum", the place name possibly derived from laurus (“laurel”).

laurent.ety: From Old French Lorenz, from Latin Laurentius.

laurenz.ety: Borrowed from Latin Laurentius. A variant of Lorenz.

lauretta.ety: An Italian pet form of Laura; first introduced into English as the name of one of the narrators in the Decameron.

laurie.ety: The given names are s of Short form of Laurence,Lawrence,Laura,Lauren -ie, all ultimately from Latin laurus (“laurel”).

lauro.ety: From the Italian surname, from a personal name derived from Latin laurus.

laverne.ety: 19th-century invention, possibly from the Californian town La Verne, named in the belief that it means "the green" in French.

lavinia.ety: Latin Lavinia, of obscure meaning. Lavinium was a town in ancient Latium.

lawton.ety: From Middle English, from Old English, from hlāw (“hill, ound”) + tūn (“homestead”) (-ton).

layne.m: A road, street, or similar thoroughfare.

layton.ety: Derived from various place names in England.

lazar.ety: Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian Lazar, ultimately from Ancient Greek Λάζαρος, from Hebrew אלעזר (ʼElʻāzār).

lech.ety: Inherited from Old Polish Lech, the name of the legendary founder of the Polish people (see Lech, Czech, and Rus), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *lęxъ, a hypocoristic form of Proto-Slavic *lęděninъ (“wasteland dweller”).

lee.ety: From Old English lēa, the dative case of lēah (“meadow”), originally to denote someone who lived near a meadow.

leena.ety: Vernacular form of Magdaleena, Matleena (“Magdalene”) and Helena. Cognate with Swedish Lena.

leeroy.ety: A less common spelling variant of Leroy.

leia.ety: From the name of a princess in the American fantasy film Star Wars (1977).

leida.ety: From 19th century literature, associated with leidma (“to find, discover”).

leigh.ety: From the nominative case of Old English lēah (“wood, meadow”), 'dweller by the wood or clearing'.

leighton.ety: Various place names in England, Old English leac (“leek”) + tun (“settlement”), also in the sense of a herb garden.

leire.ety: From the name of the monastery San Salvador de Leyre.

leiv.ety: From Old Norse Leifr, which is derived from the feminine noun leif, whence also leiv and leivd. The name is a short form of Old Norse names ending in -leifr, such as Þorleifr (> Torleiv).

lejla.ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ليلى (Leylâ), from Arabic لَيْلَى.

leland.ety: Shortened from McLeland, McClellan, from Irish Mac Giolla Fhaoláin, "son of servant of (Saint) Faolán (=Little Wolf)".

lena.ety: The female name is from the Scandinavian, German and Russian pet form of Helena, Magdalena and Yelena (also spelled Elena).

lenard.ety: Of Germanic origin, it means: as brave as a lion.

lene.ety: From Helene and Magdalene. Cognate with English Lena.

lenin.ety: Borrowed from Russian Ле́нин Borrowed from Russian Ле́нин.

lenita.ety: Variant of Leena, perhaps via a Spanish-Italian(-like) diminutive; could be considered a Blend of Leena + Anita.

lenka.ety: From a diminutive form of Helena and Magdaléna.

lennon.ety: From Irish (“descendant of Lover (Leannán)”) and from Ó Lonáin (“descendant of Blackbird (Lonán)”).

leon.ety: Ultimately from Latin Leo and leo (“lion”), from Ancient Greek Λέων and λέων (“lion”), likely ultimately from a non-Indo-European language.

leonard.ety: From Old French Leonard, name of a 6th century Frankish saint, from Old High German leo (“lion”) or Old High German liut (“person”) and hart (“hard”).

leonid.ety: Borrowed from Леони́д or Ukrainian Леоні́д, from Ancient Greek Λεωνίδας. Cognate with the English historical name Leonidas.

leonida.ety: From Latin Leonida, from Ancient Greek Λεωνίδας.

leonidas.ety: From Ancient Greek Λεωνίδᾱς (“son of Leon / lion”).

leonie.ety: From French Léonie, from Latin Leonia, feminine of Leonius, derived from leo (“lion”).

leonora.ety: From the Italian short form of Eleonora, cognate to Eleanor.

leopold.ety: From Old French Leopold, from Old High German liut (“people”) + bald (“bold”). The first part is sometimes associated by folk etymology with Latin leo (“lion”), as in Leo and Leonard.

leora.ety: Possibly a variant of the modern Israeli name transliterated as Liora, from Hebrew, ליאורה "my light", or an American contraction of Leonora.

leroy.ety: Transferred from the common French surname Leroy, meaning "the king".

lesley.ety: From a placename in Aberdeenshire, originally Lesslyn, Scottish Gaelic lios cuileann (“garden of hollies”).

leslie.ety: From a placename in Aberdeenshire, originally Lesslyn, Scottish Gaelic lios cuileann (“garden of hollies”).

lester.ety: As an English surname, from the placename Leicester.

lesław.ety: From Lech + sława, possibly Coined by Roman Zmorski.

letitia.ety: Name of an obscure Spanish saint, Leticia, from Latin laetitia "gladness".

levin.ety: From Russian Левин, from Леви + -ин (“forming possessives & adjectives”), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew לֵוִי (“Levi”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of Levine.

lewis.ety: From Middle English Lewis, Lowis, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French Louis, from Frankish *Hlūdawīg. Doublet of Louis.

lexa.ety: A short form of Alexa or Alexandra.

leya.ety: Borrowed from Turkish Leya and Arabic لَيْيَا.

leyton.ety: From the name of the River Lea + Old English tūn (“enclosure; settlement, town”). Doublet of Luton.

león.ety: From Spanish León, from Latin legiō (“legion”), named for the Legio VII Gemina, which settled there. Doublet of legion via Old French.

lia.ety: Apocoped variant of Ilìa, from Latin Ēliās, from Ancient Greek Ἠλίας, from Hebrew אֵלִיָּה (ēliyā́, “Jah is my God”).

lilah.ety: Short form of Delilah; also a variant of Leila.

lilia.ety: Borrowed from Latin lilia, plural of lilium (“lily”), or a Latinization of the English Lily.

lilian.ety: Used since the sixteenth century, possibly originally a pet form of Elizabeth, but generally accepted as a variant of Late Latin lilium (“lily”).

lill.ety: Short form of Lillian, Lilly, and other names containing the syllable -li-. Also associated with lille (“little”).

lilli.ety: Pet form of female given names containing the syllable -li-, such as Eliisabet and Aliide. Also explained as Estonian lill (“flower”).

lillian.ety: Used since the sixteenth century, possibly originally a pet form of Elizabeth, but generally accepted as a variant of Late Latin lilium (“lily”).

lillianna.ety: A less common form of Liliana.

lillyanna.ety: Variant of Liliana, or from Lily + Anna.

lily.ety: A 19th-century flower name, from lily. Also a diminutive of Lilian and sometimes Elizabeth.

lilyana.ety: Transliteration of Bulgarian Лиляна, equivalent to English Lilian.

lina.ety: Short form of any female name ending in -lina, such as Angelina, Carolina, Evelina. It can also be construed as a rare feminine form of Linus.

lincoln.ety: Inherited from Middle English Lincolne Inherited from Middle English Lincolne, from Old English Lincolle, Lindcolen, Lindcylene, from Latin Lindum Colōnia (“the Roman settlement Lindum Colonia”).

linda.ety: Latinised short form of Germanic compound names ending in -lind, -linde (“tender, soft”) (English -inda), such as Sieglinde and Dietlinde, and earlier names such as Old High German Irmilinda and Old Dutch Frithelind.

linden.ety: As a Dutch, German and Jewish surname, plural form of Linde. As a Dutch and West Flemish surname, from several placenames called Linden or Lienden.

lindsay.ety: From Lindsey in Lincolnshire, from Old English Lindesēġe, Lindesīġe (“Isle of Lind”), the Old English name of the city of Lincoln, Lincolnshire.

lindsey.ety: From Old English Lindesege, ultimately from Proto-Brythonic *llɨnn (“pool”), from Proto-Celtic *lindos (“lake, liquid”) (as in Lincoln) + Old English ēġ (“island (of land)”).

line.ety: From Caroline or, less often, from Nicoline, Pauline or similar names.

linette.ety: In modern use a spelling variant of Lynette, though it is also identical with a rare French name, diminutive of Line, from Caroline, Pauline and other female names ending in -line.

linn.ety: A 1940s creation, possibly a variant of Line and Lina, short for names ending in -lin (Ingelin, Elin, Malin, etc).

linnea.ety: A flower name coined in the eighteenth century, from, twinflower, named after the Swedish botanist Carl von Linné (1707-1778).

linwood.ety: From Old English lind (“linden tree”) + Old English wudu (“woods, forest”).

lisa.ety: Diminutive of Elisabeth in several European languages. The computer is named after Lisa Brennan-Jobs, officially explained as an acronym for “Locally Integrated Software Architecture”.

lise.ety: From Low German Lise (“female given name”), a short form of Elisabet (“female given name”), from Latin Elisabeth, from Ancient Greek Ἐλισάβετ (Elisábet), from Biblical Hebrew אֱלִישֶׁבַע (ʾĔlîšéḇaʿ, “my God is an oath”).

liselotte.ety: Lise + Lotte, an adaptation of German Lieselotte.

lisette.ety: From Elisabeth. The spelling of Elizabeth used in the Authorized Version of the New Testament.

lisha.ety: Short form of Alicia,Felicia//Felisha, and other names ending with the same sound.

lita.ety: A Dutch short form of names beginning with the element Liut-, from Old High German liut (“people”). Also associated with liten (“little”).

liva.ety: Variant of Liv, also recorded as a diminutive of Olivia. Compare Latvian Līva.

livia.ety: From Latin Līvia, feminine form of Līvius, name of a plebeian Roman gens.

llorenç.ety: Inherited from Latin Laurentius Inherited from Latin Laurentius.

lluc.ety: Inherited from Latin Lūcās, from Koine Greek Λουκᾶς.

lochlan.m: land of the lochs, loch or fjord land, i.e. Scandinavia

loic.ety: From Medieval Latin Ludovicus. Doublet of Louis.

loke.ety: From loke (“rose”); also borrowed from the English Rose.

loki.ety: Borrowed from Old Norse Loki, where further etymology is shown.

lolita.ety: Borrowed from Spanish Lolita The name is from Spanish Lolita, diminutive of Lola, from the given name Dolores.

london.ety: Inherited from Middle English Londoun From Middle English Londoun, from Old English Lunden, from Proto-Celtic via Latin Londinium – see for details. Doublet of Londinium.

londynn.ety: Modern variant of London, influenced by Lynn.

lone.ety: Shortened from Abelone, a Danish form of Apollonia, name of an early martyr, derived from the Ancient Greek god Apollo.

lorcan.ety: A diminutive of Lorc, epithet of Lóegaire Lorc, a High King of Ireland, the actual meaning of which is disputed.

lorelei.ety: Borrowed from German Lorelei (“murmuring rock or lurking rock”), but not used as a given name in Germany.

lori.ety: In some cases, a 20th century spelling variant of Laurie, from Laura. In other cases, a diminutive form of names such as Loretta and Lorraine.

lorna.ety: Blackmore for his novel Lorna Doone, possibly from the Scottish place name Lorn(e) in Argyll.

lorraine.ety: Inherited from Middle English Loreyne, from Old French Loherraine, from loherenc (“Lotharingian”); compare Early Medieval Latin Lotharingia (ultimately named for Lothair II, who ruled it); compare Doublet of Lotharingia, German Lothringen.

louise.ety: From French Louise, the feminine form of Louis.

loup.ety: From the Latin given name Lupus.

lourenco.ety: From Latin Laurentius, from Laurentum (“city in Latium”).

lourenço.ety: From Latin Laurentius, from Laurentum (“city in Latium”).

lovely.ety: Borrowed from English Lovely, from lovely.

lowell.ety: A Middle English diminutive of Old French lou + -el, meaning "little wolf". Akin to Wolfie.

loïc.ety: From Medieval Latin Ludovicus. Doublet of Louis.

lu.ety: Short form of Lucy, Lucille, and similar names.

luana.ety: Borrowed from English Luana. Made known in Hawaii by the play (1912) and film (1932) Bird of Paradise and later explained as Hawaiian luana (“leisure”).

luann.ety: From Lu. Short form of Lucy, Lucille, and similar names.

luba.ety: From Slavic Luba From Ukrainian Люба.

luc.ety: From Late Latin Lūcās, from Koine Greek Λουκᾶς.

luce.ety: Probably a patronymic surname from a variant of Luca, or a matronymic surname from a variant of Lucia.

lucette.ety: From a diminutive of the Latin name Lucia.

luci.ety: A modern nonstandard spelling of Lucy, from Lucia, from the Latin feminine form of the Latin praenomen Lucius, from lux "light".

lucia.ety: Latinate variant of Lucy, or today borrowed from modern Italian. Name of a Sicilian martyr, Latin Lūcia, feminine form of the Roman praenomen Lūcius.

lucian.ety: From Latin Lūcianus, either a derivative of the Roman praenomen Lūcius, from lūx (“light”); or from Ancient Greek Λουκιανός, of obscure meaning.

lucina.ety: From Middle English Lucina and Lucyna, from Latin Lūcīna.

lucinda.ety: Derived from Lucia with the suffix -inda, first used by Cervantes in Don Quixote (1605).

lucretia.ety: Originally from Latin lucrum (“gain, profit”). Many people with the given name have no doubt been named after others so named, not necessarily after the 6th-century-BC Roman noblewoman.

lucy.ety: From Middle English Lucy, from Old French Lucie (notably after the Christian martyr Lucia of Syracuse), from Latin Lucia (feminine of Lucius, a Roman praenomen), from lux (“light”).

ludmiła.ety: Compare Russian Людмила and Slovak Ľudmila.

ludovic.ety: From French Ludovic, from Medieval Latin Lūdovīcus.

luka.ety: From the common Slavic (, etc) male given name Luka and from Лука́, all cognates of English Luke and Lucas.

lula.ety: 19th-century variant of Lulu, nickname of Louisa and Lucy. In rare cases, shortened from Tallulah.

luther.ety: Borrowed from German Luther, from Old High German Liutheri (“male given name”), from Proto-West Germanic *Liudihari, composed of *liudi (“person, people”) and *hari (“army”).

luís.ety: Adaptation of Old French Louis, Looïs, Luis, from Latin Ludovīcus, from Old High German *Hlūtwīg or Frankish *Hlōdowig, from Proto-Germanic *hlūdaz (“loud, famous”) + *wīgą (“battle”).

lykke.ety: From medieval Danish Lydik, Lydike, from Middle Low German Ludeke, diminutive of Germanic compound names beginning with the element Liut' ("folk"), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *liudiz (“folk, people”).

lyndsey.ety: Spelling variant. A less common spelling of Lindsay or Lindsey.

lyne.ety: As an English surname, spelling variant of Lind and Line; as an Irish surname, spelling variant of Lane.
lyne.m: A road, street, or similar thoroughfare.

lynette.ety: Anglicized form of Welsh Eluned, first used by Tennyson in the Idylls of the King(1859-85), altered by folk etymology to be Lynn + -ette.

lyra.ety: Borrowed from Latin Lyra/lyra, from Ancient Greek λύρα (“a lyre; the constellation Lyra”). Doublet of lira and lyra and lyre.

lysandre.ety: Borrowed from Latin Lysander, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Λύσανδρος.

léon.ety: From Spanish León, from Latin legiō (“legion”), named for the Legio VII Gemina, which settled there. Doublet of legion via Old French.

lía.ety: Apocoped variant of Ilìa, from Latin Ēliās, from Ancient Greek Ἠλίας, from Hebrew אֵלִיָּה (ēliyā́, “Jah is my God”).

mabel.ety: Short form of Amabel, from Latin amābilis (“lovable”).

macario.ety: Borrowed from Latin Macarius, from Ancient Greek Μακάριος.

mace.ety: As an English surname, from the personal name Masse, probably shortened from Matthew. Compare Massey, Massett.

macey.ety: As an English surname, variant of Massey. As a Slavic surname, Americanized from Slovak Macej, Carpathian Rusyn (Mačej), Polish Maciej, all variants of Matthew.

mack.ety: (In sense one) From either the male name Mack or mack, itself from mackerel, which comes from Old French maquerel, from Dutch makelaar. Compare French mec.

mackenzie.ety: Of Scots MacKenȝie with the letter ⟨ȝ⟩ confused with ⟨z⟩. Ultimately from Scottish Gaelic MacCoinnich, itself from mac + Coinneach.

macklin.ety: Ultimately from Irish Mac Gille Eoin.

macon.ety: An anglicized form of French Mâcon, from earlier Mascon and Medieval Latin Masconis, a syncopated form of Madasconis and Matisco, probably from Gaulish matus (“bear”) and a suffix equivalent to -iscus (“-ish: forming adjectives”).

macy.ety: Norman baronial surname from places named Massy in France, derived from a Gallo-Roman personal name Maccius.

madalena.ety: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese Madalena, after the town of Magdala, from Hebrew מגדל (migdál, “tower”).

madalynn.ety: Variant of Madeleine, influenced by Lynn.

maddison.ety: From Madde (a medieval diminutive of Maud and Magdalene) -son.

maddy.ety: Short form of Madeleine or Short form of Madison + -y.

madeleine.ety: From French Madeleine. Doublet of Magdalene.

madeline.ety: Anglicized from French Madeleine, from Ancient Greek Μαγδαληνή or from Old High German Madalinde. Doublet of Madeleine and Magdalene and Madelinde.

madison.ety: Usually derived from Mathieson (Matthew + -son), occasionally from Middle English Maddy (“Maud”) + -son. In the movie Splash, its use as a given name derives from Manhattan’s Madison Avenue.

madonna.ety: From Italian madonna, from Old Italian ma (“my”) + donna (“lady”). The given name is derived from the English term, not used as a given name in Italy.

mads.ety: Borrowed from Danish Mads, a medieval Danish contraction of Mathias, historically also associated with Matthæus.

mael.ety: Borrowed from Breton Mael, from mael, literally “prince”.

maelle.ety: Borrowed from Breton Maelle, from maelle, literally “princess”.

maeve.ety: Anglicized form of the Irish Méabh, from Middle Irish Medb, literally “intoxicating” and Meadhbh in Medieval irish. The name of a legendary queen of Connacht in the Ulster Cycle of Irish mythology.

mafalda.ety: Originally a medieval Portuguese form of Matilda. This name was borne by the wife of Afonso, the first king of Portugal.

magali.ety: Borrowed from Occitan Magalí Borrowed from Occitan Magalí.

magdalena.ety: From Ancient Greek Μαγδαληνή (“woman from Magdala”).

magna.ety: From Old Norse Magna (“female given name”), either by continuation or revival. The Old Norse name is the feminine form of Magni (“male given name”), from magn (“might, strength”).

magnar.ety: A modern Norwegian formation. The initial element Magn- was probably taken from names such as Magnus or Magnhild, while final -ar follows an ending common in Norwegian male given names. in Norway.

magne.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Magni (“male given name”), from magn (“might, strength”). in Norway.

magnhild.ety: From Old Norse Magnhildr (“female given name”), probably an Old Norse adaptation of Old High German Maginhild (“female given name”), whose Germanic name elements mean “might, power” and “battle”.

magni.ety: A spelling variant of Magny. The latter was possibly formed through association with Magnhild and Dagny.

magny.ety: Possibly formed in Norwegian by association with Magnhild and Dagny.

mahaut.ety: Old French Mahaut, from Frankish *Mahtihild, from Proto-Germanic *Mahtihildiz.

mahir.ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ماهر (Mahir), from Arabic مَاهِر.

mai.ety: Chinese surname with several origins: from Mandarin 麥 (“wheat”), from Mandarin and Cantonese 買 (“buy”) Cantonese form of 米 (see Mi). Romanized from 马 (see Ma) Romanized from 梅 (see Mei).

maiara.ety: From ma'e (“wealth, riches”) + îara (“lord, lady”), literally “the lady of riches”.

maicon.ety: Rendering of English Michael, having become popular due to Michael Jackson’s fame. The ending may be due to the nasalization of the original final diphthong >.

maiken.ety: Nickname for Maria, cognate with Swedish Majken and German Meike.

maila.ety: Originally a baby talk form of Maria; in some cases also from Amalia.

maisa.ety: A diminutive of names like Maria, Maija-Liisa, Marja-Liisa and Mailis.

maisie.ety: From May (a pet form of Margaret) + -sie.

maissa.ety: From dialectal Arabic مَايْسَة, from Arabic مَائِسَة.

maja.ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Μαῖα.

makenna.ety: A variant of McKenna invented in the 1980s.

malachy.ety: From Irish Maolmhaodhóg and Maolseachnaill/Maolseachlainn, influenced by the etymologically unrelated name Malachi, which is of Hebrew origin.

malcolm.ety: Royal name in Scotland, anglicised from various historical Goidelic names equivalent to Scottish Gaelic Maol Chaluim or Calum, Irish Maol Colm, Middle Irish Máel Coluim, Old Irish Máel Columb.

malek.ety: From Czech Málek, Polish Małek, Slovene Malek, or a variant of the Muslim name Malik.

malia.ety: Borrowed from Hawaiian Malia (“Mary”) and in some cases from Mālia (“calm”).

malinda.ety: Variant of Melinda, used since the eighteenth century.

maliyah.ety: Probably a fanciful spelling of Malia, from Hawaiian Malia.

mallory.ety: From an Anglo-Norman nickname for an unfortunate person, from Old French maleure, malheure (“unhappy, unlucky”) (whence French malheur), from mal (“bad”) + eur (“fortune”).

malte.ety: Diminutive of the male given name Helmolt, from Old High German helm (“helmet”) + *waltan (“to rule”).

mamadou.ety: Ultimately from Arabic مُحَمَّد, via North and West African languages such as Hausa Muhammadu. Doublet of Mahomet and Mohammed.

manasses.ety: From Latin Manasses, from Koine Greek Μανασσῆς, from Biblical Hebrew מְנַשֶּׁה (Mənaše) + Ancient Greek -ς.

manfred.ety: (perhaps as opposed to divine peace); from Old High German man (“man”; “human”) + fridu (“peace”).

manon.ety: Borrowed from French Manon, pet form of Marie.

maple.ety: English surname, from the noun maple.

mara.ety: From Hebrew מָרָא (mara, “bitterness”), derived from Hebrew מַר (mar, “bitter”). The modern given name may also be shortened from Maria or Tamara.

marcal.ety: From Latin Mārtiālis, from mārtiālis (“pertaining to Mars”).

marcel.ety: Borrowed from French Marcel, from Latin Marcellus, diminutive of Marcus. Doublet of Marcellus.

marcelino.ety: Borrowed from Latin Mārcellīnus, diminutive of Mārcellus, in turn a diminutive of Mārcus.

marcellus.ety: Borrowed from Latin Marcellus. Doublet of Marcel.

marcia.ety: From Latin Marcia, feminine form of Marcius, a derivative of Marcus, ultimately from Mārs, the god of war.
marcia.m: of pertaining to the gens Marcia, Marcian

marciana.ety: From Marciana and their etymon Latin Mārciāna, feminine of Mārciānus.
marciana.m: of pertaining to Mārcus Mārcius, Marcian

marciano.m: of pertaining to Mārcus Mārcius, Marcian

marcjanna.m: of pertaining to Mārcus Mārcius, Marcian

marcus.ety: Borrowing of Latin Marcus. Doublet of Mark.

maren.ety: From Danish Maren, from Latin Marina.

margaret.ety: From the name of 3rd century Saint Margaret the Virgin, from Middle English Margaret, from Old French Margaret (French Marguerite), from Latin Margarita, from Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης (“pearl”), ultimately from an Indo-Iranian source.

margareta.ety: From Latin Margarita, from Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης (“pearl”). Cognate with English Margaret.

margaretta.ety: Rare Latinization of Margaret. Compare Margareta.

margery.ety: From Old French; ultimately from Ancient Greek.

marguerite.ety: Borrowed from French Marguerite in the 1860s. Doublet of Margaret, ultimately from the Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης (“pearl”).

mari.ety: Short for Maria; also identical with Estonian mari (“berry”).

marian.ety: A variant of Marion, a medieval derivation of Mary, often also interpreted as a contraction of Mary and Ann, or as a variant of Mariana.

mariangela.ety: From Italian Mariangela, Portuguese Mariângela, and Spanish Mariángela.

maribel.ety: Borrowed from Spanish Maribel, from a Blend of María + Isabel, from Spanish María Isabel. Maria + Isabel.

marigold.ety: From the flower. The rubber gloves are generally bright yellow in colour.

marika.ety: Borrowed from Hungarian Marika, a diminutive form of Mária (“Mary”).

marilyn.ety: A twentieth-century blend of Mary and Lynn.

marion.ety: From Middle English Marion, from Old French Marion, a diminutive of Marie, used in England since the Middle Ages.

maristela.ety: From Latin maris (“of the sea”) + stella (“star”), after Stella Maris (Mary, Star of the Sea), a title for the Virgin Mary.

marit.ety: Contraction of Margareta (“Margaret”) first recorded in the 15th century.

marita.ety: Borrowed in the late 19th century from Norwegian Marita. By folk etymology, explained as a Spanish diminutive of Maria, by analogy with Anita.

maritza.ety: From Spanish Maritza, a diminutive of: María, from Marīa, from Μαρίᾱ, from מרים (miryām, “rebellion”); and Marta, from Martha, from Μάρθα, from מרתא (mārtā, “lady, mistress, ruler”), female counterpart of מרא (mārā, “lord, master, ruler”).

marius.ety: From Latin Marius, a Roman family name probably derived from Mars. By folk etymology seen as a masculine form of Maria.

marjorie.ety: Variant of Margery, a medieval vernacular form of Margaret.

marley.ety: From several different places in England, from Old English mære (“boundary”) or myrig (“pleasant”) or mearþ (“marten”) + lēah (“woodland clearing”).

marnie.ety: Possibly a contraction of Marina or a diminutive of Marian.

marsha.m: of pertaining to the gens Marcia, Marcian

marshall.ety: As an English surname, from the noun marshal. As a French surname, variant of Mercier.

marthe.ety: Borrowed from French Marthe and Norwegian Marthe.

marti.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Mārtīnus Latin Mārtīnus.

martial.ety: From Latin Martialis (“Roman cognomen”), from martiālis (“belonging or dedicated to the Mars, the Roman god of war, or to war”), from Mārs (“the god Mars; the planet Mars”) + -ālis.

martins.ety: From Latin Martinus (“of or like Mars" or "little Mars”), Mars, Martis + -inus (diminutive suffix). Cognate to English Martin.
martins.m: of or like Mars" or "little Mars

marvin.ety: From Welsh Merfyn (“Mervyn”), probably from mêr (“marrow”) + myn (“eminent”).

maryna.ety: Transliteration of Мари́на. From Latin Marina, feminine form of Marinus, from marīnus (“of the sea”).

maría.ety: From Latin Maria, from Ancient Greek Μαρία, Μαριάμ, from Aramaic מרים (maryām).

matei.ety: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic Матѳеи.

mateus.ety: From Old Galician-Portuguese Mateus, from Latin Matthaeus, from Ancient Greek Ματθαῖος, from Hebrew מַתִּתְיָהוּ.

matheo.ety: From an archaic spelling of the Spanish Mateo and Italian Matteo in the 2000s, partly through the equally fashionable French Mathéo.

mathias.ety: Borrowed from Danish Mathias, a spelling variant of Matthias, from Latin Matthias, from Ancient Greek Ματθίας (Matthías), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew מַתִּתְיָהוּ (Mattīṯyāhū, “gift of Yahweh”).

mathéo.ety: From Matheo, an archaic spelling of the Spanish Mateo and Italian Matteo. A modern variant of the standard French Matthieu.

mats.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Mats, a short form of Mattis, itself a Nordic form of Latin Matthias, from Ancient Greek Ματθίας (Matthías), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew מַתִּתְיָהוּ (Mattīṯyāhū, “gift of Yahweh”).

matthieu.ety: Inherited from Old French Mathieu, from Latin Matthaeus, from Ancient Greek Ματθαῖος, from Hebrew מַתִּתְיָהוּ (mattiṯyāhū), literally “gift of the Lord”.

matti.ety: Vernacular form of Matias and/or Matteus (both of the same origin), brought to Finland as Catholic saint's names. Already attested as a Finnish given name in medieval records.

mattias.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Mattias, a Nordic spelling of Latin Matthias, from Ancient Greek Ματθίας (Matthías), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew מַתִּתְיָהוּ (Mattīṯyāhū, “gift of Yahweh”)..

mattis.ety: Patronymic surname from a pet form of the personal name Matthew.

matylda.ety: Borrowed from Old French Mathilde, from Old High German maht, meht + hild, hilta.

maud.ety: From Old French Mahaut. Doublet of Matilda.

maureen.ety: Anglicized from Irish Máirín, diminutive of Máire, an Irish equivalent of Mary.

mauri.ety: A vernacular form of the Latin saints' name Mauritius, and less often of Maurus.

maurice.ety: From Middle English Maurice, from Late Latin Mauritius, derived from Maurus (“Moor; dark, swarthy”). Popularized by a 3rd-century Roman soldier martyr.

maurycy.ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin Mauritius.

maverick.ety: The surname is most famously associated with Samuel Maverick, a rancher from Texas who did not brand his cattle.

mavis.ety: Coined at the end of the 19th century from mavis, a poetical name for the song thrush.

max.ety: Borrowed from German Max, diminutive of Maximilian in the 19th century, later also used as a nickname for Maxwell.

maxim.ety: As a given name, from Latin Maximus (“greatest”), of magnus (“great”). Borne by several early Christian saints.

maximilian.ety: From German Maximilian, ultimately of Latin origin.

maxine.ety: From Max + -ine. An English feminine form of Max coined at the end of the nineteenth century..

maxwell.ety: From an earlier form Mackeswell, meaning "Mack's well or spring", from Old English welle (“well”).

mayson.ety: As a surname, Middle English May's son, personal name shortened from Matthew and many other origins. The modern given name is mostly a spelling variant of Mason.

maël.ety: Borrowed from Breton Mael, from mael, literally “prince”.

maëlle.ety: Borrowed from Breton Maelle, from maelle, literally “princess”.

maïa.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Μαῖα Borrowed from Ancient Greek Μαῖα.

maïssa.ety: From dialectal Arabic مَايْسَة, from Arabic مَائِسَة.

małgorzata.ety: Inherited from Old Polish Margorzata, from Latin Margarita, from Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης, from Indo-Iranian.

mckayla.ety: Modern variant of Michaela, influenced by Mc-.

mckenzie.ety: Rare spelling variant of the surname MacKenzie.

meabh.ety: From Middle Irish Medb, from Proto-Celtic *medwā, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰu. Compare Middle Irish medb (“intoxicating”), from Proto-Celtic *medwos.

mecca.ety: From Arabic مَكَّة of uncertain etymology. In American place names, in reference to the Arabian city.

medard.ety: Borrowed from Latin Medardus, which probably has a Germanic origin.

medine.ety: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish مدینه, from Classical Persian مَدِینَه, from Arabic اَلْمَدِينَةُ.

megan.ety: Borrowed from Welsh Megan, cognate with English Margaret, ultimately from an Indo-Iranian source.

mehmet.ety: From Ottoman Turkish محمد (Mehmed, Mehmet), from Arabic مُحَمَّد. Doublet of Muhammad and Mahomet and Baphomet.

meilani.ety: Modern American coinage, rhyming with Leilani. Can be interpreted as Hawaiian Mei + lani "heavenly May".

mekhi.ety: An African-American coinage, popularized by the actor Mekhi Phifer.

melanie.ety: Borrowed from French Mélanie From French Mélanie, from Latin Melania, the name of two Roman fifth century saints, from Ancient Greek μέλας (“black, dark”).

melba.ety: Coined by Nellie Melba as a pseudonym; derived from Melbourne.

melchior.ety: From Latin Melchior, from Hebrew מלכיאור (“king of light”), from מלך (“king”) + אור (“light”).

melinda.ety: Coined in the eighteenth century from names such as Melanie and Melissa + -inda.

melody.ety: From the noun melody; in regular use since the 20th century.

melvin.ety: Variant of the Scottish surname Melville, from a place name Malleville in Normandy, from Latin mala (“bad”) + Old French ville (“settlement”).

mercy.ety: From mercy in the 17th century; one of the less common Puritan virtue names. In modern use sometimes used to anglicize Spanish Mercedes.
mercy.m: ; forbearance to cause or allow harm to another.

merida.ety: Possibly a coinage based on Mary, or transferred from the Spanish place name Mérida.

merita.ety: From Latin merita, the feminine of meritus.

merle.ety: English 19th-century bird name from merle (“blackbird”), possibly also a variant of Muriel, Merrill, etc.

merlin.ety: From Middle English Merlyn, from Medieval Latin Merlinus and Old French Merlin, from Proto-Brythonic *Mor-ðin, literally “sea-hill”, from Proto-Celtic *mori (“sea”) + *dūnom (“stronghold, rampart”).

merrie.m: ; forbearance to cause or allow harm to another.

merry.m: ; forbearance to cause or allow harm to another.

mervyn.ety: Welsh Merfyn, probably from mer (“marrow”) (from Proto-Brythonic *mer) + myn (“eminent”) (compare Irish mín (“smooth, elegant, courteous”)).

meyer.ety: As a German and Alemannic German surname, from the noun Meier (“leaseholder of a manor”). Compare Maier, Mayer, Meier, Myer.

mia.ety: A German, Dutch and North Germanic diminutive of Maria.

miah.ety: Modern usage, probably a variant of Mia.

micael.ety: From Old Leonese Migael, from Latin Micaēl.

micha.ety: Borrowed from Biblical Hebrew מִיכָה (mīḵāh), whence also English Micah; see there for more information.

michaela.ety: From Michael + -a. Latinate feminine form of Michael, first appearing as an anglicisation of the Portuguese ("Micaela") and Spanish ("Micaela").

michalina.ety: From Polish Michalina or a variant of Michaelina.

michaël.ety: From Vulgar Latin Michaēl, found in the Vulgate Bible, from Classical Latin Michahēl, from Biblical Hebrew מִיכָאֵל (mîḵāʾēl), literally “who is like God?”.

michał.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Michaēl Compare Michal.

micheal.ety: From Latin Michael, Michahel, from Biblical Hebrew מִיכָאֵל (mîḵāʾēl, “who is like God?”).

michel.ety: From Old French Michel, from Latin Michāēl,Michāēlem, borrowed from Koine Greek Μῐχᾱήλ, in turn borrowed from Biblical Hebrew מִיכָאֵל (mikha'él, “Michael”), literally “Who is like God?”.

michelle.ety: Borrowed from French Michelle, feminine form of French Michel (“Michael”), Hebrew מִיכָאֵל (mikhaél, “who is like God?”). Doublet of Michaela.

mickael.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Michael See Michaël.

mickaël.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Michael See Michaël.

mieczysław.ety: Miecz + -y- + sława, Coined by Jan Długosz to explain the origin of the name Mieszko. Compare Miecisław.

mignon.ety: Borrowed from French Mignon. Occasionally of Walloon origin.

mika.ety: Ultimately from Biblical Hebrew מִיכָה (mīḵāh), shortened form of מִיכַיְהוּ (mīḵāyᵊhū, “who is like Yahweh”).

mikail.ety: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish میكائیل (mikail), from Arabic مِيكَائِيل, ultimately from Biblical Hebrew מִיכָאֵל.

mikalai.ety: Transliteration of Мікала́й. From Ancient Greek Νικόλαος.

mikhail.ety: From Russian Михаи́л (“Michael”), from Hebrew מיכאל. Doublet of Michael.

miko.ety: From Mikko. Vernacular form of Mikael (“Michael”) attested since medieval times.

milda.ety: From Old Lithuanian mild-ìngai (“friendly”) or Sudovian (Jatvingian) miłdat (“to love”).

mildred.ety: From the name of an 8th-century English saint, Old English Mildþrȳþ.

mildrid.ety: Apparently from Old English Mildþrȳþ, cognate to modern English Mildred. Recorded in Norway since about 1300.

miles.ety: From Old French given name Milo, of problematic origin, possibly from an unknown Germanic element, or a short form of Slavic names beginning with mil- "grace, favor".

miley.ety: Popularised as a female name by American pop singer Miley Ray Cyrus (nicknamed Miley from "smiley").

milka.ety: From Biblical Hebrew מלכה (milká). Vilkuna considers this a variant of Emilia.

milla.ety: From Latin Aemilia. Shortened from Estonian Emilie.

miller.ety: English surname, capitalization of miller. Doublet of Muller.

miloud.ety: Borrowed from Arabic مِيلُود Borrowed from Arabic مِيلُود.

milton.ety: The English place names are from Old English mylen (“mill”) or middel (“middle”) + tun (“settlement”).

mio.ety: From the children's book Mio, min Mio by Astrid Lindgren. The book title is word play on Italian mio (“my”).

miranda.ety: Thumb|Miranda as the ice-covered moon of planet Uranus Coined by William Shakespeare for a character in The Tempest; feminine of Latin mirandus (“admirable”).

mireia.ety: Borrowed from Provençal Mirèlha/Mirèio. Invented by the poet Frédéric Mistral for his poem of the same title (1859).

mireille.ety: From Provençal Mirèio/Mirèlha. Invented by the poet Frédéric Mistral for his poem of the same title (1859).

mirela.ety: Borrowed from Italian Mirella, from Provençal Mirèlha/Mirèio. Invented by the poet Frédéric Mistral for his poem of the same title (1859).

miren.ety: Coined by Sabino Arana, from Hebrew מִרְיָם (miryām).

miro.ety: Probably from Slavic names like Proto-Slavic *Miroslavъ, Russian Влади́мир.

miron.ety: Transliteration of Міро́н. Borrowed from Ancient Greek Μύρων.

misha.ety: A transliteration of the Russian Ми́ша, a hypocoristic for Михаи́л, the Russian equivalent of Michael, from Hebrew מיכאל.

misty.ety: From the adjective misty, but sometimes also (like Missy) used as a nickname for Melissa.

mitchell.ety: From a Middle English vernacular form of the Old French given name Michel (“Michael”), or in some cases from a Middle English nickname muchel (“big”).

mitzi.ety: Borrowed from German Mitzi in the 20th century.

miłosz.ety: From miły + -osz. Cognate with Czech Miloš.
miłosz.m: nice, pleasant, dear, gentle, mild, soft, polite

moacir.ety: Coined by Q455703, as the name of a character in the novel Iracema. The author derived it from Old Tupi moasy (“to regret”), although he translated it as "son of the pain" in the book.

modesto.ety: Inherited from Latin Modestus From Latin Modestus.

mohammad.ety: Borrowed from Arabic مُحَمَّد (“praised, commendable”), through a Latin-script transliteration of the Arabic name.

moira.ety: Anglicized from Irish Máire, a cognate of Mary. Doublet of Maura.

moise.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Mōysēs Latin Mōysēs.

moises.ety: Borrowed from Portuguese Moisés and Spanish Moisés.

molly.ety: From Moll, diminutive lambdacism of Mary -y.

mona.ety: Anglicized from Irish and Scottish Gaelic Muadhnait, from Middle Irish múad (“noble”).

monica.ety: From Latin Monica, name of the mother of St. Augustine, of uncertain meaning but probably Berber or Phoenician origin.

monika.ety: From Latin Monica, name of the mother of St. Augustine, of uncertain origin and meaning; suggestions include Ancient Greek μόνος (“alone”) and Latin moneō (“to advise”), but likely of Punic origin.

monroe.ety: From Old English mann (“human being, person, man”) + Roe, a river in Northern Ireland, meaning "man from the River Roe".

mons.ety: A Norwegian vernacular form of Magnus, which is from Latin Magnus (“male given name”), ultimately from the adjective magnus (“great, large”).

montana.ety: Borrowed from Spanish montaña From Latin montāna the US state via Spanish montaña (“mountain”) the surname from Spanish Montaña topographic surname.

montgomery.ety: From a Norman surname, from a place in Normandy (Old French for "Gomeric's hill").

morgan.ety: From Old Welsh Morcant, possibly from *mor (“sea”) (Welsh môr) or *mọr (“great”) (Old Welsh maur) + *kantos (“circle”) (Welsh cant), meaning “great chief” or “sea chief”.

morgana.ety: From Old Welsh or Old Breton Morgen, literally “sea-born”.

moris.ety: Transliteration of Maurice. From Middle English Maurice, from Late Latin Mauritius, derived from Maurus (“Moor; dark, swarthy”).

moritz.ety: From Middle High German, from Latin Mauritius, from the 3rd-century Egyptian Saint.

morris.ety: The surname has converged from several origins; see Morris.

morten.ety: Borrowed from Danish Morten, a vernacular form of Martin, from Latin Martīnus (“of Mars, dedicated to Mars”), from Latin martinus (“of Mars, martial”), from Latin Mārs (“Mars”) (genitive Martis), the name of the Roman god of war.

morton.ety: From Old English mōr (“moor, marsh”) + tūn (“settlement”).

mouloud.ety: From dialectal Arabic مُولُود, from Arabic مَوْلُود.

mourad.ety: Borrowed from Arabic مُرَاد. Equivalent to English Murad, Turkish Murat.

moussa.ety: Borrowed from Arabic مُوسَى (“Moses”). Doublet of Moïse.

muriel.ety: Anglicized form of Scottish Gaelic Muireall, from muir (“sea”), from Old Irish muir, from Proto-Celtic *mori, from Proto-Indo-European *móri; + geal (“white, bright”), from Old Irish gel, from Proto-Celtic *gelos (“yellow.

murilo.ety: Borrowed from Spanish Murillo Borrowed from Spanish Murillo.

murphy.ety: From Irish Ó Murchadha (“descendant of Murrough”), Mac Murchaidh (“Son of Murrough”), etc.

murray.ety: Scottish surname derived from the place name Moray in northeastern Scotland, from Medieval Latin Moravia, Morauia, from Scottish Gaelic Moireibh, Moireabh, Moreb, ultimately from Proto-Celtic *mori (“sea”) + *trebā (“settlement”).

my.ety: Coined by Tove Jansson, via the character Little My in the Moomin books, named for my (“mu, the Greek letter μ”), because she was the smallest thing that there is.

myah.ety: Rare fanciful spelling of Mya, Maia, Maya.

mykyta.ety: Transliteration of Мики́та. From Ancient Greek Νικήτας Compare Belarusian Мікі́та.

myra.ety: First used by the poet Fulke Greville, possibly as an anagram of Mary.

myrna.ety: An anglicization of Irish Muirne (“beloved”). Popularized by the American actress Myrna Loy.

myrtle.ety: After the plant, myrtle; used since the end of the 19th century.

målfrid.ety: Old Norse Malmfríðr, from malm (“ore”) and fríðr (“beautiful”).

nabila.ety: Borrowed from Arabic نَبِيلَة, feminine of نَبِيل (“noble”).

nadege.ety: From the Russian virtue name Наде́жда (“Hope”).

nadezhda.ety: Transliteration of Russian Наде́жда, from наде́жда (“hope”).

nadzieja.ety: Doublet of Nadia. Cognate with Russian Наде́жда.

nadège.ety: From the Russian virtue name Наде́жда (“Hope”).

naima.ety: Variant of Naimi, from Naemi, the equivalent of English Naomi in older versions of the Finnish Bible.

nana.ety: Not certain whether directly derived from Armenian Նանե, or by association with the ancient Iranian goddess of the same name.

nancy.ety: Medieval diminutive of Ann and Agnes. Compare Betsy, Patsy.

napoleon.ety: From French Napoléon, from Italian Napoleone, name of an early saint, of uncertain origin; possibly from the Germanic clan name Nibelung.

nassim.ety: Borrowed from Arabic نسيم or Persian نسیم.

nassima.ety: From Arabic نسيمة and Persian نسیما.

natalie.ety: From the French form of the Late Latin saint's name Natalia, from nātālis (diēs) (“birthday [of Christ], Christmas”). Doublet of Natalya.

natalino.ety: From Natale, from diminutive> From Natale + -ino.

natalio.ety: Borrowed from Latin Nātālius, name of an antipope, or created as the masculine version of Natalia.

nataliya.ety: Transliteration of Ната́лья. Ultimately from Latin Natalia.

natalya.ety: Transliteration of Russian Ната́лья. Doublet of Natalie.

nathaniel.ety: Modification, under influence of Daniel, of Nathanael, from Ancient Greek Ναθαναήλ, from Biblical Hebrew נְתַנְאֵל (Netan'el), literally “God has given”.

nazareth.ety: From the Ancient Greek Νᾱζᾰρέθ (“Nazareth”), probably from the Hebrew נָצְרַת (Nāṣraṯ).

ned.ety: From rebracketing of the phrase mine Ed to my Ned.

neela.ety: Through spelling pronunciation from English Neela, from Sanskrit नील.

neil.ety: Anglicized form of Goidelic/Irish Niall. Doublet of Niall.

neill.ety: Variant spelling of Neil, anglicised form of Goidelic/Irish Niall.

nelci.ety: From Nélson, from English Nelson, from Middle English Neil + -son — or Nell + -son.

nele.ety: From a Middle Low German pet form of Cornelia.

nella.ety: Possibly borrowed as a diminutive from German Cornelia.

nelle.ety: From Ellen spelled backwards. Popularized by author Harper Lee, whose first name Nelle was so derived from her grandmother’s.

nelli.ety: Possibly borrowed as a diminutive from German Cornelia.

nellie.ety: Suffixed with -ie, compare Noll and Neddie, respectively from Oliver and Edward.

nels.ety: Anglicization of Norwegian Nils and Swedish Nils, reflecting the pronunciation of the name among Scandinavian immigrants to North America, or matched to Nelson.

nena.ety: Popularized by the singer Nena, from Spanish nena (“girl”).

neo.ety: Recent coinage from the prefix neo- (“new”). Popularized by a character in the science-fiction film The Matrix (1999), where it is explained as an anagram of "(the) One".

nerijus.ety: Borrowed from Latin Nereus, ultimately From Ancient Greek Νηρεύς.

nerissa.ety: Coined by Shakespeare for The Merchant of Venice, apparently from Ancient Greek Νηρηΐς (“sea-nymph”).

nestor.ety: From Ancient Greek Νέστωρ, possibly from νέομαι (“to return safely”), νόστος (“homecoming”).

neta.ety: Possibly borrowed as a diminutive from Swedish Agneta.

nettie.ety: Suffixed with -ie, compare Neddie and Nellie, respectively from Edward and Eleanor.

nevaeh.ety: From heaven, spelled backwards. Popular since 2000 when the rock singer Sonny Sandoval gave the name to his baby daughter.

neville.ety: A Norman baronial surname, de Neville, from place names in Normandy, Néville, from Old French Neville, literally “Néel's estate” or Neuville, literally “new settlement”, equivalent to nuef + ville.

nevin.ety: A rare Anglicization of Irish Naomhán, a diminutive of naomh (“saint”).

newton.ety: Inherited from Middle English Neweton, from Old English nēowa tūn (“new town”). Compare same construction in Italian Napoli (“Naples”) and in Arabic نَابُلُس (“Nablus”).

neymar.ety: Borrowed from Portuguese Neymar in the 2010s after the Brazilian footballer Neymar da Silva Santos Júnior.

nicholas.ety: From Middle English Nicholas, from Old French Nicholas, from Latin Nīcolāus, from Ancient Greek Νικόλαος, from νίκη (“victory”) + λαός (“people”).

nicolae.ety: Taken from Old Church Slavonic Николаи, from Ancient Greek Νικόλαος. Doublet of Nicoară.

nicolau.ety: Borrowed from Latin Nīcolāus, from Ancient Greek Νικόλαος.

nicolette.ety: From Nicole. Feminine form of Nicolas (“Nicholas”).

nicolina.ety: Borrowed from Bulgarian Николина, from Ukrainian Ніколіна.

niels.ety: Medieval contraction of Latin Nicolaus, Nicholaus, from the Ancient Greek Νικόλαος. Cognate with English Nicholas.

nigel.ety: English form of Latin Nigellus, from nigellus (“slightly black”), diminutive of niger (“black”), used in the Middle Ages to Latinize Norman Néel and Old Irish Níall, from which the former is derived via Old Norse Njáll.

nihad.ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish نهاد (Nihâd), from Arabic نِهَاد.

nikita.ety: From the Russian Ники́та, a male given name, from Ancient Greek Νικήτας (“conqueror”) also a male given name (and name of various saints). The Greek word derives from νῑ́κη (“victory”).

niklas.ety: Vernacular form of Nikolas, Nikolaus, probably fairly recently borrowed from Swedish Niklas.

nikole.ety: Borrowed from the French Nicole, from Ancient Greek Νικόλαος (Nikólaos), from νίκη (níkē, “victory”) + λαός (laós, “people”).

nilda.ety: Short form of Germanic given names composed of a first element ending in -n and the second element hild (“battle”), such as Brunilda, Zunilda or Leonilda.

nils.ety: Borrowed from Swedish Nils. A variant of the more common Danish Niels.

nina.ety: Borrowed into English in the nineteenth century, apparently from several sources.

ninni.ety: Originally a diminutive of various female names containing the letters i and n, such as Elin, Ingrid, Linnea, Signe.

nita.ety: Short form of Anita and other names ending in nita.

nixon.ety: From Nick + -son, an alteration of Nickson, originally a patronymic meaning "son of Nicholas".

noam.ety: From Hebrew נועם (“pleasantness; a male name”).

noble.m: An aristocrat; one of aristocratic blood.

noel.ety: Inherited from Middle French Noël, from Old French Noel, Naël, inherited from Vulgar Latin, from Latin nātālis [diēs Dominī] (“birthday of the Lord”) with dissimilation of the first -a- to -o-.

noelle.ety: From French Noëlle, the feminine form of the male given name Noël.

noemi.ety: Borrowed from Hebrew נָעֳמִי (no'omí), literally “my pleasantness”, from + ־ִי (-í, “my, of me”).

nola.ety: From Finola, from Irish Fionnghuala. In the US, also under the influence of the male name Nolan (which see).

nolan.ety: Anglicized from Irish Ó Nualláin, literally “descendant of Nuallán”, diminutive of nuall (“chariot-fighter, champion”).

nolwenn.ety: Borrowed from Breton. See also Gwennoal.

nona.ety: Feminine form of the Roman gens name Nōnus, from nōnus (“the ninth”).

nora.ety: Short form of Eleanor or, rarely, of Honora.

norman.ety: From Middle English Norman, from Old English Norman (a variant of Norþman) and Old French Normant.

norris.ety: An Anglo-Norman surname, from Old French norreis (“a northerner, a migrant from the north”). More at French norois.
norris.m: a northerner, a migrant from the north

norton.ety: From Old English norþ (“north”) + tūn (“enclosure; settlement, town”).

norwood.ety: From north + wood. Doublet of Northwood.

novella.ety: From novella, feminine form of novello (“new, early”).

nuria.ety: From the Roman Catholic Catalan epithet of the Virgin Mary La Mare de Déu de Núria (“The Mother of God of Núria”), from the place name Núria (Vall de Núria, “Núria valley”).
nuria.m: The Mother of God of Núria

néo.ety: Recent coinage, associated with the prefix néo- (“new”), popularized by a character (Neo in English) of the science fiction film The Matrix (1999).

oakley.ety: Inherited from Middle English From Old English Āclēa, from āc (“oak”) + lēah (“woodland clearing, glade”), thus a clearing in an oak forest; equivalent to oak + -ley (“lea”).

ocean.ety: From ocean (“sea”), inspired by the fashionable French female name Océane.

oceane.ety: Modern feminine form of Océan, from Latin Ōceanus, Ancient Greek Ὠκεανός, the god of sea and the name of an early Christian saint.

octavian.ety: From Latin Octavianus, from Octāvius + -ianus (“-ian: forming adjectives”), initially used to distinguish the future Roman emperor upon his adoption by his uncle Gaius Julius Caesar.

octavius.ety: From Latin Octāvius (“Roman praenomen and nomen”), from octavius (“eighth”), probably initially in reference the child's birth order or the month of their birth in the Roman calendar.

océane.ety: Modern feminine form of Océan, from Latin Ōceanus, Ancient Greek Ὠκεανός, the god of sea and the name of an early Christian saint.

odd.ety: English surname, from the Middle English name Ode, either from Anglo-Norman Ode (see Oates) or from Old English Odda, Old Norse Oddr, or a conflation of all.

oddbjørg.ety: From Old Norse oddr (“sharp point”) and bjǫrg (“salvation”).

oddbjørn.ety: Old Norse oddr (“sharp point”) and bjǫrn (“bear”).

oddlaug.ety: From Old Norse oddr (“sharp point”) and laug (“consecrated, dedicated”).

oddny.ety: From Old Norse Oddný, from oddr (“sharp point”) and ný (“new”).

oddrun.ety: From Old Norse Oddrún, from oddr (“sharp point”) and rún (“rune, secret knowledge”).

oddvar.ety: Newer name; from odd (“sharp or thin point”) and the old name element -var (“protector”). Also a variant of Oddvard.

oddveig.ety: A 19th-century invention from Old Norse elements that would mean "sharp point" (Old Norse oddr) and "strength, war" (Old Norse víg).

odessa.ety: Uncertain; possibly from the placename, with usage influenced by the name Odysseus.

odhran.ety: From Old Irish Odrán, originally from odur + -án. odhar (“dun”) + -án.

odie.ety: Separate origins as diminutives of British name Odell and Germanic name Odin; later used as nickname for additional given names.

odile.ety: Name of a 7th/8th century saint of Alsace; derivative of a short form of Germanic compound names beginning with the element od-, ot- "riches," from Frankish *aud.

oisin.ety: From oisín (“fawn”), from os (“deer”) + -ín; name of a hero in Irish mythology.

oksana.ety: Transliteration of Окса́на. A form of the name Ксе́ния, from Ancient Greek ξενία (“hospitality”).

olai.ety: From Latin Eulalia, from Ancient Greek Εὐλαλία, from εὔλαλος (“sweetly speaking”).

olav.ety: From Old Norse Óláfr, from Proto-Norse *ᚨᚾᚢᛚᚨᛁᛒᚨᛉ. Name of an 11th century king, the patron saint of Norway.

olaya.ety: From Latin Eulalia, from Ancient Greek Εὐλαλία, from εὔλαλος (“sweetly speaking”). Cognate with Spanish Eulalia, Galician Olalla and French Eulalie.

oleg.ety: Borrowed from Russian Оле́г, a Varangian name, ultimately from Old Norse Helgi (“holy, sacred or blessed”). Cognate to modern Scandinavian Helge.

oline.ety: A feminine form of Ole; possible also shortened from Caroline.

olive.ety: Medieval form of the Latin saint's name Oliva "olive"; revived in the 19th century when flower and plant names became fashionable.

oliver.ety: Inherited from Middle English Oliver, from Old French Olivier, by folk etymology derived from the Latin name Olīvārius.

oliverio.ety: Borrowed from Spanish Oliverio Compare English Oliver).

olivier.ety: Borrowed from French Olivier. Doublet of Oliver.

olivio.ety: Originally used as the masculine form of Olivia.

ollie.ety: From Germanic, from Latin olivarius (“olive tree”) (from oliva (“olive”)), and from Welsh.

olve.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Ǫlvér, also found as Ǫlvir, from Proto-Norse *Aluwīhaz. The first element has been interpreted as meaning “luck; protection” and the second as “giant, warrior”.

olympia.ety: From Ancient Greek Ὀλυμπία, from Ὄλυμπος (“Olympus”).

oma.ety: Coined as a feminine equivalent of Omar.

omari.ety: Borrowed from Arabic عمري. The surname is predominantly found in Tanzania.

onesimo.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ὀνήσιμος, from ὀνήσιμος (“profitable, useful”).

oona.ety: Borrowed from Irish Úna; doublet of Una.

ophelia.ety: Borrowed from Italian Ofelia, coined by the poet Jacopo Sannazaro in his poem Arcadia (1504), probably from the Ancient Greek ὠφέλειᾰ (“help, aid, succour”).

ophelie.ety: Borrowed from Italian Ofelia, coined by Jacopo Sannazaro from Ancient Greek ὠφέλειᾰ (“help”, “aid”, “succour”).

ophélie.ety: Borrowed from Italian Ofelia, coined by Jacopo Sannazaro from Ancient Greek ὠφέλειᾰ (“help”, “aid”, “succour”).

ora.ety: First appeared in the 19th century when similar sounding names like Cora, Dora and Nora were in fashion.

orion.ety: From Middle English Orioun, from Latin Ōrīōn, from Ancient Greek Ὠρίων, speculatively from Akkadian 𒌋𒊒𒀭𒈾 (Uru-anna, “heaven's light”), though without any firm evidence.

orland.ety: Used to sound more English, the name Orlando often erroneously attributed to Spanish.

orville.ety: Invented by Fanny Burney for the hero of her novel Evelina. It has been suggested that it is based on the very old Welsh forename of Eurfyl, meaning 'gold'.

ostap.ety: Transliteration of Ukrainian Оста́п, ultimately from Ancient Greek Εὐστάθιος. Doublet of Eustace.

oswald.ety: Inherited from Old English Ōsweald, from ōs (“god, deity”) + weald (“power”). Cognate with German Answald, Ásvaldur, and Norwegian Nynorsk Åsvald.

othilie.ety: Variant spelling of Otilie, from the German name tradition. The name goes back to Latin Otilia, originally Odilia, Latinised forms of Old High German Odila and Otila, pet forms of names such as Oda.
