othmar.ety: From Old High German Audomar, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *Audamār, from a compound of Proto-Germanic *audaz (“treasure”) and *mērijaz (“famous”). Compare French Omer.

otilia.ety: From Latin Otilia, originally Odilia, a Latinised form of Old High German Odila and Otila, pet forms of names such as Oda.

otilie.ety: One of several Norwegian spellings of a female given name going back to Latin Otilia, originally Odilia, a Latinised form of Old High German Odila and Otila, pet forms of names such as Oda.

otis.ety: A patronymic surname derived from Middle English genitive case of the Germanic given name Ote, Ode, cognate to modern Otto.

oualid.ety: Borrowed from Arabic وَلِيد Borrowed from Arabic وَلِيد.

ove.ety: From Old Danish Aghi, possibly a short form of compound names beginning with Germanic agh "blade" or Old Norse agi "awe". Related to German (Frisian) Uwe.

owain.ety: Borrowed from Welsh Owain. Doublet of Owen.

oxana.ety: Transliteration of Окса́на. A form of the name Ксе́ния, from Ancient Greek ξενία (“hospitality”).

paco.ety: Borrowed from Spanish Paco, of Spanish Francisco. See also Spanish Pancho.

padraig.ety: From Latin Patricius, likely via Old Welsh. Replaced Old Irish Cothraige, a much earlier borrowing as shown by the replacement of Latin p with c.

paige.ety: Variant of Page, from page, from Old French page, possibly via Old Italian paggio, from Late Latin pagius (“servant”), probably from Ancient Greek παιδίον (“boy, lad”), from παῖς (“child”).

palmer.ety: From Middle English palmer (“a pilgrim from the Holy Land”), from Old French.
palmer.m: a pilgrim from the Holy Land

palmira.ety: Borrowed from Latin Palmȳra, Palmīra, from Ancient Greek Παλμύρα, Παλμίρα, of uncertain origin.

pamela.ety: Invented by Sir Philip Sidney for his pastoral poem The Countess of Pembroke's Arcadia (c 1593).

paris.ety: Inherited from Middle English Parys From Middle English Parys, Paris, from Old French Paris, from the Late Latin name of an earlier settlement, Lutetia Parisiorum (“Lutetia of the Parisii”), from Latin Parīsiī, a Gaulish tribe.

pascal.ety: From Latin Paschālis, from paschālis (“Paschal; of or pertaining to Easter”), from pascha (“Easter”) + -ālis, for birth on Easter, or in honor of the 9th-century pope Paschal I (died 824).
pascal.m: Paschal; of or pertaining to Easter

pascale.m: Paschal; of or pertaining to Easter

pascaline.m: Paschal; of or pertaining to Easter

patience.ety: From patience, a virtue name first used by Puritans in the sixteenth century.

patrice.ety: 20th century variant of Patricia, probably borrowed from the French male given name Patrice.

patrik.ety: From English Patrick, from Latin Patricius.

patsy.ety: From the Short form of Patricia or Patrick + -sy.

paulette.ety: Borrowed in the twentieth century from French Paulette, a diminutive feminine form of Paul.

paulin.ety: From a Middle English form of the Latin saint's name Paulīnus.

paulina.ety: From Latin Paulīna, feminine form of Paulīnus, derivative of Paulus, from paulus (“small”). Name of a third-century saint.

pauline.ety: From French Pauline, in turn from Latin Paulīna; in regular use since the 19th century.

paxton.ety: From Old English *Pæcces + tūn, literally “settlement of (a person named) *Pæcc”.

payton.ety: Habitational surname from a minor place in Sussex, from the Old English personal name Pǣga + tūn (“enclosure; settlement, town”).

pearl.ety: From Chinese 珠江 (Zhūjiāng, Zyu1 Gong1, “Pearl River”); calque of Chinese 珠 (zhū, zyu1, “pearl”). From Hawaiian Wai Momi (“pearl water”); calque of Hawaiian momi (“pearl”).

pearline.ety: Coined at the end of the 19th century from Pearl + -ine. Compare Pauline, Earline.

pelagia.ety: Borrowed from Latin Pelagia, from Ancient Greek Πελαγία. Doublet of Pelagie.

pepe.ety: Perhaps from a the last syllable of Josepe, an older variant of José, or from the Latin expression Pater Putativus (“supposed father”) (P.P.), which appeared next to the name of Saint Joseph (José de Nazareth) in texts.

percival.ety: From Old French Perceval, name of a knight in a twelfth century Arthurian romance by the French poet Chrétien de Troyes.

percy.ety: Thumb|A statue of Sir [[w:Henry Percy (Hotspur)|Henry Percy (1364–1403; ') in Alnwick, Northumberland, England, United Kingdom.

pericles.ety: From Latin Periclēs, from Ancient Greek Περικλῆς (“far-famed”), from περί (“around”) + κλέος (“glory”).

pernille.ety: From Latin Petronella. Recorded in Denmark since 1375.

perpetua.ety: Borrowed from Latin Perpetua, name of an early saint, from perpetuus (“continuous, perpetual”).

perrin.ety: From a Middle English pet-form of Peter, from an Old French diminutive of Pierre.

peta.ety: A rare feminine form of Peter.

peterson.ety: English, Scottish, and German surname, from Peter + -son.

petru.ety: Ultimately from Ancient Greek Πετρος, from πέτρος (“stone, rock”), related to πέτρα.

petrus.ety: From Middle Dutch Petrus, from Latin Petrus, from Ancient Greek Πέτρος, from πέτρος (“rock, stone”), as a name a loan translation of Aramaic כֵּיפָא (“stone, rock; Peter, Cephas”).

phaedra.ety: From Latin Phaedra, from Ancient Greek Φαίδρᾱ.

phil.ety: Shortened from Philip, from Ancient Greek Φίλιππος, which see for more information.

philibert.ety: From a Germanic given name consisting of Frankish *filu (“many”) + *berht (“bright”). The spelling with Ph instead of F is due to influence of the given name Philippe.

philipp.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Φίλιππος (“fond of horses”), from φιλέω (“I like”) + ἵππος (“horse”).

philippa.ety: Feminine form of Philippus from Ancient Greek Φίλιππος, literally “Lover of Horses”.

phillip.ety: A less common spelling of Philip.

phillis.ety: A less common spelling of Phyllis.

philomena.ety: From Latin Philomēna, from Ancient Greek Φιλουμένη, literally “beloved”. Name of an alleged early martyr whose remains were discovered in 1802 in Rome.

philomene.ety: From French Philomène. Doublet of Philomena.

phineas.ety: From Ancient Greek Φινέας, alternative form of Φινεύς. Alternative source from Hebrew (פִינְחָס).

phoenix.ety: Borrowed from Latin phoenīx, from Latin Phoenīx From Latin phoenīx, Phoenīx, from Ancient Greek φοῖνῐξ, Φοῖνῐξ.

phyllis.ety: From the masculine Ancient Greek Φύλλις or from the feminine Φυλλίς.

pia.ety: From Latin Pia, feminine form of the papal name Pius, from pius (“pious”).

piedad.ety: From Nuestra Señora de la Piedad, an epithet of the Virgin Mary as "Our Lady of Pity".

pierre.ety: Inherited from Middle French Pierre Inherited from Middle French Pierre, from Latin Petrus, from Ancient Greek Πέτρος, from πέτρος (“stone, rock”), related to πέτρα (compare pierre (“stone, rock”)).

pierrot.ety: From Pierre, from diminutive suffix> From Pierre (“Peter”) + -ot.

plinio.ety: Borrowed from Latin Plīnius, of obscure origin.

polly.ety: Nickname for Mary, created by rhyming with Molly.

porter.ety: From Middle English Porter, from porter (“porter”), From Old French portier (“doorman”), from porte (“door”) From Old French portour (“bearer”), from porter (“to carry”).

portia.ety: From Latin Porcia, a feminine form of the gens name Porcius (the gens of the Cato the Elder and his famous descendants), from porcus (“pig”).

preben.ety: Contraction of Pridbjørn, a medieval Danish rendering of the Wend name Pritbor, from Slavic elements meaning "first" and "battle".

presley.ety: The English surname is usually a variant of Priestley, from Old English prēost (“priest”) + lēah (“wood, clearing”). Equivalent to priest + -ley (“lea”).

preston.ety: From Old English, from prēosta (“priests'”) + tūn (“settlement”). Doublet of Prestatyn.

primrose.ety: The surname derives from a place name in Fife, Scotland; Watson (1926) derived this from Pictish/Proto-Brythonic *prenn (“wood, tree”) + *rros (“moor, heath”).

princeton.ety: From prince + -ton (“town”), originally in honor of crown princes or princes of the British Empire but later chiefly in honor of others with the name Prince or locations named Princeton.

prisca.ety: Latin feminine form of the cognomen Prīscus, from prīscus (“former, ancient, old-fashioned”).

purificacion.ety: From purificación (“purification”), shortened from María (de la) Purificación, a Roman Catholic epithet of the Virgin Mary on the feast day of purification after childbirth.

pål.ety: From Old Norse Páll, from Latin Paulus. Cognate with English Paul.

queenie.m: The wife, consort, or widow of a king.

quentin.ety: From Old French. The name of a third century French martyr, from Latin Quīntīnus, a derivative of the Roman praenomen Quīntus, from quīntus (“fifth”).

quincy.ety: A Norman surname of Old French origin, from a place name Quincy or Quincey in France, ultimately from Latin Quintus (“fifth [born]”).

quinn.ety: The surname is Borrowed from Irish Ó Coinn (“descendant of Chief”).

quintin.ety: Derived from French Quentin, from Latin Quīntīnus, derivative of the Roman praenomen Quīntus, from quīntus (“fifth”) (used to distinguish the fifth-born child as per Roman naming conventions).

quinton.ety: Variant of Doublet of Quentin, merged with an Old English place name meaning "queen's town".

rachelle.ety: 20th-century variant of Rachel, from French Rachelle, or possibly coined independently of it.

rachid.ety: Borrowed from French Rachid, itself from Arabic رَاشِد.

ragna.ety: Short form of female compound names beginning with the element Ragn-, from Old Norse rǫgn (“counsel”), such as Ragnhild.

ragnvald.ety: From Old Norse Rǫgnvaldr, from Proto-Germanic *Raginawaldaz.

raiden.ety: Possible a modern variant of Rayden, or a coinage rhyming with Braiden, Jaiden, etc.

raimundo.ety: From Old Galician-Portuguese Reimundo, from Old French Raimund, from Frankish *Raginmund, from Proto-Germanic *Raginamunduz, composed of *raginą (“advice”) + *mundō (“protection”).

rainer.ety: Variant of Rayner, a patronymic surname from a medieval given name from Proto-Germanic *raginą (“counsel by the gods”) + *harjaz (“army”). Also borrowed from modern German.

rainey.ety: Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó Raighne (“descendant of Raighne”), a Gaelicized form of the Old Norse personal name Rognvaldr.

raisa.m: easy; easy to understand, easy to do

rajmund.ety: From Old French, from Frankish, from Proto-Germanic *raginą + *mundō.

raleigh.ety: From Old English rā, rāha (“roe deer”) + lēah (“woodland, clearing”). Equivalent to roe + -ley (“lea”).

ralf.ety: From German Ralf. Borrowed from English Ralph.

ralph.ety: Inherited from Middle English Radulf From Middle English Radulf, from Old English Rǣdwulf (also as Raulf), from Proto-West Germanic *Rādawulf, from Proto-Germanic *Rēdawulfaz.

rami.ety: Borrowed from Arabic رَامِي, masculine singular construct form of رَامٍ (rāmin). This surname is predominantly found in Morocco and India.

ramon.ety: From Old French Raimunt, from Frankish *Raginmund, from Proto-Germanic *raginą (“advice”) + *mundō (“protection”).

ramsey.ety: From Old English hramsa (“wild garlic”) + īeġ (“island”).

ran.ety: After Rán, Old Norse goddess of the sea, whose name is from the noun rán (“robbery”).

rand.ety: From Afrikaans rand, from English rand; compare English rand.

randall.ety: A Middle English variant of Randolph, preserved as a surname and revived in the twentieth century.

randi.ety: Contraction of Ragnfrid, from Old Norse Ragnfríðr, from ragn (“advice, judgment”) + fríðr (“beautiful”).

raoul.ety: From Germanic, first attested in Old French as Raol.

rasmus.ety: From the Latin saints' name Erasmus, from Ancient Greek Erasmos "beloved". Used in Denmark since the fifteenth century.

raul.ety: From Raoul. From Germanic, first attested in Old French as Raol.

ray.ety: As an English surname, from pet forms derived from the root of Raymond. Also as an English surname, from Old French rei (“king”).

rayden.ety: From Raydon or Reydon in Suffolk.

raylan.ety: Modern coinage from Ray, compare Rylan, Braylon.

raymond.ety: From Old French Raimund, from Frankish *Raginmund, from Proto-Germanic *Raginamunduz, composed of *raginą (“advice”) + *mundō (“protection”).

reagan.ety: Anglicized from Irish Gaelic Ó Riagáin (“descendant of Riagán”), a personal name possibly derived from ríodhgach (“impulsive, furious”), an alternative form of ríogach.

rebekka.ety: From Hebrew רִבְקָה (Riḇqāh, “enchantingly beautiful, captivating, snare”).

reed.ety: As an English and Scottish surname, from the adjective red. Also as an English surname, from Old English rēodan (“to clear out”), from Proto-West Germanic *reudan.

reese.ety: As a given name and British surname generally from Welsh Rhys, literally “ardor”. Chiefly in North America, the surname may also be from unrelated German Reese, literally “giant”.

reginald.ety: From Latin Reginaldus, Latinization of names deriving from Proto-Germanic *Raginawaldaz.

reidar.ety: From Old Norse Reiðarr, Hreiðarr, from hreiðr (“nest, home”) + -arr. Cognate with Faroese Reiðar, Icelandic Hreiðar, Swedish Redar, Danish Reder and Old Swedish Rēdhar.

reilly.ety: From Irish Ó Raghallaigh, a surname meaning "descendants of Raghallach".

reine.ety: A more gallicized form of Régine, from Latin Regina (“queen”).

reinhard.ety: From Middle High German Reinhart, from Old High German Reginhart (also Raginhart), from Proto-Germanic *Raginaharduz, a compound of *raginą and *harduz. Cognate with English Reynard.

reinhold.ety: From Old High German Raginald, from Proto-Germanic *Raginawaldaz; see there for cognates and further etymology.

remi.ety: A sixth-century French saint, Latin Rēmigius, from rēmex (“oarsman”).

remington.ety: The surname is from Rimington, from Old English rima (“edge, border”) + -ing + -tun, literally “settlement by the boundary stream”.

remy.ety: From French Rémy, a French short form of Latin Remigius. In Norwegian, Remy is used as a spelling variant of Remi.

renata.ety: Feminine form of Latin saint's name Renatus, from renatus (“reborn”).

rene.ety: From Latin Renātus, name of a legendary 5th century French saint, from renātus (“reborn”), with identical meaning in French (rené).

renee.ety: From French Renée, meaning reborn, stemmed from Latin Renata. Feminine form of male René.

renesmee.ety: Coined by Stephenie Meyer as the name of Renesmee Cullen (a character in her novel Breaking Dawn (2008), the fourth in the Twilight series, who also appeared in The Twilight Saga, a film series based on the novels).

renée.ety: From French Renée, meaning reborn, stemmed from Latin Renata. Feminine form of male René.

rex.ety: From Latin rēx (“king”). Doublet of rajah and roy.

reynold.ety: From Anglo-Norman Reinald From Anglo-Norman Reinald, from Proto-Germanic *Raginawaldaz brought to England by Normans and partly merged with the earlier equivalent Ronald, from Old Norse Rǫgnvaldr.

rhett.ety: Name of a South Carolina family, anglicized from Dutch de Raedt, from Middle Dutch raet (“advice”).

rhian.ety: From rhiain (“maiden”), from Middle Welsh riein, first used in fiction.

rhianna.ety: A variant spelling of Rihanna, from Arabic رَيْحَانَة. This spelling is possibly influenced by unrelated Welsh names such as Rhiannon.

rhodes.ety: From rodes, the plural form of Middle English rode, from Old English rod, rodu.

rhonda.ety: Modern coinage explained as Welsh rhon (“pike, lance”) + da (“good”).

riad.ety: Borrowed from Arabic - Borrowed from Arabic.

rian.ety: A re-Gaelicisation of the given name Ryan, which comes from the Irish surname Ó Riaghain//Ó Riain, literally “descendant of Riaghan//Rian”. Thus, reviving the original Irish given name Riaghan//Rian.

rich.ety: The surname also derives from rich as a nickname.

richmond.ety: From Middle English Rychemund, from a name cognate to French Richemont (“town in Normandy”). Equivalent to rich + mound.

ricki.ety: As a female name also from Erica.

ridley.ety: Place names in England, Old English hrēad (“reeds”) or rydde (“cleared land”) + lēah (“wood, clearing”). Thus, equivalent to reed or rid + -ley (“lea”).

rigmor.ety: Medieval Danish variation of Old High German Ricmuda, from rihhi (“rule”) + muot (“mood”) (from Proto-West Germanic *mōd).

rikke.ety: Short form of Frederikke, the feminine form of Frederik, and less often of other female names ending in -rikke.

riley.ety: From Ryley in Lancashire, from Old English ryge (“rye”) + leah (“clearing, meadow”). Equivalent to rye + -ley (“lea”).

rina.ety: Short form of names ending in -rina, such as Katrina, Marina and Larina. Also borrowed from other European languages, such as Italian, in the 20th century.

ripley.ety: From the Old English folk name for the Anglian tribe, *Hrype + Old English lēah (“woodland clearing”).

rivka.ety: From Hebrew רִבְקָה (rivká) or Yiddish רבֿקה (rivke). Doublet of Rebecca.

roald.ety: From Old Norse Róaldr, Old Norse Hróaldr, from earlier Hróðvaldr, from Proto-Germanic *Hrōþiwaldaz, *Hrōþawaldaz, from *hrōþiz (“praise, fame”) + *waldaz (“ruler, chieftain”).

roar.ety: Old Norse Hróarr, from hroðr "fame" + geirr "spear".

robin.ety: From Middle English Robin, from Old French, diminutive of Robert. From the bird, robin, or from Germanic.

rochelle.ety: Habitational or topographic name from places in France, La Rochelle, from Old French rochelle diminutive form of roche (“rock”).

rocio.ety: From rocío (“dew”), shortened from María (del) Rocío, an epithet of the Virgin Mary in Almonte, Spain.

rock.ety: As an English surname, from the noun rock. Also as an English surname, misdivision of Middle English atter oke (“at the oak”).

rod.ety: Abbreviated form of Rodney and of Roderick, both with roots originating from Germanic *hrōþiz (“fame”).

rodney.ety: From Old English placename Hrōdanīeġ, Hrōdanīġ, literally “Hroda's island”, from Proto-Germanic *hrōþiz (“fame”) and *awjō (“island”).

roel.ety: Shortened from Roelof, Roeland and other names starting with Roel-.

roger.ety: From Old French Rogier, from the Frankish equivalent of Old English Hrōþgār (see Hroðgar), from Proto-Germanic *Hrōþigaizaz (“fame-spear”). Compare also Rutger.

rogerio.ety: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin Rogerius.

rohit.ety: Transliteration of Hindi रोहित, Transliteration of Bengali রোহিত, etc.

roksana.ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Ῥωξᾱ́νη.

rolf.ety: From Old Norse Hrólfr, and from its Old French equivalent, cognates of Rudolph.

rolv.ety: From Old Norse Hrólfr, from *Hróðolfr, *Hróðulfʀ, from Proto-Germanic *Hrōþiwulfaz. Cognate with Faroese Rólvur, Icelandic Hrólfur, German Rudolf and English Rudolph.

roma.ety: From Latin and Italian Roma (“Rome”). Doublet of Rome and Rum.

rommel.ety: From the Dutch surname, from rommelen (“to rumble”). Also a spelling variant of Rummel.

romuald.ety: From the name of a 10th–11th century Italian saint, from Old High German ruom (“fame”) + waltan (“to rule”).

romualdo.ety: From Proto-Germanic *hrōmą (“glory”) (the same root of German Ruhm) + *waldiz (“powerful”).

ronald.ety: From Scottish Gaelic Raghnall Anglicized from Scottish Gaelic Raghnall, itself derived from Old Norse Rǫgnvaldr, from rǫgn (“advice”) + valdr (“power”), later partly merged with the Continental Germanic equivalent Reynold.

ronaldo.ety: Borrowed from English Ronald Borrowed from English Ronald, anglicized from a Scottish Gaelic form of Old Norse Rǫgnvaldr, from rǫgn (“advice”) + valdr (“power”), later partly merged with the Continental Germanic equivalent Reynold.

roni.ety: 20th century rendering of English Ronnie. It can also be explained as a short form of the Latin (ultimately Ancient Greek) saint's name Hieronymus and of biblical Aaron.

ronin.ety: From modern films and comics, perhaps literally "a ronin". Compare also Ronan.

ronja.ety: Borrowed from Swedish Ronja, from the book of Lindgren. Transliteration of Russian Роня, diminutive of Вероника.

ronny.ety: Shortening of Ronald + -y. A less common spelling of Ronnie.

roosevelt.ety: From a Dutch name of a farm, either Rozenveld (one in Zeeland) or Ruiseveld (one in Brabant), from Middle Dutch; the former could be a compound of rose (“wild rose / poppy?”) + velt (“open country.
roosevelt.m: wild rose / poppy? + open country; field

rory.ety: Anglicized form of Scottish Gaelic Ruairidh and Irish Ruairí (“red-haired king”), from Old Irish Ruaidrí (“red king”).

rosaleen.ety: Anglicized from Irish Róisín, a diminutive of Rose.

rosalie.ety: From French Rosalie, from the Latin saints’ name Rosālia, from rosa (“rose”). Doublet of Rosalia.

rosalind.ety: From Proto-Germanic *hrussą (“horse”) and *linþaz (“soft; weak, tender”), associated by medieval folk etymology with Spanish rosa linda "lovely rose".

rosaline.ety: An elaborate form of Rosalie, or a simplified form of Rosalind.

rosanna.ety: Blend of Rose + Anna, possibly also inspired by Roxana.

rosanne.ety: Blend of Rose + Anne, possibly also inspired by Roxanne.

rosaura.ety: From Spanish rosa + aurea. Invented by w:Pedro Calderón de la Barca in w:Life is a Dream.
rosaura.m: the bit and reins of a horse, bridle

roscoe.ety: From a place in Lancashire, from Old Norse rá (“roebuck”) + skógr (“forest”).

rose.ety: As an English, Scottish, French, Walloon, Danish, Jewish (Yiddish רויז), and German surname, all from the noun rose.

rosemary.ety: A combination of Rose + Mary, referring to the flower as a symbol of Virgin Mary, first recorded in the eighteenth century. It is found in continental Europe as Rosemarie and Rosa Maria.

rosendo.ety: Surname from transferred use of given name, of Spanish, Galician, or Portuguese origin, from Medieval Latin Rudesindus, from the Germanic (Gothic) name Rudesind, composed of the elements *𐌷𐍂𐍉𐌸𐍃 (“glory.

rosina.ety: An Italian pet form of Rosa borrowed in the nineteenth century, particularly from the character in Rossini's opera The Barber of Seville (1816).

roslyn.ety: A variant of Rosaline inspired by the Scottish place name Roslin or Rosslyn.

ross.ety: As a Scottish surname, from several places such as Roose in Cumbria or Roos in Yorkshire, both from Scottish Gaelic ros (“promontory”) or a Brythonic parallel of its source such as Welsh rhos (“moor, heath”).

rowan.ety: Anglicised from the Irish saints' name Ruadhán (“little red one”), or as a surname from Ó Ruadháin (“descendant of Ruadhán”).

rowena.ety: From the name of the daughter of Hengist and wife of Vortigern in Geoffrey of Monmouth's 12th century pseudohistorical Latin work Historia regum Britanniae.

roxane.ety: From French Roxane, from Ancient Greek Ῥωξᾱ́νη, from Old Persian *rauxšnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂. Doublet of Lua and Luna.

roy.ety: From various sources: Anglo-Norman roy (“king”) a variant of Old French roi, from Latin rēx, rēgem from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs (“ruler, king”). Doublet of Rey.

royal.ety: A habitational surname, shaped by folk etymology, from places in England, Riehale, Righale, Ryhill and Ryall, Old English ryge (“rye”) + hyll (“hill”), and Royle, rā (“roe”) + hyll (“hill”).

royce.ety: Derived from the Middle English given name Rose. See English Rose.

ruby.ety: The female name derives from ruby in the 19th century. The programming language was named after the gemstone.

rudolf.ety: Borrowed from Czech Rudolf and German Rudolf.

runa.ety: From Old Norse Rúna, from rúna. Also a short form of compound names with the element run.

runar.ety: 19th century construction of run + -ar; from rún (“secret; rune”), and Proto-Germanic *harjaz or *warjaz.

rune.ety: From Old Norse Rúni, from rúni (“good friend”). Also a short form of compound names with the element run (such as Runolv).

rupert.ety: A German name, brought to England by Prince Rupert of the Rhine in the seventeenth century. Doublet of Robert.

rush.ety: As an English surname, from the noun rush (“waterside plant, plant in marshes”). Also as an English surname, from the archaic noun rush (“beehive”), from French ruche.

ruslana.ety: A transliteration of the female given name Русла́на.

russell.ety: Inherited from Middle English Russel, from Anglo-Norman Russel. Doublet of Rousseau/Roussel.

rut.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Ruth Latin Ruth.

rylan.ety: Possibly a variant of Ryland, meaning "rye field" and from Old English.

régis.ety: An occupational surname for an official, from French régir; also from Latin rēgis (“of the king”), for service in a king's household, or as a nickname.

rían.ety: A variant of Rian, based on a folk etymology found on baby name websites that claim the name is a compound of rí (“king”) + -án.

sabine.ety: From the Latin saint's name Sabina.

sabra.ety: Borrowed from Hebrew צַבָּר (tsabár, “prickly pear cactus”), from Arabic صَبَّار (“cactus”).

sadhbh.ety: From Middle Irish Sadb, from Old Irish Sadb, from Proto-Celtic, feminine derivative of *swādus (“sweet”).

safira.ety: Borrowed from Italian Saffira, from Ancient Greek Σαπφειρη, likely from σάπφειρος.

sage.ety: As an English and French surname, from sage, a nickname for a wise person. The given name, in general use since the 1990s, is also associated with the sage plant.

saima.ety: 19th-century coinage from, the name of a lake.

sajid.ety: Borrowed from Arabic سَاجِد. This surname is mostly found in Pakistan.

salah.ety: As an Islamic/Arabic surname, as well as a Jewish adoption of it, from صَلاة (“prayer”) or صَلاح (“righteousness”).

salete.ety: Probably from French placename Notre-Dame de la Salette.

salina.ety: Possibly a variant of, or a coinage inspired by, Selina. The place name seems an unlikely source.

sallie.ety: A less common spelling of Sally; see -ie.

sally.ety: A diminutive lambdacism of Sarah. Compare Hal from Harry and Moll from Mary.

salomao.ety: From Old Galician-Portuguese Salomon, from Latin Salomon, from Ancient Greek Σολομών, Σαλομών, from Hebrew שְׁלֹמֹה.

salvadora.ety: Created as a female form of the given name Salvador.

samanta.ety: From English Samantha in the end of the 20th century.

samantha.ety: It was recorded in the 17th century in England.

samatha.ety: From Sanskrit समाधान (śamatha) meaning "tranquility" and "concentration" (referring to Buddhist meditation) or "equality".

sander.ety: Short form of Aleksander, also used as a short form of Alexander (“male given name”).

sanders.ety: From the Middle English Sander, a shortened form of Alexander + suffix -s.

sandra.ety: Short form of Aleksandra, also used as a short form of the spelling variant Alexandra.

sandrine.ety: Sandra + -ine short form of Alexandrine, from Latin Alexandrīna.

santos.ety: From Romance Santos (Spanish Santos, Portuguese Santos, Italian Santos).

sanya.ety: Variant of Saniyah, Saniyya, from Arabic سنيّة (“radiant”).

sarai.ety: From Hebrew שרי (Saráy), from the plural form of שר (“master, chief”).

sariah.ety: Name of a character in the Book of Mormon. Compare Sarah and Maria.

sariyah.ety: Borrowed from Arabic سَارِيَة, the meaning “a cloud that comes by night”.
sariyah.m: a cloud that comes by night

sascha.ety: Russian Саша, a pet form of Александра ( =Alexandra), cognate to Sasha.

sasha.ety: Borrowed from the Slavic diminutive form of Alexander and Alexandra; in English mostly from Russian Са́ша, a diminutive form for both Алекса́ндр (“Alexander”) and Алекса́ндра (“Alexandra”).

saskia.ety: Probably formed from compound names beginning with the Germanic element *Sas- (“a Saxon”). Best known as the name of Rembrandt's wife.

saturnina.ety: From Old French saturnin, derived from Latin Saturninus, meaning “of Saturn”.

savannah.ety: The cities are named after the Savannah River, possibly derived from Shawnee or Algonquian.

sawyer.ety: As an English occupational surname, from sawyer (“one who saws”). Senses loaned from various languages include Jewish/German Seger and Sager, Slovene Žagar.

saxon.ety: Partially from Middle English Saxe, Sax; from Old English *Seaxa (attested in plural Seaxan), from Proto-West Germanic *Sahsan, plural of Proto-West Germanic *Sahsō.

schuyler.ety: A Dutch surname (cf. scholier) from German Schüler (“scholar, student”); brought to America by seventeenth-century Dutch immigrants. Doublet of scholar and schooler.

scot.ety: Inherited from Middle English Scot, from Old English Sċottas (“people from Ireland, Irishmen”), from Late Latin Scōttī (see Scōtī for more).

seamus.ety: Anglicization of Irish Séamas (“James”), itself from English James.

sean.ety: Anglicised form of Irish Seán, from Old French Jehan, from Latin Johannes, variant of Ioannes, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yōḥānān), literally “God is gracious”.

sebastian.ety: From Latin Sebastiānus, name of an early Christian saint, from ancient city of Sebaste in Asia Minor (modern Sivas, Turkey), from Ancient Greek Σεβαστός (“august, venerable, exalted”), itself a translation of the Roman title Augustus.

sedona.ety: Originally coined by Sedona Schnebly's mother. From the given name of Sedona Schnebly (1877-1950).

selah.ety: Biblical Hebrew סֶלָה (selāh); according to some scholars, from סָלָה (salah, “to hang”, implying “to weigh”, “to measure”).

selena.ety: Either a variant of Selina, from Latin Caelīna (“heavenly”), or from Selene, the Ancient Greek goddess of the moon.

selim.ety: From Swedish Selim, from Arabic سليم; partly also from forms of Anselmi.

selin.ety: Possibly from Turkmen selin, a perennial large grass growing in the desert.

selina.ety: From Selene. From the Ancient Greek Σελήνη, from σέλας (“light”).

selma.ety: Taken to use in the 19th century when similar-sounding names, Elma, Thelma, Alma, Wilma, etc. were in vogue.

september.ety: From Middle English, from late Old English, from Old French septembre, Latin September (“seventh month”), from septem (“seven”), which see; September was the seventh month in the Roman calendar.

seraphina.ety: From Late Latin Seraphina, name of obscure early martyrs, from biblical seraphim.

sergey.ety: Transliteration of Russian Серге́й, from Latin Sergius.

serghei.ety: Borrowed from Russian Сергей. Doublet of Sergiu and Serghie.

serhiy.ety: Transliteration of Ukrainian Сергі́й, from Latin Sergius.

seyed.ety: Borrowed from Iranian Persian سید (seyyed), from Classical Persian سَیِّد, from Arabic سَيِّد.

seymour.ety: From a Norman surname from a place in Normandy, from Old French Saint-Maur, from Late Latin Sanctus Maurus (“Saint Maurus”). The name is cognate to Murry and Maurice.

shana.ety: Anglicized variant of the Welsh name Siân (pet form Siana) - or a version of the French name Jeanne.

shanae.ety: Anglicization of Irish Sinéad q.v. based on its modern Irish pronunciation.

shane.ety: Anglicized form of the Northern Irish pronunciation of Irish Seán, from Old French Jehan, from Latin Johannes, variant of Ioannes, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yōḥānān), literally “God is gracious”.

shanelle.ety: From French Chanel, after Coco Chanel and under influence from -elle.

shaniqua.ety: Popularized in the 1970s among African Americans, possibly influenced by Swahili shani (“novelty”) or Welsh Siân (Joanna, "God is gracious"); compare other names starting with Shan- like Shanice, Shanika, Shanita.

shaquille.ety: A fanciful spelling of Arabic شَكِيل (“handsome”).

sharee.ety: A variant of Sherry or coined from French chéri, chérie (“darling”).

sharon.ety: Biblical place name, Hebrew שָׁרוֹן (šārōn, “the Sharon plain”).

shaun.ety: A variant of Sean, from Irish Seán, from Old French Jehan, from Latin Johannes, variant of Ioannes, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yōḥānān), literally “God is gracious”.

shauna.ety: From Shaun + -a, variant of Irish Seán, from Old French Jehan, from Latin Johannes, variant of Ioannes, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yōḥānān), literally “God is gracious”.

shavon.ety: A 20th-century phonetic spelling of Irish Siobhán.

shavonne.ety: Anglicization of Irish Siobhán as pronounced in modern Irish, under probable influence from Yvonne.

shawn.ety: A variant of Sean, from Irish Seán, from Old French Jehan, from Latin Jōhannēs, variant of Iōannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (yōḥānān, yokhanán), literally “God is gracious”.

shawnee.ety: Ultimately from Shawnee saawanwa (“Shawnee”) or saawanoki (“southerners”), a hypothetical intermediary term is sometimes supposed to have facilitated the entry into English, such as Munsee sawanow.

shay.ety: Variant of Shea, from Irish Ó Séaghdha.

shayna.ety: Borrowed from Yiddish שיינע, a feminine inflection of שיין (“beautiful”).

sheena.ety: Anglicization of Scottish Gaelic Sìne and Síne, ultimately from Latin Joanna, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννα, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָה (Yôḥānāh), literally “God is gracious”.

sheila.ety: From Hindi शीला, from Sanskrit शील (“character, good conduct”).

shelby.ety: From a medieval name, of Of unknown origin origin, yet likely an alteration of Middle English Selby, Salibi (“dweller of the willow place”), from salwe (“willow, sallow”) + -by (“settlement, farm”).

sheldon.ety: From Old English scylf (“shelf”) + dūn (“hill”) or denu (“valley”).

shelley.ety: From Old English, meaning "clearing on a bank".

shelton.ety: From Old English scylfe (“deck, shelf”) + tun (“town”). Doublet of Skelton.

sheridan.ety: As a surname, from Irish Ó Sirideáin.

sherman.ety: From Middle English schereman, scherman; equivalent to shear + -man.
sherman.m: A shearman; a person who shears sheep.

shirley.ety: English place name from Old English sċīr (“county”) + lēah (“meadow”). Equivalent to shire + -ley (“lea”).

shiv.ety: Variant of Shiva, from Sanskrit शिव (Śivá, “the auspicious one”).

shlomo.ety: Transliteration of Biblical Hebrew שְׁלֹמֹה (šəlōmōʰ), from שָׁלוֹם (šālôm, “peace”). Doublet of Solomon.

shmuel.ety: Borrowed from Yiddish שמואל (Shmuel), from Hebrew שְׁמוּאֵל (šəmūʾḗl).

shona.ety: Scottish Anglicized form of Seonag ( =Joan) and an American variant of Shauna.

shonda.ety: Perhaps a Blend of Shona + Rhonda.

shyla.ety: A 20th-century coinage, possibly inspired by Sheila.

sian.ety: An anglicization of Welsh Siân, ultimately from Latin Joanna, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννα, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָה (Yôḥānāh), literally “God is gracious”, the feminized form of יְהוֹחָנָן (Yəhōḥānān) which produced John and its many doublets.

sibyl.ety: Latin Sibylla, Ancient Greek Σίβυλλα (“sibyl”), name of ancient Greek prophetesses.

sibylle.ety: Latin Sibylla, from Ancient Greek Σίβυλλα.

sidney.ety: From Old English *Sīdaneġ, the name of a place in Surrey, from sīd (“wide”) + eġ (“island”).

sidonie.ety: From Sidon (“Saïda”) + -ie. Naming pertaining to the Phoenician city of Sidon.

siegfried.ety: From Middle High German Sîfrit, from Old High German Sigifrid, from Proto-West Germanic *Sigifriþu, from Proto-Germanic *Sigifriþuz.

sigbjørn.ety: Old Norse Sigbjǫrn, from sigr (“victory”) + bjǫrn (“bear”).

sigfrid.ety: Germanic "victory" + "peace", a variant of German Siegfried and Danish Sigfred.

sigmund.ety: From Old Norse Sigmundr, from sigr (“victory”) + mundr (“protection”), from Proto-Norse *ᛗᚢᚺᛞᚢᛉ (munduʀ), and ultimately from Proto-Germanic *mundō (“protection, security”).

signe.ety: Old Norse Signý. Name of heroines in Norse mythology.

sigrun.ety: Old Norse Sigrún, from sigrún, from sigr (“victory”) + rún (“secret”).

sigve.ety: Old Norse Sigviðr, from sigr (“victory”) + viðr (“wood”).

sihem.ety: Borrowed from Arabic سِهَام Borrowed from Arabic سِهَام.

silvano.ety: From a derivative of Latin silva (“wood”).

silver.ety: As a surname, anglicised from the German Jewish ornamental surname Silber.
silver.m: silver (chemical element with the symbol Ag)

silverio.ety: Inherited from Latin Silverius Inherited from Latin Silverius.

silvestre.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Silvester Latin Silvester.

silvo.ety: Mainly from a vernacular form of Sylvester, perhaps via Middle High German Silvester. In Eastern Finland, the surname could also derive from vernacular forms of Ancient Greek Σιλουανός.

simao.ety: From Old Galician-Portuguese Simon, from Latin Simon, from Ancient Greek Σίμων, from Hebrew שִׁמְעוֹן.

sinclair.ety: Derived from Saint Clare, to whom the clan's churches were dedicated.

sindy.m: Cynthian (of or relating to Mount Cynthus)

sinead.ety: Anglicization of Irish Sinéad, from Old Northern French Jeanette, from Middle French Jehanne + -ette, from Medieval Latin Johanna, variant of Latin Ioanna under influence from Latin Iōhannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννα.

siri.ety: From Norwegian Siri, a variant of Sigrid, whence also English Sigrid.

siril.ety: A 20th century coinage from the given name Siri + the Old Norse ending -hild, as in Toril, Torhild, etc.

sissel.ety: From Cecilie. From Latin Caecilia, feminine form of Caecilius, a Roman family name possibly derived from the byname caecus (“blind”).

siv.ety: From Old Norse Sif, from sif (“kindred, kinswoman”), from Proto-Germanic *sibjō.

sivert.ety: From a German variant of Sigvard, cognate to Sigurd.

sky.ety: As a surname, a translation of German Himmel and an anglicization of Ashkenazic surnames ending in -sky.

skye.ety: Derived from Scottish Gaelic An t-Eilean Sgitheanach, of long disputed (probably non-Indo-European substrate) origin, with several theories proposed and none widely accepted; see Etymology of Skye.

smith.ety: From smith or Middle English Smith (“a surname”), alternative form of Smyth, itself from smyth (“smith”). Doublet of Schmidt and Smid and Smit.

snorre.ety: From Old Norse Snorri, from snerra (“attack, onslaught”).

socrates.ety: Via Latin Socrates, from Ancient Greek Σωκράτης. Doublet of Sokratis.

sofiane.ety: Borrowed from Arabic سُفْيَان Borrowed from Arabic سُفْيَان.

soizic.ety: Borrowed from Breton Soazig, diminutive of Soaz.

solange.ety: Name of a 9th-century French saint, Late Latin Sollemnia, from sollemnis (“solemn”).

solbjørg.ety: Old Norse Salbjǫrg, from salr (“house", "hall”) + bjǫrg (“salvation”).

solfrid.ety: Created at the end of the nineteenth century, from the elements Sol- as in Solveig, from Old Norse salr (“hall”) (by folk etymology interpreted as modern Norwegian sol (“sun”) ) and -frid as in Målfrid, Ingrid, etc, meaning "beautiful".

sondre.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Sundri (“male given name”), of uncertain meaning.

sonya.ety: Borrowed from Со́ня, an informal pet form of Со́фья, Софі́я or Софи́я (“Sofia, Sophia”), from the Ancient Greek σοφία (“wisdom”).

sophie.ety: From the English Sophie, the pet form of Sophia or from French Sophie. From Ancient Greek σοφία (“wisdom”).

sorin.ety: Possibly derived from or related to soare (“sun”).

spencer.ety: An occupational surname from Middle English Spenser, Spencer, Spensier, from the common noun spenser (“spencer”), denoting someone who works in a spense (“spence”), or as a butler or steward.

spenser.ety: From Middle English Spenser, from Middle English spenser (“spencer”), from spense (“spence”).

stacey.m: ancient name, also of Christian Saint

stacie.m: ancient name, also of Christian Saint

stafford.ety: From Old English stæþ (“landing place”) + ford.

stanford.ety: Various placenames from Old English stān (“stone”) + ford (“ford”).

stanley.ety: From places in England, Old English stān (“stone”) + lēah (“meadow”). Equivalent to stone + -ley (“lea”).

star.ety: As a German and Jewish surname, from Star (“starling”). Also as a German and Jewish surname.

starla.ety: Possibly derived from the word star.

starr.ety: As an English surname, from the noun star. As a Jewish surname, spelling variant of Star.

stefan.ety: From Ancient Greek στεφανίζω (“to crown”) & Ancient Greek στέφανος (“that which surrounds, crown, wreath”).

steffan.ety: From Late Latin Stephanus, from Ancient Greek Στέφανος.

steffen.ety: Borrowed from Danish Steffen (“male given name”), a Danish form of Stefan (“male given name”), also found in Low German.

stein.ety: From Old Norse Steinn, from steinn (“stone”), whence also stein. Also a short form of compound names with the element.

steinar.ety: From Old Norse Steinarr, from Proto-Norse ᛊᛏᚨᛁᚾᚨᚹᚨᚱᛁᛃᚨᛉ, from Proto-Germanic *stainaz (“stone”) + *warjaz (“defender”). Cognate with Steinar, Swedish Steinar and Danish Stener.

sten.ety: From Old Norse Steinn, from steinn (“stone”).

stephan.ety: Ultimately from Ancient Greek στεφανίζω (“to crown”) & Ancient Greek στέφανος (“that which surrounds, crown, wreath”).

stephane.ety: Borrowed from Latin Stephanus, from Ancient Greek Στέφανος, becoming popular beginning in the 1950s.

stephani.ety: Two main origins: Borrowed from German Stephani, a Latinized patronymic surname from the personal name Stephanus. Variant spelling of Italian Stefani.

stephanie.ety: Borrowed from French Stéphanie. The standard English feminine form of Stephen.

stetson.ety: A variant of Stitson, a habitational name from Stidston (“site in the Parish of South Brent”), from Middle English Stidewardesdoune, Stidewardeston, Stitewardeston, Styddeston.
stetson.m: site in the Parish of South Brent

steve.ety: Shortening of various names ultimately derived from Latin Stephanus, from Ancient Greek Στέφανος from στέφανος (“crown, wreath”).

steven.ety: Inherited from Middle English Stevene, Steven, from Anglo-Norman Estievne, Estievene, from Latin Stephanus, from Ancient Greek Στέφανος, from στέφανος (“crown, wreath”), from στέφω (“to put round, to surround”).

stewart.ety: Borrowed from Middle Scots stewart (“steward”), from Early Scots stewart, from Old English stiġweard.

stig.ety: From Old Norse Stígr, made famous by Stig Hvide, a legendary Danish chieftain.

stine.ety: A short form of Kristine. Recorded as a given name since the 17th century.

sture.ety: A medieval byname, famous in the history of Sweden, possibly from the verb stura "to sulk", for a stubborn person. Used as a given name since the 18th century.

sturla.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Sturla, probably originally a nickname. Related to sturla (“to disturb, drive crazy”).

stéphane.ety: Borrowed from Latin Stephanus, from Ancient Greek Στέφανος, becoming popular beginning in the 1950s.

stéphanie.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Stephania Latin Stephania.

sueli.ety: From the Germanic root suel, meaning "shining". Alternatively a variant of Suélen.

suellen.ety: Blend of Sue + Ellen. short form of Sue-Ellen/Sue Ellen.

sunniva.ety: From Old English Sunnġifu, from sunne (“sun”) + ġifu (“gift”).

susan.ety: English form of the biblical Susanna, from Biblical Hebrew שׁוֹשַׁנָּה (šōšannā, “lily”), ultimately from Egyptian (zšn).

susanne.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Σουσάννα, the New Testament form of Hebrew שׁוֹשַׁנָּה (šōšannā, “lily”).

sutton.ety: From Old English suþ (“south”) + tun (“town”). Doublet of Southtown.

suzanne.ety: From French Suzanne. Doublet of Susanna.

svanhild.ety: Old Norse Svanhildr, from svan (“swan”) + hildr (“battle”).

svea.ety: From old singular feminine form of svear (“Swedes”). Popularized as a name by Esaias Tegnér's poem Svea, published in 1817.
svea.m: Swedes (members of a North Germanic tribe)

svein.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Sveinn, originally a byname based on the common noun sveinn (“boy, young man, servant”), from Proto-Germanic *swainaz (“relative, kinsman; young man; herder”).

sven.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Sveinn, originally a byname based on the common noun sveinn (“boy, young man, servant”).

svend.ety: Borrowed from Danish Svend, the Danish form of Svein, ultimately from Old Norse Sveinn, originally a byname based on the common noun sveinn (“boy, young man, servant”).

svenja.ety: Modern German feminine form of Sven.

svenn.ety: A spelling variant of Sven, with doubled final n; ultimately from Old Norse Sveinn, originally a byname based on the common noun sveinn (“boy, young man, servant”).

sverre.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Sverrir, originally a byname derived from sverra (“to swing around, spin; move violently”), and interpreted as “troublemaker; wild, restless person”.
sverre.m: to swing around, spin; move violently

svetlana.ety: Transliteration of Russian Светла́на, from свет (“light”). Made up by Alexander Vostokov in 1802, later borrowed into English and other languages.

sviatlana.ety: Transliteration of Святла́на. Transliteration of Russian Светла́на, from свет (“light”).

svitlana.ety: Transliteration of Ukrainian Світла́на, from свет (“light”). Made up by Alexander Vostokov in 1802, later borrowed into English and other languages.

sydney.ety: For the surname and given name, see Sidney. The cities in Australia and Canada are named after British politician Thomas Townshend, 1st Viscount Sydney (1733–1800).

syeda.ety: Borrowed from Arabic سَيِّدَة. From Urdu سیدہ, from Arabic سَيِّدَة.

sylvestre.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Silvester Latin Silvester.

sylvi.ety: A vernacular or short form of Sylvia.

sylviane.ety: From Latin Silviana, feminine derivative of Silvius, silva "forest".

synthia.m: Cynthian (of or relating to Mount Cynthus)

søren.ety: Medieval vernacular form of the Latin Severinus.

tabata.ety: From Tabita, from Aramaic טביתא (Ṭabītā’, “doe, roe, gazelle”).

tabita.ety: Borrowed from Aramaic טביתא (Ṭabītā’, “doe, roe, gazelle”).

tadeu.ety: From Latin Thaddaeus, from Ancient Greek Θαδδαῖος, from Aramaic תַדַּי (Ṯaday), of uncertain origin.

tage.ety: From Old Danish Taki "a guarantor", used as a given name since the 17th century.

tahar.ety: Borrowed from Arabic طَهَر Borrowed from Arabic طَهَر.

tai.ety: From the Wade–Giles romanization of the Mandarin pronunciation of Chinese 代.

taina.ety: Eastern Finnish diminutive of the Russian given name Татья́на, identical with a dialectal form of taimi (“seedling”).

taira.ety: Borrowed from Japanese 平 (Taira) or Japanese 平良 (Taira).

tais.ety: From Ancient Greek Θαΐς, related to θαυμάζω (“to admire”). Became known as the name of the mistress of Alexander the Great.

talitha.ety: From Aramaic טליתא (ṭalyəṯāʾ, “female child, girl, maiden”). From a passage in the New Testament (Gospel of Mark) in which Jesus restores to life a little girl.

tallulah.ety: Borrowed from Cherokee Tallulah, name of a river in Georgia. See etymology section of Wikipedia article Tallulah River.

talon.ety: The surname derives from Old French talon (“heel”) as a nickname for a deformity, or for a swift runner; also diminutive of Talbot and Talleyrand.

tamer.m: the one who is completely mannish

tamia.ety: A 20th-century coinage popularized by the Canadian singer Tamia Hill.

tammy.ety: A diminutive of Tamsin and Tamara, later also used for new names beginning with Tam such as Tamika and Tamiya.

tamsin.ety: A medieval contraction of Thomasina, a feminine form of Thomas, revived in the UK in the twentieth century.

tanguy.ety: Borrowed from Breton Tangi, from tan (“fire”) + ki (“dog”).

tanya.ety: Borrowed in the twentieth century from the Russian pet form Та́ня of Татья́на (“Tatiana”).

tarah.ety: From Tara. Borrowed from Irish Teamhrach, genitive of Teamhair, from Old Irish Temair, literally “high place”.

taran.ety: From Torunn. From Old Norse Þórunn, from Þórr (“Thor”) and unna (“to love”).

taryn.ety: A 20th-century coinage, apparently from Tara combined with names like Karen. In the case of the American actress Taryn Power, derived from her father's given name Tyrone.

tate.ety: From Middle English *Tate, partially from Old English Tāta, from Proto-West Germanic *tait, from Proto-Germanic *taitaz (“radiant, glad, cheerful, tender”); and partially from Old Norse Táta, a personal name of unknown meaning.

tatiana.ety: Popular saints' name in the Eastern Orthodox Church, feminine of Latin Tatiānus, from Tatius (a Roman family name of obscure origin) + -ānus. Modern English usage is derived from Russian Татья́на.

tatjana.ety: Borrowed from Russian Татья́на, from Latin Tatiana. Cognate to English Tatiana.

tatum.ety: From Tatham, from Old English Tāta, a personal name of unknown meaning + hām.

tea.ety: Short form of Dorotea (“Dorothea”). Cognate with Scandinavian and English Thea.

teagan.ety: A diminutive of the Irish male name Tadhg, from tadhg (“poet”) A variant of Tegan, from Welsh tegan (“pet, darling”).

ted.ety: Shortened form of Edward, Theodore, Thaddeus or Edmund.

tegan.ety: 20th-century coinage from Welsh tegan (“pet, darling”). Transferred use of Irish Ó Tadhgáin, a surname.

temperance.ety: From temperance. A virtue name first used by Puritans in the 16th century.

tenley.ety: From Tineley in Northumberland or Teenley in West Yorkshire.

teodor.ety: From the Ancient Greek Θεόδωρος (“gift of god”). Cognate with English Theodore.

terence.ety: From Latin Terentius, a Roman family name of obscure origin, borne by a Roman playwright and by early Christian saints. In Ireland, it has been used to represent Turlough.
terence.m: of pertaining to the gens Terentia.

teri.ety: A spelling variant of Terry, from Teresa.

terje.ety: From Estonian tera "grain", or from Terhenetär in the Kalevala, Finnish terhen "mist".

terra.ety: From Latin Terra (“goddess of the earth; the land itself”).
terra.m: goddess of the earth; the land itself

terrance.m: of pertaining to the gens Terentia.

terrence.m: of pertaining to the gens Terentia.

tetyana.ety: Popular saints' name in the Eastern Orthodox Church, feminine of Latin Tatiānus, from Tatius (a Roman family name of obscure origin) + -ānus. Modern English usage is derived from Ukrainian Тетя́на.

thais.ety: From Ancient Greek Θαΐς, became known as the name of the mistress of Alexander the Great.

thea.ety: Shortened from Dorothea and Theodora, ultimately from Ancient Greek θεά (“goddess”).

theadore.ety: Spelling alteration of Theodore, from Ancient Greek Θεόδωρος.

thelma.ety: A literary invention, first appeared in the Swedish novel Kyrkoinvigningen i Hammarby (1840-1841) by Emilie Flygare-Carlén, translated into English as "The Magic Goblet" (1845).

theo.ety: Short form of Theodore, or of the rare given names Theobald, Theophilus or Theodoric, or of Theodora.

theodor.ety: From Teodor. From the Ancient Greek Θεόδωρος (“gift of god”).

theophile.ety: Borrowed from Latin Theophilus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek Θεόφιλος.

theresa.ety: First used in Spain, supposedly derived from Latin Thēra, from Ancient Greek Θήρᾱ, name of a city in Santorini, Greece.

thibault.ety: From Early Medieval Latin Theobaldus, a borrowing from Old English Þēodbald, from Proto-West Germanic *Þeudubalþ.

thompson.ety: Variant of Thomson, from Tom + -son, originally meaning "son of Thomas".

thora.ety: Short form of Old Norse female given names beginning with Þórr (“Thor”).

thorvald.ety: Old Norse Þorvaldr, from Þórr (“Thor”) + valdr (“rule”).

théophile.ety: Borrowed from Latin Theophilus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek Θεόφιλος.

tia.ety: Invented in the latter half of the twentieth century. It can be explained as a short form of Letitia or Venetia, or from Estonian Tiia, pet form of Dorothea.

tiago.ety: Reinterpreting it as São Tiago rather than Santo Iago by analogy to other saints such as São Mateus, São Marcos and São Paulo. Doublet of Iago and Jacó and Jaime.

tiana.ety: Modern contraction of Tatiana and Christiana. In the USA it is also explained as a form of Diana in such unrelated languages as Samoan and Cherokee (but the author Tiana Bighorse is a Navajo).

tiare.ety: From Tahitian Tiare, from tiare, a small white gardenia (Gardenia tahitiensis ), the national flower of Tahiti.

tierney.ety: Anglicized from Irish Gaelic Ó Tiarnaigh "descendant of Tiarnach", a diminutive of tiarna (“lord, master”).

tiffany.ety: From Old French Tifinie, Tiphanie, from Latin Theophania (“Epiphany”), from Ancient Greek θεο- (“god”) (combining form of θεός (“god”)) + φαίνω (“to shine, appear”). Doublet of theophany.

till.ety: Medieval diminutive of compound given names beginning with Diet- (such as Dieter or Dietrich), from Old High German thoit (“people”).

tilly.ety: Shortened from Matilda, -y. The surname may also have origins as a matronymic from Matilda.

timea.ety: Coined by Mór Jókai as Timéa in his 1872 novel Az arany ember (The Man with the Golden Touch, literally The Golden Man).

timeo.ety: From Latin Tīmaeus, from Ancient Greek Τῑ́μαιος.

timo.ety: Short, vernacular form of Timoteus, perhaps in Eastern Finland via short forms of Russian Тимофе́й. The standard Finnish equivalent of the English given name Timothy.

tina.ety: Short form of Christina or of any female name ending in -tina, such as Martina or Albertina; frequently from Latin -ina.

tino.ety: Probably from Italian Tino and reinforced by Timo; mostly from the (very) late 20th century.

tinsley.ety: From the unattested Old English personal name *Tynni + -s- + lēah (“woodland clearing, glade”).

tiny.ety: Hypocoristic form of Martijn/Martinus, Constantijn and other names ending in -tijn.

tito.ety: From Romance Tito (Spanish Tito, Portuguese Tito, Italian Tito); from Latin Titus.

tiziana.m: of pertaining to the gens Titia.

tiziano.m: of pertaining to the gens Titia.

toby.ety: The Middle English vernacular form of Tobias.

tom.ety: From Middle English Thomme. of Thomas. The dollar-bill sense is from the portrait of Thomas Jefferson featured on it.

tomas.ety: Borrowed from Spanish Tomás, from Ancient Greek Θωμᾶς, the Biblical Greek transcription of Aramaic תאומא (te'oma, “twin”).

tome.ety: From Latin Thōmās, from Ancient Greek Θωμᾶς, the Biblical Greek transcription of Aramaic תאומא or תאמא (“twin”), the nickname of one of the Twelve Apostles.

tomi.ety: 20th-century rendering of Swedish Tom and English Tom.

tommi.ety: A traditional diminutive or vernacular form of Tuomas (“Thomas”) and Tuomo. Used as a formal given name since 20th century, reinforced by English Tommy, with which it is often associated.

tonya.ety: Phonetic rendering of Russian То́ня, an informal pet form of Антони́на (“Antonina”).

tora.ety: From Old Norse Þóra, a female form of Þórr, or a short form of compound names with the element. Cognate with Faroese Tóra and Icelandic Þóra.

torben.ety: Borrowed from Danish Torben, a spelling variant of Danish Thorben.

torbjørg.ety: From Old Norse Þorbjǫrg, from Þórr (“Thor”) + bjǫrg (“salvation”).

torbjørn.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Þorbjǫrn. The Old Norse name consists of Þórr (“Thor”) + bjǫrn (“bear”), literally “Thor-bear”.

tord.ety: From Old Norse Þórðr, from Þórr (“Thor”) + friðr (“peace”).

tore.ety: From Old Norse Þórir, from older *Þórvér, from Proto-Germanic *Þunrawīhaz. Also a short form of names with the element Þórr.

torgeir.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Þórgeirr (“male given name”), from Þórr (“Thor”) + geirr (“spear”), literally “Thor's spear”.

torgunn.ety: From Old Norse Þórgunnr, cognate to Icelandic Þórgunnur.

torild.ety: Apparently a dialectal form of Torvald.

torje.ety: A younger Norwegian form of Torjei and Torgeir, ultimately from Old Norse Þórgeirr, from Þórr (“Thor”) + geirr (“spear”), hence “Thor's spear”.

torkel.ety: From Old Norse Þorkell, akin to English Torquil.

torkil.ety: From Old Norse Þorkell, a compound of Þórr (“Thor”) and ketill (“cauldron”), akin to English Torquil.

torleiv.ety: From Old Norse Þorleifr, whence also Torlav.

tormod.ety: From the Old Norse adjective þormóðr (“brave”), or a compound name ("Thor" + "mood", "emotion").

torstein.ety: From Old Norse Þorsteinn, Þórsteinn, from Þórr (“Thor”) + steinn (“stone”). Cognate with Faroese Torstein, Tórstein, Icelandic Þorsteinn, Torsten, and English Thurstan.

torsten.ety: Old Norse Þorsteinn, the root of English Thurstan, from Þórr (“Thor”) + steinn (“stone”).

torunn.ety: From Old Norse Þórunn, from Þórr (“Thor”) and unna (“to love”).

torvald.ety: From Old Norse Þorvaldr, from Þórr (“Thor”) + valdr (“wielder, ruler”). Doublet of Torald.

tory.ety: Short for Victoria when used as a female name, and for Victor or Salvatore when used as a male name.

tove.ety: Medieval short form of Old Norse female names composed of Þórr- "Thor" and a second element beginning with b-, f- or v-, such as Torbjørg, or Þórr "Thor" + fríðr "beautiful" ( =Turid).

tracy.ety: A Norman baronial surname from places in France, derived from the Gallo-Roman given name Thracius which referred to Thrace + the Celtic suffix *-āko (place, property).

travis.ety: From an Old French word meaning "to cross over," related to traverse. Probably a name for a gatekeeper or the toll collector of a bridge.

trent.ety: Inherited from Middle English Trent, from Old English Trēonte; Koch (2006) derives the river name from Proto-Celtic *tri-sent(o)-on-ā-, from the elements *trei (“through”) + *sentus (“path”).

trenton.ety: Originally named "Trent's town" in the 17th century, after a Quaker, William Trent.

trevon.ety: From several sources, such as Britain, Germany, Norse, and Welsh. Combination of Tre("three") and von ("hope"/"expectation"/"little"/"from").

tristan.ety: Old French, the name of a knight, lover of Iseult in medieval romance Tristan and Iseult, from Celtic Drystan derived from drest meaning "riot" or "tumult".

trond.ety: From Old Norse Þróndr, Þrándr, either from þróndr (“man from Trøndelag”) or of the same origin, the present participle of þróa(sk). Another suggested origin is Proto-Norse ᚦᚱᚨᚹᛟᚹᛁᚾᛞᚢᛉ.

troy.ety: From Latin Troia, from Ancient Greek Τροία.

trude.ety: Possibly borrowed from German Trude, a short form of names ending in -trud, especially Gertrud.

trudi.ety: In some cases, a 20th-century spelling of Trudy; in other cases borrowed from German Trudi.

truls.ety: A variant of Danish Troels, from Old Norse Þorgísl (“Thor" + "pledge”) or Þorgils (“Thor" + "arrow”).

trygve.ety: From Old Norse Tryggvi, a byname from the adjective tryggr "reliable". Revived in the 19th century.

tránsito.ety: From tránsito (“transit”), shortened from Tránsito de María, a feast known as "Dormition of the Mother of God.".

tudor.ety: Probably a variant of Teodor, ultimately from Ancient Greek Θεόδωρος. Compare also Toader, Sântoader.

turid.ety: From Old Norse Þorriðr, from Þórr (“Thor”) + fríðr (“beautiful”).

turner.ety: From Middle English Turner, Turnur, Turnure, Turnour, from Middle English turner, turnare, tornere, an occupational surname for a turner or tumbler.
turner.m: One who or that which turns.

tuva.ety: From Norwegian Tuva. Sometimes interpreted as a plant name from tuva.

twyla.ety: A 20th-century American coinage, derived from twilight.

ty.ety: Short form of Tyrone, Tyler, Tyson, Tyron, and other male given names beginning with "Ty".

tyler.ety: From Middle English Tyler, Tylere, Tygler, Tygheler, Tyghelere, Tyghelare, Tygelere, from Middle English tiler, tylere, tylare, tylier (“tiler”).

tyreese.ety: A modern invention possible formed as a Blend of Tyrone + Reese.

tyrese.ety: Uncertain, possibly a Blend of Tyrone + Reese or Maurice.

tyrone.ety: From Irish Tír Eoghain, literally “land of Eoghan”.

tyson.ety: A variant of Tison. A nickname from Old French tison (“firebrand”).

uladzimir.ety: Transliteration of Уладзі́мір. Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic Владимѣръ; cognate with Russian Влади́мир.

uladzislau.ety: Transliteration of Уладзісла́ў. Cognate of Russian Владисла́в.

ulf.ety: From Old Norse Úlfr, from úlfr (“wolf”).

ulla.ety: From Swedish Ulla. Diminutive form of Ulrikke.

ulrich.ety: Inherited from Old High German Uodalrich (Odalric, Udalric), from uodal (“heritage, homestead”) + rihhi (“ruler”). English sources also suggest Old English wulf (“wolf”) + ric (“ruler”).

ulrik.ety: From German Ulrich, from Old High German Uodalrich (Odalric, Udalric), from uodal (“heritage, homestead”) + rihhi (“ruler”). Cognate with Old Norse Óðalríkr.

ulysses.ety: From Latin Ulyssēs, a frequent alternative form of Ulixēs (“Odysseus”), influenced by the Ancient Greek Ὀδυσσεύς. Doublet of Odysseus.

una.ety: From Latin una (“one”), or possibly from English Una.

unn.ety: From Old Norse unna (“to love”), a popular element in female given names. Possibly also from Unnr (“wave”), a daughter of the Norse sea god.

urban.ety: Latin Urbānus, name of eight early popes, from urbānus (“of the town or city, urbane”). Doublet of Orban.
urban.m: of the town or city, urbane

urs.ety: Borrowed from Latin Ursus From Latin Ursus.

ursula.ety: From Latin Ursula, the name of a fourth century saint. Via Proto-Indo-European *h₂ŕ̥tḱos cognate with Arcady.

usman.ety: Via an intermediary language, such as Classical Persian عُثْمَان, or Malay Usman, from Arabic عُثْمَان.

ute.ety: Inherited from Middle High German Uote. High German variant of Oda, short form of names beginning with Germanic ot (“riches”); name of a queen in the Nibelungenlied.

uwe.ety: A Frisian name of debated origin; possibly a short form of Germanic compound names beginning with *ob- "industrious" or Old High German agil- (“sword”) (etymologically allied with Latin acūtus, Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”)).

vagna.ety: Feminine form of the name Vagn.

valarie.m: to be healthy, to be strong

valborg.ety: From the name of an eighth century German saint, Walburg, with a feast day on May 1st; from Old High German waltan (“to rule”) + burg (“fortress”).

valda.ety: Feminine form of Valdis, from valdīt (“to rule”), and shortened from compound names containing the similar Germanic name element.

valdemar.ety: Danish rendering of Russian Владимир, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *Voldiměrъ, which see for more.

valdimar.ety: Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *Voldiměrъ. Cognate to Danish Valdemar, German Waldemar, Ukrainian Володи́мир, Belarusian Уладзі́мір/Уладзі́мер.

valdinei.ety: From the name of the American film producer and entrepreneur Walt Disney.

valencia.ety: From Spanish Valencia, from Latin Valentia, from valentia (“power, vigour”). Doublet of Valence.

valentin.ety: Latin Valentinus (“Valentine”), from valentia (“strength, health”) + -inus (“-ine: forming adjectives”).

valentine.ety: From Latin Valentīnus, a patronymic from Valēns, itself nominalized from vālens (“strong, healthy”) + -īnus (“-ine”). Doublet of Valentinus and Valentino and Valentina and Valentini.

valeriana.ety: From Spanish Valeriana. The archaeological site was named after Laguna la Valeriana, a neighbouring lake.

valerie.ety: From French Valérie, from Latin Valeria. Doublet of Valeria.
valerie.m: to be healthy, to be strong

valery.ety: From French Valéry, from Latin Valerius. Doublet of Valerius.
valery.m: to be healthy, to be strong

valérie.m: to be healthy, to be strong

vance.ety: From a Southern English dialectal form of Old English fenn (“marsh, bog”).

vanderlei.ety: From the Dutch van der Leij.

vanessa.ety: Coined by Jonathan Swift as a pseudonym for a lady friend named Esther Vanhomrigh (or Van Homrigh), an Irish woman of Dutch descent.

vanja.ety: From Russian Ваня, diminutive of the male name Ива́н (“John”) and the female name Иванна (“Jane”).

vanya.ety: Romanization of Ва́ня (“Johnny”), a diminutive of Ива́н, Іван (“John”).

varvara.ety: Borrowed from Russian Варва́ра. Doublet of Barbara.

vasco.ety: Borrowed from Portuguese Vasco; see there for more.

vasile.ety: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic Василии, from Ancient Greek Βασίλειος. Cognate with English Basil.

vasilios.ety: From a transliteration of Modern Greek Βασίλειος, a male given name used in (modern) Greece, which in turn derives from Ancient Greek Βασίλειος, from βασίλειος (“of the king, kingly, royal”), from βασιλεύς (“king”).

vaughan.ety: Borrowed from Welsh Vychan, from bychan, diminutive of bach (“little”).

vaughn.ety: A variant of Vaughan, from Welsh bychan (“small”).

vebjørn.ety: From Old Norse Vébjǫrn, from vé (“home”) + bjǫrn (“bear”).

vegard.ety: From Old Norse Végarðr, from vé (“home; sanctuary”) + garðr (“enclosure; protection”).

velma.ety: Coined at the end of the 19th century, by analogy with Thelma and Wilma.

venancio.ety: From Spanish Venancio, from Latin venatium or venator (“hunter”).

venceslau.ety: From Latin Wenceslaus, a Latinization of Old Czech Vácslav, from Proto-Slavic *Vęťeslavъ.

veneranda.ety: From Latin veneranda (“venerated”). Name of an obscure Sicilian or Albanian saint.

venus.ety: Based on Latin Venus (“Venus, the Roman goddess; the planet Venus”), from the common noun Latin venus (“loveliness, beauty, charm”), from Proto-Indo-European *wénh₁-os (“loveliness”), from the root *wenh₁- (“to wish, love”).
venus.m: Venus, the Roman goddess; the planet Venus

verna.ety: Coined in the 19th century, from Latin vernus (“spring-like”) or as a feminine of Vernon.

vernon.ety: From Transalpine Gaulish (“alder”) (from Proto-Celtic *wernā, from Proto-Indo-European *wern-) + -o, -onis, literally “place of alder trees”.

verona.ety: Borrowed from Italian Verona, from Latin Vērōna.

vesta.ety: From Middle English Vesta, from Latin Vesta, related to Ancient Greek ἑστία (“to dwell”) and Ἑστία (“Hestia”), all from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wes-; see also Old High German and Old English wesan (“to be”), Gothic wisan.

vetle.ety: A regional form of Vetterlide, Vetlide, from Old Norse Vetrliði, from vetrliði (“one-year-old bear”).

vibeke.ety: Borrowed from Middle Low German Wiebke and Frisian Wiebke; made famous by a mistress of king Christian IV.

vicent.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Vincentius Latin Vincentius.

vicky.ety: From English Vicky, diminutive of Victoria, from Latin Victōria, from victōria (“victory”).

victor.ety: From a Late Latin personal name Victor, borne by several saints, from victor (“conqueror”). Doublet of victor.

victoriana.ety: From Spanish Victoriana and its etymon Latin Victōriāna, feminine of Victōriānus. Victoria + -ana or Victorian + -a.

victoriano.ety: From Victoriano, a given name from Latin Victōriānus.

victorina.ety: From Latin Victōrīna, feminine of Victōrīnus.

vidar.ety: From Old Norse Víðarr, from víðr (“wide”) + herr (“army”).

vienna.ety: From Italian and Medieval Latin Vienna, from German Wien, Middle High German Wienne, and Old High German Wienna, probably from Proto-Celtic *widus (“wood”) or *weidus (“wild”) via unattested Vulgar Latin *Vedunia.

vigdis.ety: Old Norse Vígdís, from víg (“war”) + dís (“minor goddess”).

viktar.ety: Transliteration of Ві́ктар. Ultimately from Latin Victor.

viktor.ety: From Swedish Viktor, from Latin victor (“victor, conqueror, winner”).

viktorija.ety: From Latin Victoria. The Australian state was borrowed from English Victoria.

vilhelm.ety: From Swedish Vilhelm, from Old High German Willahelm (meaning something like ).

vilja.ety: From, found as an element in pre-Christian Finnish names (probably male given names), and revived in the 19th century as a female given name.

vincent.ety: Borrowed from French Vincent Borrowed from French Vincent, from Latin Vincentius, from vincēns (“conquering”), from the verb vincō.

vinicius.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Vīnicius, a Roman gens name.

violaine.ety: Coined name of a character in the play L'Annonce faite à Marie (1912) by Paul Claudel, as a variant of Violette or transferred from a place name.

violet.ety: A 19th century flower name from violet, sometimes as an anglicisation of the earlier French Violette.

violetta.ety: From violetta (“violet”) or a diminutive form of the older given name Viola. Name of the supposedly French heroine of Verdi's opera La traviata (1853).

violette.ety: From violette (“violet”). Cognate with English Violet.

virgil.ety: From Middle English Vyrgyle, from Latin Virgilius, from the Roman clan name Vergilius, from Etruscan and of unknown meaning.

virgilio.ety: Inherited from Latin Virgilius Inherited from Latin Virgilius.

vita.ety: From Latin vita (“life”), also a feminine form of Vitus.

vivaan.ety: Borrowed from Hindi विवान, from Sanskrit विवान (“plaiting, twisting”).

vivaldo.ety: Of Proto-Germanic origin. The second element is certainly *waldą (“might, power, force”), while the first one remains uncertain.

vivi.ety: Pet name for female given names containing the syllable -vi-, such as Lovise, Olivia, Viola; later also used as a pet name for Vivian.

vivian.ety: Early saints' name from Latin Vīviānus, and of its feminine form Vīviāna, probably from vīvus (“alive”).

viviane.ety: From French Viviane, from Latin vivus (“living”).

vladimir.ety: From Russian Владимир, as well as from other Slavic cognates, and reinforced by Medieval Latin Vladimirus, name of several saints in the Eastern Orthodox Church, from Old East Slavic Володимѣръ, Old Church Slavonic Владимѣръ.

vojtěch.ety: Cognate with Slovak Vojtech and Polish Wojciech.

volker.ety: Equivalent to Old High German folc (“people, folk”) (from Proto-West Germanic *folk) + heri (“army”). Cognate to Middle English Fulcher.

volodymyr.ety: From Ukrainian Володи́мир, Old East Slavic Володимѣръ. A Ukrainian cognate of Russian Влади́мир.

văn.ety: Implies an educated or scholarly person.

waldemar.ety: From an Old High German compound name, from the elements waltan (“rule, govern”) (from Proto-West Germanic *wald) + māri (“famous, great”) (from *mārī).

waldo.ety: English surname, from the obsolete English given name Waltheof, from Old English weald (“power”) + þēof (“thief”), as in "one who snatched victory from battle." Comparable to, or ultimately Anglicized from.

waleria.m: to be healthy, to be strong

wallace.ety: An Old English byname for a Welshman or Breton, from Anglo-Norman waleis (“foreign”); see wǣlisċ.

walter.ety: A Germanic name, from Middle English Walter, from Old Northern French Waltier, from Frankish *Waltheri (compare Old High German Waltheri, which see for more details), from Proto-West Germanic *Waldahari.

walton.ety: Variously from Old English weall (“wall”) or wealh (“Celt, Welshman”) + tūn (“settlement”).

waltraud.ety: From the name of a seventh century saint, from Old High German waltan (“rule”) + *þruþi (“strength”).

wanda.ety: Borrowed from Polish Wanda, possibly derived from an ethnic term for “a Wend”.

wanja.ety: Borrowed from Russian Ва́ня, diminutive of the male name Ива́н (“John”) and the female name Иванна (“Jane”).

ward.ety: As an English surname, from the noun ward and related cognates such as warden, guard etc. As an Irish surname, reduced from McWard, from mac an bard (“son of the poet”).

warner.ety: English, Norman, and German surname, all corresponding to German Werner. Also see Warrener.

warren.ety: From the Anglo-Norman surname (de) Warenne, a reference to a place called Varenne, a hamlet near Arques-la-Bataille, along the river Varenne in Normandy, from Medieval Latin Warinna, a hydronym of Celtic/Gaulish origin.

washington.ety: Washington (the town in Tyne and Wear, northeast England): probably from the Old English place name Hwæssingatūn, literally “a settlement of the household of *Hwæssa”, from *Hwæssa + -ing (“belonging to”) + tūn (“homestead, settlement”).

waylon.ety: Variant of Wayland popularized by the American singer Waylon Jennings who was originally named Wayland.

wayne.ety: An occupational surname for a cartwright, Old English wægen (“wagon”).

wells.ety: From Old English wella, genitive plural of well (“spring”), in reference to a residence near a group of springs. The original use of the genitive case here would've indicated origin.

wenceslao.ety: Latinazation of Old Czech Venceslav, a Slavic (Old Czech) name, from Proto-Slavic *Vęťeslavъ. Doublet of Vyacheslav.

wenche.ety: From Middle Low German, German Low German, Dutch Low Saxon Wenke, the diminutive of several female given names beginning with the Germanic element *win- (“friend”).

wendell.ety: Short form of Germanic compound names beginning with the tribal name Wendel-, "a Wend".

wendy.ety: Popularized by the character in J.

werner.ety: Germanic: *waraz (“cautious; heedful; wary; watchful”) + *harjaz (“army; army leader”); roughly equivalent to English Warner.
werner.m: cautious; heedful; wary; watchful + army; army leader

wesley.ety: Several places in England, from Old English west (“west”) + lēah (“wood, clearing”). Equivalent to west + -ley (“lea”).

wesson.ety: A patronymic surname from Wes + -son, literally son of Wes, the latter a diminutive of the male given name Wesley.

whitney.ety: From Old English hwītan, dative of hwīt (“white”) + īeġ (“island”), "white island".

wilbur.ety: From an Old English female given name Wilburg, from wil (“will”) + burh (“fortress”).

wilfred.ety: The name of two early Anglo-Saxon saints Wilfriþ, from Old English wil (“will”) + friþ (“peace”).

wilfrid.ety: Inherited from Old English Wilfriþ, from wil (“will”) + friþ (“peace”).

wilfried.ety: Borrowed from German, equivalent of English Wilfred. Doublet of Wilfrid.

wilhelmina.ety: Borrowed from German Wilhelmina, equivalent to Wilhelm + -ina.

will.ety: Short form of William or Willow, less often, other given names beginning with Wil-, such as Wilfred or Willard.

willa.ety: Derived from Wilhelmina and recoined in the 19th century in America based on the male given names Will and William.

willard.ety: From Old English wil (“will”) + heard (“brave, strong”).

willem.ety: From Dutch Willem, from Middle Dutch Willem.

william.ety: Inherited from Middle English William From Middle English William, from Anglo-Norman Willame, from Old High German Willahelm, from Proto-Germanic *Wiljahelmaz (> Latin Gulielmus).

wilmer.ety: From Old English willa (“mind, will, determination, purpose, desire, wish”) + mǣre (“famous”), from Proto-Germanic *Wiljamērijaz, from *wiljô + *mērijaz.
wilmer.m: mind, will, determination, purpose, desire, wish + famous

windy.ety: Often a diminutive of names starting with Wi-, such as Wilhelmina and Winifred, with -y. Influenced by windy.

winfred.ety: From Old English Wynnfriþ, from wynn (“joy”) + friþ (“peace”).

winifred.ety: From Old English Winfriþ, from Welsh Gwenfrewi.

winona.ety: From Dakota winúŋna (“firstborn daughter”). While not originally used as a personal name by the Dakota, it has been adopted as such by English speakers.

winslow.ety: From Middle English Wynselowe, from Old English Wineshlǣw, from Wines (“Wine's”) + hlāw (“mound”).

winston.ety: From Old English personal name Wine, in the genitive singular case Wines + tūn (“farm, village”).

wojciech.ety: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *Vojьtěxъ, from *vojь + *utěxa. Cognate with Czech Vojtěch and Slovak Vojtech.

wolf.ety: From Middle English and German short forms of given names containing the Germanic element "wolf".

wolfgang.ety: Borrowed from German Wolfgang (reinforced by Medieval Latin Wolfgangus), from Middle High German Wolfgang, from Old High German Wolfgang, from wolf (“wolf”) + gang (“path, course”).

wyatt.ety: Ultimately from the Old English personal name Wigheard, from wīg (“war”) + heard (“hard, brave”), later also used as a Middle English diminutive of the names Guy and William.

wynn.ety: From the Welsh surname, from the name Gwyn. Also spelled as Wynne.

władysław.ety: Borrowed from Czech Vladislav, from Proto-Slavic *Voldislavъ. Doublet of Włodzisław, an inherited form.

xanthe.ety: From Ancient Greek Ξανθή, literally “blond-haired”, from ξανθός (“yellow”).

xaver.ety: From Spanish Xavier (older spelling of Javier), after 16th-century Catholic saint Francis Xavier.

xavier.ety: From Medieval Latin Xavierus and Spanish Xavier, variant of Javier, ultimately from Basque Xabier. Originally chiefly in honor of the Navarrese saint Francis Xavier.

xena.ety: Possibly a variant of Xenia, from Latin Xenia, from Ancient Greek ξενία (“hospitable”), the assumed name of a fifth-century saint venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church, from ξένος (“foreign, strange”).

xenia.ety: From the assumed name of a fifth-century saint venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church, Latin Xenia, from Ancient Greek ξενία (“hospitable”). Doublet of Oksana.

xerxes.ety: From Ancient Greek Ξέρξης, from Old Persian 𐎧𐏁𐎹𐎠𐎼𐏁𐎠 (“ruler among kings”). Doublet of Ahasuerus.

yaelle.ety: Borrowed from Hebrew יעל Borrowed from Hebrew יעל.

yago.ety: From Spanish Yago, from Latin Iācōbus (“James”), from Ancient Greek Ἰάκωβος, from Hebrew יַעֲקֹב (ya‘ăqṓḇ, “Jacob”), literally “he will/shall heel”, from עָקֵב (‘āqḗḇ.

yahir.ety: Transliteration of Hebrew יַאִיר, meaning "he will light up". Doublet of Doublet of Jair.

yair.ety: Transliteration of Hebrew יַאִיר, meaning "he will light up".

yamileth.ety: From Spanish, derived from Arabic جَمِيلَة (“Jamila”), literally “beautiful”.

yana.ety: Cognate to English Jane, ultimately from Hebrew, feminine form of Ioannes ( =John).

yann.ety: From Latin Ioannes. Ultimately from Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yôḥānān).

yannick.ety: From French Yannick, from Breton Yannig.

yarden.ety: From Hebrew יַרְדֵּן (yardén, “Jordan”). Doublet of Jordan.

yasmeen.ety: Variant of Jasmine, often representing a transliteration of the corresponding Arabic and Persian names.

yasmine.ety: Variant of Jasmine, often representing a transliteration of the corresponding Arabic and Persian names.

yauheni.m: good, well + born a certain way

yaëlle.ety: Borrowed from Hebrew יעל Borrowed from Hebrew יעל.

yegor.ety: Transliteration of Егор. Vernacular form of Гео́ргий.

yehuda.ety: Transliteration of Hebrew יְהוּדָה (yehudá). Doublet of Judah and Judas.

yehudit.ety: Transliteration of Hebrew יְהוּדִית (y'hudít, “Judith”). Doublet of Judith.

yelena.ety: From Еле́на, from Latin Helena, from Ancient Greek Ἑλένη. Doublet of Helena.

yelizaveta.ety: From Russian Елизаве́та. Doublet of Elizabeth.

yesenia.ety: Coined in 1970 for the heroine of a Mexican TV series of the same name, created by Yolanda Vargas, from Jessenia (bataua), the botanical name of a South American palm tree.

yevgeny.ety: From Russian Евге́ний, from Medieval Greek Εὐγένιος (“noble, high-born”).

yevhen.m: good, well + born a certain way

yisroel.ety: From Yiddish ישׂראל (yisroel, “Israel”), from Hebrew ישראל (yisra'él, “Israel”). Doublet of Israel.

yngve.ety: From Old Norse Yngvi, a name of the god Freyr, from Proto-Germanic *Ingwô. Doublet of Inge.

yngvild.ety: Old Norse Yngvildr, from Yngvi ("the god Ing/Yngvi") and hildr ("battle").

yolanda.ety: From Spanish Yolanda, the form of a medieval royal name of obscure, probably Germanic, origin. It has been identified with Latin Violante and with Ancient Greek ἴον (“violet”) + ἄνθος (“flower”).

yolande.ety: Borrowed from French Yolande. Doublet of Yolanda.

yosef.ety: Borrowed from Hebrew יוֹסֵף (yoséf), equivalent to Joseph.

yoshiko.ety: Borrowed from Japanese 美子, 芳子 (よしこ, Yoshiko), literally “good, excellent child”.

young.ety: As an English, Scottish, and northern Irish surname, from the adjective young, used to distinguish a younger brother or son.

younès.ety: Borrowed from Arabic يُونُس Borrowed from Arabic يُونُس.

youssouf.ety: Borrowed from Arabic يُوسُف (“Joseph”). Doublet of Joseph.

yu.ety: Transliteration: From Wade–Giles romanization of Mandarin (for: ㄩˊ, ㄩˇ, ㄩˋ, ㄧㄡˊ) (余, 于, 由, 魚 / 鱼, 漁, 渔, 楀, 俞, 喻, 兪, 於, 遇, 虞, 郁, 尉, 禹, 游, 尤, 庾, 娛, 娱, 茹) From Korean 유 or 류 (柳, 劉, 兪, 庾) From Japanese ゆう or ユウ (優, 夕, 友, 有, 勇, 祐, 裕.

yuli.m: Of the gens Julia, a patrician Roman family.

yulia.m: Of the gens Julia, a patrician Roman family.

yuri.ety: From Russian Ю́рий (“George”). Doublet of George.

yves.ety: Unclear still today, either short form of Germanic or Celtic compound names beginning with iv- "yew" - see Proto-Germanic *īhwaz (“yew”) and Proto-Celtic *iwos (“yew”), both from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyHw- (“yew”).

yvette.ety: Borrowed from French Yvette. The politics sense is a reference to the name of a docile young girl in a school textbook, and was popularized by separatist politician Lise Payette (1931–2018).

yvonne.ety: From the French feminine form of Yvon, variant of Yves, from a Germanic root for "yew" (see Old English iw). It might have originally been used of an archer, since yew wood was used to make bows.

zacarias.ety: From Latin Zacharias, from Koine Greek and Hebrew.

zachariah.ety: From Hebrew זְכַרְיָה (Zəḵaryā, “Yahweh has remembered”) under influence from Latin Zacharias and Koine Greek Ζαχαρίας.

zacharias.ety: From Latin Zacharias, from Koine Greek Ζαχαρίας, the New Testament form of the figure's name in the Old Testament, Hebrew זְכַרְיָה (Zəḵaryā, “Yahweh has remembered”).

zacharie.ety: From Latin Zacharias, from Koine Greek, from Hebrew.
