zachary.ety: From clipped forms of Zachariah and Zacharias + -y, from Hebrew זְכַרְיָה (Zəḵaryā, “Yahweh has remembered”) via Latin Zacharias and Koine Greek Ζαχαρίας.

zahid.ety: Inherited from Malay Zahid, from Arabic زَاهِد.

zakhar.ety: Borrowed from Заха́р. Doublet of Zachary.

zane.ety: The usage seems to date from the American writer Zane Grey (1875-1939), born Pearl Zane Gray. It was the surname of his mother's family, of unknown meaning.

zara.ety: A 20th-century variant of Sarah, or explained as Arabic زَهْرَة (“flower”); given to the daughter of Princess Anne in 1981.

zayden.ety: American 21st-century coinage, rhyming with Jayden, Brayden, Aidan, etc.

zaylee.ety: Modern coinage; compare Zayden, Kaylee, Jaylee.

zbigniew.ety: Inherited from Old Polish Zbygniew, from Proto-Slavic *Jьzbygněvъ, from *jьzbyti (“chase away”) + *gněvъ (“anger, wrath”). zbyć + gniew. Compare Old Czech Zbyhněv, whence Modern Czech Zbyněk.

zeb.ety: From Zebadiah, Zebedee, Zebulon or Zebulun.
zeb.m: gift of God, God has bestowed

zenilda.ety: Brazilian creation in comparision to other names ending in the root -ilda (Hilda, Matilda, etc.), from Proto-Germanic *hildiz.

zenilde.ety: Brazilian creation in comparision to other names ending in the root -ildo (Matilde, Clotilde, etc.), from Proto-Germanic *hildiz.

zenildo.ety: Brazilian creation in comparision to other names ending in the root -ildo (Ivanildo, Hildo, etc.), from Proto-Germanic *hildiz.

zenobia.ety: From Latin Zēnobiā, from Ancient Greek Ζηνοβίᾱ, name of a third century Queen of Palmyra.

zeus.ety: From Ancient Greek Ζεύς. Doublet of Dyeus and Jove.

zhanna.ety: Borrowed from Russian and Ukrainian Жа́нна, doublet of Johanna and Joanna.

zinaida.ety: Borrowed from Russian Зинаи́да, cognate with the English historical name Zenaida, from Ancient Greek Ζηναΐς, meaning "belonging to Ζεύς".

zinedine.ety: Borrowed from Arabic زين الدين, from زين + الدين, from دين + ال... Variant of Zayn ad-Din.

zion.ety: From Middle English Sion, from Old English Syon, from Ecclesiastical Latin Sīōn, from Koine Greek Σῑών, from Biblical Hebrew צִיּוֹן (ṣiyyôn).

zofia.ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin Sophia.

zoja.ety: Borrowed from Russian Зо́я, equivalent to Czech Zoe and English Zoe.

zoltan.ety: From Hungarian Zoltán, from szultán (“sultan”), from Ottoman Turkish سلطان (sultan), from Arabic سُلْطَان (“ruler”). Doublet of sultan.

zoé.ety: From Ancient Greek ζωή (“life”). It was the name of a third century martyr venerated in the Orthodox Church.

zoë.ety: From Ancient Greek ζωή (“life”). It was the name of a third century martyr venerated in the Orthodox Church.

zulma.ety: Possibly from Arabic سُلَيْمَان (“Solomon”); see that entry for more. The name is popular in Latin America because of an Argentine actress of that name.

zuzanna.ety: Ultimately from Hebrew. Cognate to English Susan.

zygfryd.ety: Borrowed from German Siegfried, from Middle High German Sîfrit, from Old High German Sigifrid, from Proto-Germanic *Segafriþuz, from *segaz + *friþuz.

ådne.ety: From a regional variant of Arne with differentiation (rn > dn) and a lengthening of the a to å (< á). Compare Árni with a similar development.

åsa.ety: From Old Norse Ása, short form of female compound names beginning with the element áss, ǫ́ss (“god”). Cognate with Ása, Swedish Åsa and Danish Åse.

åse.ety: From Old Norse Ása, short form of female compound names beginning with the element áss, ǫ́ss (“god”). Cognate with Ása, Swedish Åsa and Danish Åse.

åshild.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Áshildr, from Proto-Germanic *Ansuhildiz, equivalent to Old Norse áss (“god; one of the Æsir”) + hildr (“battle”), literally “god-battle”.
åshild.m: god; one of the Æsir + battle

åsmund.ety: Ås + -mund; from Old Norse Ásmundr, from áss + -mundr. Cognate with Ásmundur.

élodie.ety: From the Spanish saint's name Alodia.

éloïse.ety: From Éloi + -se (“-ess: feminizing nouns”), from Medieval Latin Eligius, chiefly after Saint Eligius, from Latin ēligere (“to pick, to choose from”) + -ius (“-y: forming adjectives and names”).

émile.m: striving to equal or excel, rivaling

ömer.ety: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عمر (ömer), from Arabic عُمَر.

ørjan.ety: Borrowed from Low German Jürgen, from Middle Low German Jurian, from Latin Geōrgius.

øystein.ety: From Old Norse Øysteinn, Eysteinn, from ey (“luck”) + steinn (“stone”). Cognate with Faroese Oystein, Icelandic Eysteinn, Swedish Östen and Danish Østen.
